chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: “Harvest is ended and summer is gone,” quoted Nell Harcourt, looking out over the harvested fields in a dreamlike way. Isolde Pembroke and she had been gathering apples in the orchard at Grey Shutters, but they were currently taking a break from their work in a sunlit nook, where light swarms of thistledown floated past carried by a breeze that remained summer-sweet with the fragrance of ferns from the Whispering Wood.

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: Yet all details of the surrounding countryside proclaimed that it was autumn. Deeply and hollowly, the ocean resounded far off, while the empty, withered fields were draped in golden rod, purple asters of an otherworldly shade spilled through the brook valley beneath Grey Shutters, and the Lake of Glassy Waters possessed a blue—blue—blue hue; this was not spring's shifting shade of blue, nor summer's light azure, but a distinct, unchanging, peaceful blue, appearing as though the water had outlived every emotional shift and phase to rest in a calmness undisturbed by fleeting dreams.

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: “It’s been a pleasant summer,” Isolde stated, a smile on her face as she turned the newly acquired ring on her left hand. “And the crowning moment of it all appeared to be Miss Rosalind’s wedding. I imagine that Mr. and Mrs. Stanhope have reached the Pacific coast by this time.”

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: “It appears to me that their absence has lasted long enough for a journey around the globe,” Nell sighed.

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: “It seems impossible that a mere week has passed since their wedding. Everything is different now. With Miss Rosalind along with Mr. and Mrs. Wace departed, the manse appears so desolate with all its shutters drawn! Passing by it yesterday evening, I felt as though every single occupant within had perished.”

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: “We will not ever obtain a different minister who is as pleasant as Mr. Wace,” Isolde stated, possessing a dismal certainty. “I imagine that various supplies will be provided to us during this winter, while preaching will be entirely absent for half of the Sundays. Furthermore, with both you and Hugh having departed—the time is going to be dreadfully boring.”

text: “When is Mrs. Sowerby going to move up?” asked Isolde, acting as though she had failed to hear what Nell said.

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: “Tomorrow. I am pleased that she is arriving—though it signifies yet another shift. Thirza and I removed all the contents from the spare room yesterday. Would you believe that I disliked doing so? Naturally, it was foolish—yet it felt almost as though we were perpetrating sacrilege. To me, that ancient spare room has perpetually felt like a sacred space. As a youngster, I regarded it as the most marvelous chamber on earth. You recall my overwhelming longing to spend a night in a spare room bed—yet certainly not the one at Grey Shutters. Oh, absolutely not there! It would have been far too terrifying—awe would have kept me awake the entire night. Whenever Thirza dispatched me there on a task, I never simply walked across that space—indeed, I crept on tiptoe and suspended my breathing, just as if I were inside a church, feeling a sense of ease only upon leaving it. Hanging there, positioned on either side of the looking glass, were the portraits of Laurence Whitefield and the Duke of Wellington, who glowered at me with great severity the whole time I remained inside, particularly if I took the risk of glancing into the glass, which happened to be the sole mirror in the dwelling that failed to distort my features slightly. It was a constant mystery to me how Thirza possessed the audacity to clean that space. Yet at present, it has not merely been tidied, but emptied completely. Laurence Whitefield and the Duke have been banished to the hallway on the upper floor. ‘So passes the glory of this world,’” Nell finished, offering a chuckle that carried a subtle tone of sorrow. Having our former sanctuaries defiled is never an agreeable experience, even after we have advanced beyond them.

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: “When you depart, I will feel terribly lonely,” Isolde lamented as she had done a hundred times before. “And it’s unbearable that your departure is next week!”

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: “However, we remain united even now,” Nell remarked brightly. “We cannot permit the coming week to take away the happiness of the present one. Despising the prospect of departing is something I feel personally—my home and I share such a strong bond. Speaking about feeling isolated! I am the one who ought to lament. You will remain in this place surrounded by a multitude of your former companions—and Gideon! Whereas I will find myself solitary in the midst of unfamiliar people, without a single acquaintance!”

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change

Naturally, Nell was equally unaware of them herself.

Christmas will appear to be a thousand years in the future.”

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: “It seems we have reached a point where our paths separate,” Nell observed meditatively. “It was inevitable that we would reach this stage. Isolde, do you believe that adulthood is actually as pleasant as we assumed it was going to be during our childhood?”

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: “I don’t know—there are some nice things about it,” Isolde replied, touching her ring once more with that faint smile that invariably caused Nell to feel abruptly excluded and lacking in experience. “But there are so many puzzling things, too. At times I feel as though becoming an adult simply scares me—and during those moments I would do whatever it takes to be a young girl once more.”

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: “Eventually, I expect we will become accustomed to adulthood,” Nell remarked in a cheerful manner. “As time goes on, it won’t hold quite as many surprises—even if, when all is said and done, I suspect those very surprises are what make life interesting. Isolde, we are eighteen. Two years from now, we will reach twenty. Back when I was ten years old, twenty struck me as an advanced age. Before long, you will have turned into a respectable, middle-aged married woman, whereas I will be pleasant, elderly single Aunt Nell, arriving to stay with you during holidays. You will always reserve a spot for me, won’t you, Izzy dear? Naturally, not the guest room—unmarried women cannot aim for guest rooms, and I will be just as ’umble as Uriah Heep, perfectly happy with a small nook above the porch or adjacent to the parlor.”

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: “Nell, the things you say are so silly,” Isolde said with a laugh. “Your future husband will be a magnificent, attractive, and wealthy man—and every guest bedroom in Brierley won't come close to being grand enough for your stay—and you will look down on everyone you used to know as a girl.”

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: “It would be a shame; my nose is rather pretty, but I am afraid that upturning it would ruin its appearance,” Nell remarked while tapping the well-formed feature. “My attractive traits are not numerous enough for me to ruin the ones I possess; therefore, I guarantee I will not snub you, Isolde, even were I to wed the King of the Cannibal Islands.”

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: Giggling once more, the young women parted ways, as Isolde went back toward Pear Hill and Nell headed on foot to the Post Office. chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: “I wonder if it will be—can be—any more beautiful than this,” whispered Nell, gazing about herself with the affectionate, spellbound eyes belonging to people for whom “home” will forever remain the most gorgeous place on earth, regardless of how much lovelier the territories under foreign stars might be.

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change

Memories cast a delicate and delightful trance upon the two youths.

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: “I must go home,” she cried out, pretending to be quite unconcerned. “Thirza’s head was aching this afternoon, and I feel certain the twins are up to some terrible trouble now. Truly, I ought not to have been absent for such a length of time.”

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: She talked without stopping or making much sense all the way to Grey Shutters lane, leaving poor Hugh with scarcely any opportunity to speak. Nell experienced a sense of relief once they said goodbye. Ever since that brief instant of understanding in the garden at Echo Cottage, a novel and hidden self-awareness had taken root in her heart concerning Hugh. An unfamiliar element had broken into their former, flawless, school-day companionship—an element that endangered its harmony.

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: “I have never been pleased to witness Hugh’s departure until now,” she pondered, feeling partly resentful and partly sorrowful, while making her way up the lane by herself. “Should he persist in this foolishness, our connection will be ruined. It must not be ruined—I refuse to allow it. Oh, why are boys incapable of simply being reasonable!”

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: Nell felt a troubled suspicion that it was hardly “sensible” for her to continue sensing the warm squeeze of Hugh’s hand on hers, just as clearly as when his had stayed there for that brief instant; and even less sensible that this feeling was not at all disagreeable—completely unlike the one that had accompanied a comparable gesture from Wilfred Mott, while she sat through a dance with him during a Pale Sands gathering three evenings earlier. Nell shuddered at the unpleasant memory. However, every issue regarding smitten suitors disappeared from her thoughts as she walked into the unpretentious, matter-of-fact setting of the Grey Shutters kitchen, where an eight-year-old boy wept bitterly upon the couch.

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: “Oh, Robin!” Nell suppressed a wicked burst of laughter. “Do you think it is fun when poor little Lucy falls down the stairs and hurts herself?”

text: “She didn’t get hurt very badly,” Robin said, in a defiant tone. “Naturally, I would have felt genuinely sorry if she had died, Nell. However, killing a Farrow isn't that simple. Yet he managed to emerge alive, having broken merely three bones. Mrs. Sowerby claims that certain people cannot be killed even with a meat-axe. Nell, will Mrs. Sowerby be coming here tomorrow?”

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change

chapter_title: Chapter I The Shadow of Change
text: Following Robin's departure for bed, Nell strolled down to Victoria Island and remained seated by herself, enclosed in a delicate, moonlit dusk, as the surrounding water chuckled through a combined harmony of wind and brook. That brook had perpetually held a special place in Nell's heart. Over its shimmering current, she had fashioned numerous dreams throughout bygone times. She banished thoughts of enamored young men, the biting remarks from spiteful neighbors, and every dilemma belonging to her youthful life. Within her mind, she navigated across legendary oceans that lap against the remote, radiant coasts of “faery lands forlorn,” where forgotten Atlantis and Elysium rest, guided by the evening star toward the land of Heart’s Desire. Furthermore, she possessed greater wealth within those visions than in tangible life; because visible elements perish, whereas invisible elements endure forever.

The week that came after flew by rapidly, packed with countless “last things,” to use Nell’s phrase. Farewell visits needed to be paid and accepted, proving to be agreeable or the opposite, depending on whether the visitors and those visited shared a warm enthusiasm for Nell’s ambitions, or believed she possessed too much pride regarding her college attendance and considered it their obligation to “take her down a peg or two.”

One night, at the residence of Flossie Tulk, a send-off celebration was hosted by the B.V.I.S. to celebrate Nell and Hugh; this location was selected in part due to the spaciousness and suitability of Mr. Tulk’s dwelling, and in part due to the heavy suspicion that the Tulk sisters would refuse to participate in the event if the tender of their home was rejected. The gathering proved to be quite enjoyable, as the Tulk sisters behaved politely and neither uttered nor committed anything to disturb the peaceful atmosphere of the event—a departure from their usual behavior. Flossie exhibited an extraordinary degree of friendliness—to the extent that she went so far as to patronizingly say to Nell,
“That new dress of yours suits you quite well, Nell. Truthfully, it makes you look nearly pretty.”

“It is very sweet of you to speak that way,” Nell replied, her eyes twinkling. As her humor was growing stronger, the remarks that might have pained her when she was fourteen were turning into nothing more than sources of entertainment now. Flossie had a feeling that Nell was mocking her from behind those mischievous eyes; nevertheless, while they walked down the stairs, she satisfied herself by muttering to Tibby that Nell Harcourt would act even more arrogant than before now that college was in her future—just wait and see!

Every member of the “old crowd” had gathered, packed with glee, enthusiasm, and young vivacity. There was Isolde Pembroke, flush-cheeked and marked with dimples, closely followed by the loyal Gideon; Odette Pullen, tidy, practical, and unadorned; Opal Pettigrew, appearing at her most attractive and radiant wearing a cream silk blouse, her blonde hair adorned with red geraniums; Hugh Carrow alongside Wilfred Mott, each attempting to remain as close to the slippery Nell as they could; Carrie Mott, appearing washed-out and somber due to rumors that her father had forbidden Oliver Kimball from approaching the location; Elias Purdy MacKinnon, possessing a circular face and repulsive ears that remained precisely as circular and repulsive as always; and Barney Pullen, who occupied a corner for the entire night, let out quiet laughs whenever somebody addressed him, and observed Nell Harcourt with a joyful smile across his wide, freckle-covered face.

Although Nell had been aware of the event in advance, she was unaware that, owing to their status as the Society’s founders, she and Hugh would receive a highly flattering “address” along with “tokens of respect”—which consisted of a fountain pen for Hugh, and a book of Shakespeare’s plays for her. The kind words contained in the address, which Elias Purdy recited using his most grave and cleric-like voice, caught her off guard and delighted her to such a degree that tears completely overwhelmed the shimmer in her large gray eyes. Having labored diligently and devotedly on behalf of the B.V.I.S., she felt deeply gratified that her hard work was so genuinely valued by the members. Furthermore, everyone was so pleasant, warm, and cheerful—the Tulk girls even displayed some good qualities; right then, Nell felt affection for everyone in the world.

The night brought her immense pleasure, yet its conclusion ruined everything to an extent. As they consumed their supper on the verandah bathed in moonlight, Hugh committed the error once more of uttering a sentimental remark to her; consequently, Nell displayed warmth toward Wilfred Mott to discipline him, granting the man permission to escort her home. She discovered, nevertheless, that vengeance causes the greatest harm to the person attempting to deliver it. Away strolled Hugh blithely alongside Opal Pettigrew, their cheerful laughter and conversation reaching Nell as the pair lingered in the quiet, sharp air of autumn. A thoroughly wonderful time was clearly being had by them, whereas Wilfred Mott bored her dreadfully by speaking continuously without ever, even inadvertently, making a single comment deserving of attention. Distractedly uttering a periodic “yes” or “no,” Nell reflected on the beauty Opal had possessed that evening, the extreme goggliness of Wilfred’s eyes under the moon—an impression heightened compared to daytime—and how the world, for some reason, failed to be as pleasant a realm as she had deemed it earlier that night.

“I am merely exhausted—that is what is wrong with me,” she declared, upon gratefully finding herself by herself in her private chamber. And she truly thought that was the case. Yet a particular small surge of happiness, like from a hidden, unfamiliar source, welled up inside her breast the following night, as she watched Hugh walking with long strides down through the Whispering Wood and traversing the ancient log bridge using those sure, swift paces of his. Therefore Hugh had no intention of passing this final night alongside Opal Pettigrew after all!
“Nell, you appear exhausted,” he remarked.

“I am exhausted, and, even worse, I feel discontented. My exhaustion stems from a full day of packing my trunk and doing needlework. Meanwhile, my discontent is due to six women who came by to bid me farewell, with each single one of those six contriving to utter remarks that appeared to strip all the brightness straight out of existence, rendering it just as gray and bleak and depressing as a morning in November.”
“Spiteful old cats!” was the refined remark made by Hugh.

“Oh, no, they were not,” Nell stated earnestly. “The difficulty lies right there. Had they been malicious cats, I would not have cared. However, every one of them is a pleasant, gentle, maternal person who fondles me and whom I affection, which is the reason their statements, or insinuations, possessed such disproportionate influence over me. They made it clear to me that going to Wexcombe and attempting to earn a B.A. struck them as foolish, and I have been questioning my sanity ever since. Mrs. Peter Mott uttered a sigh and expressed her wish that my endurance would last until I finished; instantly, I envisioned myself as a despairing sufferer of nervous exhaustion when my third year ended; Mrs. Eben Duckett remarked that spending four years at Wexcombe surely required a tremendous amount of money; and every part of me felt that wasting my own funds and Thirza’s on a piece of foolishness like that was unforgivable. Mrs. Jasper Bell voiced her hope that higher education would not ruin me, the way it ruined certain individuals; and I experienced a deep conviction that the conclusion of my four years at Wexcombe would find me a completely unbearable person, believing I possessed all knowledge, while despising all things and all people located in Brierley; Mrs. Elisha Duckett mentioned her understanding that female students at Wexcombe, particularly those hailing from Portmaris, were ‘terribly fashionable and arrogant,’ predicting that I probably would not fit in well with them; and I pictured myself as an ignored, unfashionable, embarrassed rural girl, dragging my feet along the traditional corridors of Wexcombe while wearing copper-toed boots.”

Nell finished, blending a laugh together with a sigh. Because of her delicate temperament, any censure carried gravity, including the censure from people whose views she held in little regard. At that moment, existence lacked zest, and her drive had vanished similar to a blown-out flame.

“They cannot possibly matter to you,” Hugh objected. “Their view of the world is as limited as you well know, despite those good souls being so fine. Whatever falls outside their own experience is utterly abominable to them. No girl from Brierley has attended college before you; and every pioneer, as you are aware, is deemed to suffer from lunatic insanity.”

“Oh, I am aware. Yet sensing it differs so greatly from understanding it. Every argument you might offer is echoed by my rational mind, though occasions arise where rationality exerts no influence upon me. Absurdity completely overwhelms my spirit. Honestly, once Mrs. Elisha departed, I scarcely possessed the spirit to complete my packing.”

“Nell, you are merely fatigued. Come along, put everything out of your mind and go for a stroll with me—a trek back through the forest past the marsh. I ought to have something to display to you there.”
“Ought to be! Are you unaware whether it is in that place?”

“No. It is only because of a thing I witnessed over there during spring that I know it ought to be. Hurry. We will act as if we are a pair of youngsters once more, and we will travel whichever way the wind blows.”

They set out cheerfully. Nell, recalling the previous night's unpleasantness, treated Hugh with great kindness; and Hugh, growing wiser, made sure to act as merely a schoolboy friend once more. Mrs. Sowerby and Thirza observed them out of the kitchen window.
“Eventually, those two will make a fine pair,” remarked Mrs. Sowerby in a tone of approval.
Thirza flinched a little. She secretly wished that it might happen, yet hearing the subject brought up in the casual, talkative manner of Mrs. Sowerby went against her nature.
“They are still merely youngsters,” she stated abruptly.
Mrs. Sowerby chuckled in a friendly way.

“Nell has reached eighteen; I had already wed by the time I was that age. We older people, Thirza, tend far too often to believe that kids remain young forever, that is the truth. Nell is now a grown woman and Hugh has become a man, and he adores the very earth beneath her feet, which is obvious to everyone. He is an excellent gentleman, and Nell could not make a finer match. I trust she will not adopt any foolish romantic ideas while at Wexcombe. I do not endorse those coeducational institutions and never have, that is the truth. I am convinced,” Mrs. Sowerby declared with gravity, “that those attending such colleges rarely accomplish much beyond flirting.”
“They have to do a bit of studying,” Thirza said, smiling.

“Very little,” Mrs. Agatha sniffed. “Still, Nell will, in my opinion. Flirting was never her way. That said, she fails to value Hugh as highly as he deserves, and that is the truth. Oh, I understand girls! Wilfred Mott is also crazy for her, yet I would not ever suggest she wed a Mott. Naturally, the Motts are decent, trustworthy, reputable folks. Even so, when everything is considered, Motts are what they are.”

Thirza gave a nod. Though declaring that Motts were Motts could seem uninformative to a stranger, she grasped the meaning. In all villages, a family of this kind exists; while they can be upright, truthful, and esteemed folks, they are Motts and are bound to stay that way perpetually, even if they converse with the voices of humans and angels.

Hugh and Nell, who were blissfully unaware that Mrs. Agatha was disposing of their destiny in this manner, were strolling amidst the shade of the Whispering Wood. Further off, an amber evening light bathed the harvest hills beneath a faint, high sky of pink and blue. The far-off spruce woods resembled polished bronze, casting lengthy shadows across the high pastures. Around the pair, however, a slight breeze whistled through the fir needles, carrying with it a suggestion of autumn.

“Former recollections truly haunt these woods now,” Nell remarked, bending down to collect a bunch of ferns that frost had turned a waxy white. “I feel as though the young girls Isolde and I once were continue to play in this place, sitting beside the Nymph’s Well when twilight falls to meet with the apparitions. Did you realize that I am unable to walk up this trail at dusk without experiencing a touch of that previous dread and trembling? A single spectre we invented was particularly terrifying—a slain child’s spirit that crawled behind a person to touch their hands with icy fingers. I must admit, even now, I am unable to avoid imagining its small, stealthy paces following me whenever I arrive here after dark. Neither the White Lady, the man without a head, nor the skeletons frighten me, yet I regret ever conceiving that infant’s phantom. Thirza and Mrs. Pembroke became so furious about that incident,” Nell ended, laughing at the memory.

Violets of distance filled the forest surrounding the marsh’s upper end, woven through with cobwebs. Beyond a stern grove of twisted spruces and a warm, sunny dale bordered by maples, the “something” that Hugh sought was discovered by them.
“Ah, here it is,” he remarked contentedly.
“An apple tree—and way back here!” Nell cried out with delight.

“Indeed, a real fruit-yielding apple tree stands right here surrounded by beeches and pines, located one mile from the nearest orchard. During a visit here last spring, I discovered it covered in white flowers. Because of that, I decided to return during the autumn to check if fruit had grown. Look how full of fruit it is. They appear appetizing as well—brownish-yellow like russets, yet featuring a dark crimson blush. The majority of wild seedlings seem green and unappealing.”

“It likely originated a long time ago from a seed dropped by accident,” Nell remarked in a dreamy tone. “And look at how the courageous, resolute creature has expanded, thrived, and maintained its position in this solitary spot surrounded by strangers!”

“A downed tree with a pillow of moss is right here. Take a seat, Nell—a forest throne can be made of it. Up I’ll go to gather a few apples. Every single one is high up—reaching toward the sun was necessary for the tree.”

The fruit turned out to be exquisite. Beneath the yellowish-brown skin lay an extraordinarily white flesh, subtly streaked with crimson; furthermore, in addition to their genuine flavor of apple, they carried a particular untamed, marvelous zest that no cultivated apple had ever held.

“The disastrous apple from Eden could not have possessed a more uncommon taste,” remarked Nell. “However, the hour has come for us to head back. Look, three minutes in the past brought dusk, and this instant brings moonlight. What a shame that we were unable to capture the instant of change. Still, I imagine those instances are never captured.”
“Shall we return by circling the marsh and taking Linger Lane back? Has your disgruntled mood lifted at all since we set off, Nell?”
“Not I. The apples were like manna for a soul that was starving. My feeling is that Wexcombe will be dear to me and that my four years spent in that place will be wonderful.”
“And following those four years—then what?”
“Oh, another turn in the path exists over by them,” Nell responded carelessly. “What could be past it is beyond my knowledge—and I prefer it that way. Not knowing is more pleasant.”
That night, Linger Lane was a beloved spot, quiet and strangely shadowy under the soft glow of the moon. Neither wanting to speak, they ambled along it together in an agreeable, friendly quiet.
“Everything would be so pleasant and straightforward if Hugh always acted the way he did tonight,” Nell thought to herself.
As Nell strolled forward, Hugh observed her closely. Her gentle grace and airy clothing brought to his mind the image of a white iris.
“I ponder whether I will ever be able to gain her affection,” he meditated, feeling a sharp ache of doubt in himself.

Wilfred Mott, Hugh Carrow, and Nell Harcourt departed from Brierley on the subsequent Monday morning. Nell had wished that the day would be fine. Isolde was scheduled to chauffeur her to the station, and the two desired that this drive, which would be their final one together for a while, might prove enjoyable. However, as Nell retired to bed on Sunday evening, the east wind was lamenting about Grey Shutters with a menacing prediction that came to pass when morning arrived. Upon waking, Nell discovered raindrops tapping against her windowpane and creating expanding circles on the gray face of the pond; fog concealed the hills and the sea, making the entire world appear dark and dismal. Nell put on her clothes in the gloomy gray twilight of dawn, since setting out early was required to make the connection for the boat train; she fought against tears that kept rising to her eyes regardless of her efforts. She was departing from the home she held so precious, and an inner feeling suggested that her departure was permanent, except for visits as a vacation retreat. Circumstances would never return to what they had been; returning for holidays would not constitute residing there. And oh, how cherished and adored every single detail was—that small white porch room, dedicated to the daydreams of her youth, the ancient Frost Maiden by the window, the stream down in the hollow, the Nymph’s Well, the Haunted Woods, and Linger Lane—every one of the countless beloved places where recollections of former years lingered. Was it possible for her to ever experience true happiness in any other place?

Morning meal at Grey Shutters on that day was quite a gloomy affair. Likely for the initial time in his existence, Robin was unable to consume food, instead weeping openly above his porridge. Except for Lucy, who consumed her portion with ease, no one else appeared to possess much of a desire to eat. Lucy resembled the famed and highly sensible Charlotte, who “went on cutting bread and butter” as the corpse of her frantic suitor was borne by on a shutter, being among those lucky individuals whom almost nothing upsets. A lot was required to disturb the calm of Lucy, even at the age of eight. Naturally, she felt regret over the departure of Nell, yet did that justify not enjoying a poached egg on toast? It certainly did not. Consequently, observing that Robin was incapable of consuming his own, Lucy consumed it in his place.

Punctually at the appointed hour Isolde arrived with horse and buggy, her flushed countenance shining over her raincoat. At that point, the farewells somehow needed to be spoken. Entering from her quarters, Mrs. Sowerby warmly hugged Nell and cautioned her to take care of her health, no matter what happened. Thirza, abrupt and without tears, lightly kissed Nell’s cheek and remarked she presumed they would receive word from her once she was established. An onlooker without intimate knowledge might have assumed that Nell’s departure was of small consequence to her—except if that onlooker had chanced to catch a clear glimpse into her eyes. Lucy gave Nell a stiff kiss and managed to produce two neat, small tears; yet Robin, who had been weeping on the back porch step from the moment they left the table, declined to bid farewell whatsoever. Observing Nell approach him, he leaped up, rushed up the rear staircase, and concealed himself inside a clothes closet, refusing to emerge. The last noises Nell caught as she departed Grey Shutters were his deadened cries.

Downpours fell unceasingly throughout the journey to Alder River, the depot they were required to travel to because the feeder line train coming from Delford failed to link up with the boat train. Upon their arrival, Wilfred and Hugh stood waiting on the station platform while the train emitted its whistle. Nell barely managed to obtain her ticket and trunk check, bid a hasty goodbye to Isolde, and rush onto the train. She longed to return to Brierley alongside Isolde, feeling certain that homesickness would be her death. Furthermore, if merely that dreary rain would cease cascading down as though all creation grieved for lost summer and gone delights! Not even Hugh’s presence offered her solace, because Wilfred Mott accompanied them as well, and Sloanishness was bearable exclusively during pleasant weather. In the rain, it was utterly unendurable.

Yet conditions improved once the vessel navigated away from the harbor at Port Marlow. Rain stopped falling, and through openings in the cloud cover, the sun started breaking through in golden flashes here and there, polishing the dull sea with a reddish-metallic glow, and illuminating the vapors draping the red coasts of the Island with flashes of gold that promised a pleasant day would come after all. Furthermore, Wilfred Mott was quickly afflicted by such intense seasickness that he was forced to head down into the cabin, leaving Nell and Hugh by themselves on the deck.

“It is a great relief to me that every Mott becomes seasick the moment they are on the water,” Nell reflected without pity. “If Wilfred were beside me feigning a sentimental gaze at it, I know I would be unable to cast my final glance upon the ‘ould sod.’”
“Well, we’re leaving,” Hugh stated without emotion.

“Indeed, Byron’s ‘Childe Harold’ comes to mind for me—except the land I am observing is not actually my ‘native shore’,” Nell remarked, her gray eyes blinking rapidly. “I guess Nova Scotia holds that title. Nevertheless, the place a person cherishes most constitutes their true native shore, and for my part, that is dear old P.E.I. That I haven't spent my entire life here seems unbelievable. A nightmare is what those initial eleven years prior to my arrival feel like. Seven years have passed since I made the passage aboard this vessel—on the same night Mrs. Tranter transported me from Hopetown. I picture my former self, clad in that hideous old wincey garment and washed-out sailor hat, investigating the decks and cabins with blissful wonder. The evening was lovely; and the way those red shores of the Island shone under the sun was remarkable. At present, I am making the strait crossing once more. Oh, Hugh, my sincere wish is that Wexcombe and Portmaris prove pleasing to me, though my certainty is that they won't!”
“Nell, where has the whole of your philosophy vanished to?”

“A massive, overwhelming surge of solitude and longing for home covers everything completely. For three years I have yearned to travel to Wexcombe—and my journey is happening now—and I desire not to go! Do not worry! Once I have simply one thorough cry, my cheerful and philosophical nature will return. I need to experience that, ‘as a went’—and my wait must continue until I reach my boardinghouse bed this evening, wherever that might be, before I am able to indulge in it. At that point Nell will return to her true self. I ponder whether Robin has emerged from the closet at this time.”

When their train arrived in Portmaris at nine o'clock that evening, they stepped into the crowded station's harsh blue-white illumination. Nell experienced a sense of terrible confusion, yet shortly afterward, Honora Hollis, who had arrived in Portmaris the previous Saturday, grabbed hold of her.
“You have arrived, my love! I assume you are just as exhausted as I was upon my arrival Saturday night.”

“Exhausted! Honora, avoid speaking about that. I am exhausted, alongside being naive, unsophisticated, and merely roughly a decade of age. For mercy's sake, escort your miserable, exhausted friend to a spot where it is possible for her to listen to her own thoughts.”
“I will escort you straight to our boardinghouse. My cab is waiting just outside.”

“Having you present is a true blessing, Sukey. Had you not been, I believe I would merely collapse upon my luggage, right this moment, and shed sorrowful tears. How reassuring a single recognizable countenance proves to be amidst a roaring sea of unknown people!”

“Does that happen to be Hugh Carrow over there, Nell? The way he has matured throughout this last year is remarkable! During my time teaching in Delford, he was merely a schoolboy. Naturally, that other person is Wilfred Mott. No change has come over him—none was possible! His appearance was identical to that at his birth, and at eighty years old he will retain that very same look. Head this direction, dear. Our arrival home will take just twenty minutes.”
“Home!” Nell groaned. “You mean we’ll be located in a terrible boardinghouse, situated in a hall bedroom that is even more terrible, facing a gloomy back yard.”

“This isn't a dreadful lodging, Nell-girl. Our cab has arrived. Get inside—our trunk will be retrieved by the cabbie. Ah, yes, regarding the lodging—it is truly quite a fine establishment for what it is, which you will acknowledge by tomorrow morning after a restful night converts your sadness to cheerful optimism. It consists of a large, aged, gray stone dwelling located on St. John Street, situated merely a pleasant short walk away from Wexcombe. High society used to consider it their ‘residence’, yet style has departed from St. John Street, leaving its structures to merely daydream about finer times. Their size is so grand that the occupants must accept lodgers simply to occupy the space. In any case, that represents the explanation our hostesses are extremely eager to emphasize to us. They are wonderful, Nell—I am referring to our hostesses.”
“What is their count?”
“Two. Miss Hannah Harvey together with Miss Ada Harvey. Their births as twins occurred approximately fifty years back.”
“It appears I am unable to escape twins,” Nell said with a smile. “They face me everywhere I travel.”

“Oh, dear, they are not twins any longer. They ceased to be twins once they turned thirty. Miss Hannah has aged, though not very gracefully, whereas Miss Ada has remained thirty, with even less grace. Whether Miss Hannah is capable of smiling or not is unknown to me; I have not yet seen her do so, but Miss Ada wears a constant smile, which is far worse. Even so, they are pleasant, good-hearted people who host two boarders annually because Miss Hannah’s thrifty nature refuses to allow room space to be 'wasted'—it is not out of necessity or obligation, a fact Miss Ada has informed me of seven times since Saturday evening. Regarding our quarters, I confess they are hall bedrooms, and my own faces the back yard. Yours is situated at the front, overlooking Old St. John’s graveyard, located directly across the street.”
“That seems horrific,” shuddered Nell. “I believe I’d prefer looking out over the back yard.”

“Indeed, you would not. Just wait and observe. Old St. John’s is a lovely location. Having functioned as a burial ground for so long, it no longer serves that purpose and has transformed into one of the attractions of Portmaris. Yesterday, I traversed the entire grounds for a recreational outing. A large stone wall together with a line of massive trees encircles it completely, and lines of trees run all through its interior, alongside the strangest old gravestones featuring the strangest and most charming epitaphs. You will head there to study, Nell, mark my words. Naturally, no one receives a burial there anymore. However, several years ago, a striking monument was erected to honor Nova Scotian soldiers who perished during the Crimean War. Located directly across from the entry gates, it offers ‘scope for imagination’, as you were accustomed to saying. At long last, your trunk has arrived—and the boys are approaching to bid us good night. Is it truly necessary for me to shake hands with Wilfred Mott, Nell? The feeling of his hands is perpetually so cold and fish-like. We ought to invite them to visit from time to time. Miss Hannah solemnly informed me that ‘young gentlemen callers’ were permitted two nights a week, provided their departure occurred at a sensible time; while Miss Ada, with a smile, requested that I ensure they refrained from sitting on her lovely cushions. I pledged to manage that; though goodness knows what other seating exists for them, short of sitting on the floor, because cushions rest upon every surface. Miss Ada has even placed an ornate Battenburg one atop the piano.”

By this time, Nell was laughing. Her spirits were cheered, as intended, by the lively talk of Honora; for the moment, her longing for home disappeared, and it failed to come back at maximum strength even when she ultimately was by herself in her small bedroom. Going to her window, she gazed outside. Shadowy and peaceful was the street underneath. On the opposite side, over the trees in Old St. John’s, the moon shone right behind the huge, dark head of the lion situated on the monument. Nell pondered whether her departure from Grey Shutters had occurred only that morning. She experienced that feeling of a lengthy duration passing which a single day filled with movement and new experiences creates.

“I guess that exact moon is shining on Grey Shutters right now,” she pondered. “However I will not dwell on it—down that path lies homesickness. I am not even going to indulge in my good cry. I will delay that until a more fitting time, and for now I will go peacefully and reasonably to bed and to sleep.”

Portmaris is a charming old town, recalling early Colonial times, and enveloped in its antique ambiance, like a refined old lady wearing clothes made after the style of her younger years. In places it shoots forth into modern times, yet down deep it remains uncorrupted; it abounds in strange relics, and is encircled by the romance of numerous tales from bygone days. At one time it was simply a frontier post on the border of the wild country, and during those times Indians prevented existence from becoming dull for the inhabitants. Afterwards it developed into a source of conflict between the British and the French, being held at times by the former and at times by the latter, coming out of every possession with a new mark of fighting countries stamped upon it.

Within its park stands a martello tower covered with the signatures of visitors, a decommissioned former French fortification occupies the hills outside the municipality, and a few old-fashioned cannons sit in its public plazas. It contains additional historical sites as well, which inquisitive people can discover, and not one is as charming and appealing as Old St. John’s Cemetery situated in the absolute center of the community, bordered by avenues of peaceful, historic residences on two flanks, and active, energetic, contemporary avenues on the remaining ones. Each inhabitant of Portmaris experiences a surge of personal pride regarding Old St. John’s, because, should he possess any status whatsoever, he possesses a forefather interred within it, having an odd, tilted stone placed at his crown, or otherwise lying flat defensively across the plot, upon which every primary detail of his life is documented. Generally, no significant artistry or craftsmanship was expended upon those ancient markers. The majority consist of coarsely carved native brown or gray stone, and a desire for decoration is present in merely a handful of instances. A few are decorated with a skull and cross-bones, and this macabre motif is often paired with the face of a cherub. Numerous stones are fallen and broken. The passage of time has eroded nearly every one, to the point where certain epitaphs are entirely erased, while others are barely readable with effort. The burial ground is extremely crowded and densely shaded, as it is encircled and crossed by lines of elms and willows, under whose canopy the rested ought to sleep without dreams, continuously lulled by the breezes and foliage above them, and entirely untroubled by the noise of vehicles immediately outside.

The following afternoon, Nell embarked on the first of numerous walks through Old St. John’s. Earlier, during the morning, she and Honora had traveled to Wexcombe to enroll as students, an errand that left them with no further duties for the remainder of the day. Being encircled by throngs of unfamiliar people—the majority of whom seemed somewhat out of place, as though uncertain of their proper standing—was far from uplifting, so the girls were pleased to make their departure.

Small, separate clusters of two or three “freshettes” were standing around, eyeing one another suspiciously; more astute in their time and era, the “freshies” had formed a single group on the main hallway’s large staircase, from which they were beltly singing glees with all the energy of young lungs to challenge their customary foes, the Sophomores, several of whom were roaming around in a superior manner, appearing suitably contemptuous of the “unlicked cubs” occupying the steps. Hugh and Wilfred could not be spotted anywhere.

“Rarely had it occurred to me that I would one day rejoice at seeing a Mott,” stated Honora while they walked across the campus, “yet I would receive Wilfred’s bulging eyes with near ecstasy. They would, if nothing else, be eyes I recognize.”

“Oh,” Nell sighed. “I am unable to put into words my emotions while I stood in that place, awaiting my turn for registration—feeling as unimportant as the smallest droplet inside a huge bucket. Feeling unimportant is awful enough, but having it forced deep into your spirit that you shall not ever, can not ever, become anything other than unimportant is intolerable, and that represents my exact feelings—like I was unseeable by the unaided eye and a few of those Sophs could crush me underfoot. I was certain that I’d enter my tomb without tears, honor, or song.”

“Just hold out until next year,” Honora offered consolingly. “At that point, we can appear just as unimpressed and worldly as any single Sophomore among them. Feeling unimportant is certainly quite unpleasant; however, I believe it surpasses feeling as huge and clumsy as I felt—like I was stretched out across the entirety of Wexcombe. I experienced that feeling—presumably since I exceeded everyone else in the gathering by a solid two inches in height. My fear wasn't that a Soph would step on me; my fear was that they would mistake me for an elephant, or a excessively large instance of a potato-nourished Islander.”

“I imagine our difficulty lies in our inability to pardon large Wexcombe for failing to be small Regent’s,” Nell stated, drawing her former sunny outlook around herself to clothe her inner desolation. “On our departure from Regent’s, we were acquainted with all the locals and occupied a position unique to us. It seems we were unwittingly anticipating that we would resume existence at Wexcombe at the exact point we ceased at Regent’s, leaving us currently feeling disoriented. It is a relief that my current mental condition is unknown to Mrs. Sowerby and Mrs. Elisha Duckett, and that they will remain ignorant of it forever. They would take delight in declaring ‘I told you so,’ believing it signaled the start of the conclusion. In truth, it merely marks the conclusion of the start.”

“Precisely. That seems more Anneish. Soon enough we will be acclimated and acquainted, and everything will be fine. Nell, did you see the girl who spent the whole morning standing by herself right outside the coeds’ dressing room door—the attractive one possessing brown eyes and a crooked mouth?”

“Indeed, I noticed. She stood out to me especially as she appeared to be the sole being present who appeared just as isolated and without companions as I felt inside. Though I possessed you, she was entirely on her own.”

“I believe she experienced a strong sense of isolation, as well. On a few occasions I noticed her start to move in our direction, yet she failed to carry it through—owing to shyness, most likely. It was my desire that she join us. Had I not experienced such a strong resemblance to the previously mentioned pachyderm, I would have approached her myself. However, I lacked the ability to clamber across that vast room while every one of those young men was shouting from the staircase. Among the new female students I observed throughout the day, she possessed the greatest beauty, though it is likely that grace proves deceptive and fairness itself counts for nothing during one's initial day at Wexcombe,” Honora said in closing, accompanied by laughter.

“I’m heading over to Old St. John’s following lunch,” Nell stated. “A cemetery might not be an ideal location for lifting one's spirits, yet it appears to be the sole accessible spot possessing trees, and I simply cannot do without trees. I intend to take a seat on an old slab, close my eyes, and pretend that I am situated within the Brierley woods.”

Instead of doing so, Nell discovered plenty to captivate her in Old St. John’s that kept her eyes fully attentive. Passing through the entrance gates, they moved beyond the unadorned, heavy stone arch capped by England's magnificent lion.
“‘And the wild bramble on Inkerman remains bloody, And in history those desolate heights shall from now on be celebrated,’”

quoted Nell, eyeing it with a shudder of excitement. A shadowy, chilly, verdant spot enveloped them, a domain where breezes enjoyed humming. Along the extended turf-covered walkways they roamed, deciphering the unusual, lengthy inscriptions, chiseled during an era possessing greater free time than ours.

“‘Here lieth the body of Albert Crawford, Esq.,’” Nell recited off a gray, weathered slab, “‘for many years Keeper of His Majesty’s Ordnance at Portmaris. He served in the army till the peace of 1763, when he retired from bad health. He was a brave officer, the best of husbands, the best of fathers, the best of friends. He died October 29th, 1792, aged 84 years.’ That is quite an epitaph, Sukey. It surely offers some ‘scope for imagination.’ What a great deal of adventure a life like that must have contained! As for his character, I do not think human praise could possibly surpass it. I wonder if people informed him of all those finest traits during his lifetime.”
“Another one is right here,” Honora remarked. “Listen—

“To the memory of Alexander Ross, who passed away at 43 years of age on September 22, 1840. Erected as a token of affection by someone he served with such fidelity for 27 years that he was considered a friend, worthy of complete trust and devotion.”

“That is a fine inscription for a tomb,” Nell remarked after a moment’s thought. “I could not ask for anything superior. Every person serves in one way or another, and provided the truth of our fidelity can be honestly carved upon our markers, nothing further is required. Sukey, take a look at this sad small slate marker—‘in remembrance of a beloved child.’ Furthermore, another one here states it was ‘built in remembrance of a person interred in another place.’ I am curious about the location of that unfamiliar resting site. In truth, Nonie, modern cemeteries can never match the fascination of this place. Your statement was correct—this location will see me frequently. My affection for it is already established. It appears other people are present—a young woman stands at the far portion of this path.”

“Indeed, and my thought is that she is the exact young woman who came under our notice at Wexcombe earlier today. My eyes have been fixed on her for five minutes. Precisely six times she has begun to walk up the avenue, and precisely six times she has wheeled around and returned. Her condition is either one of terrible shyness, or her conscience is burdened by something. We should walk out to meet her. My feeling is that making an acquaintance is simpler in a graveyard than it is at Wexcombe.”

Along the extended grassy arcade, they strolled toward the unknown woman, who sat upon a gray stone beneath a massive willow tree. She was unquestionably quite lovely, possessing a striking, uneven, captivating sort of beauty. Her satiny hair exhibited a luster resembling brown nuts, and her plump cheeks carried a gentle, mature warmth. Beneath curiously angled black eyebrows, her eyes were large, dark, and plush, while her uneven lips were the color of a red rose. She was dressed in a stylish brown suit, from under which a pair of extremely fashionable small shoes poked out; and her dull pink straw headwear, encircled by golden-brown poppies, possessed that subtle, undeniable quality belonging to the “creation” of a master hatter. Honora experienced an abrupt, sharp awareness that her own headpiece was the work of her local shopkeeper, while Nell felt an uneasy doubt about whether the shirt she had sewn herself, which Mrs. Sowerby had adjusted, appeared excessively rustic and rustic-made in comparison to the unknown woman's elegant outfit. During that instant, each girl considered retreating.

However, they had currently halted and faced the gray slab. Retracting was impossible now, because the girl with brown eyes had obviously assumed that they intended to talk with her. At once, she leaped to her feet and advanced, extending her hand with a bright, welcoming smile that appeared completely devoid of both timidness and a guilty conscience.

“Oh, I am longing to find out who you two girls are,” she cried out enthusiastically. “I have been desperate to discover it. I caught sight of you at Wexcombe earlier today. Tell me, was it not terrible there? Briefly, I found myself wishing I had remained at home and wed.”
Nell along with Honora both burst into unrestrained laughter upon hearing this unforeseen ending. Laughing as well was the girl with the brown eyes.

“I honestly did. I was capable of it, you see. Come along, let us all take a seat on this tombstone and become familiar. It will not be difficult. I am certain we will be fond of one another—I was aware of it the moment I noticed you at Wexcombe earlier today. I had such a strong desire to walk straight across and embrace you two.”
“Why didn’t you?” Honora inquired.

“For the simple reason that I was unable to resolve to act. Personal decisions are something I can never reach on my own—indecisiveness is a constant burden to me. The moment I choose a path, an inner feeling tells me that a different option would have been the right one. Though it is a terrible handicap, it is an innate trait of mine, meaning there is no point in criticizing me over it, as certain individuals are prone to do. Consequently, I was unable to reach a decision to approach and talk with you, despite my strong desire to.”
“We assumed your shyness was holding you back,” Nell remarked.

“No, no, my dear. Shyness is not one of the numerous faults—or good qualities—possessed by Cressida Lindsay—Cressy as a nickname. Please use Cressy for me from the start. Well then, what are your names?”
“That one is Honora Hollis,” Nell said while pointing.
“And that one is Nell Harcourt,” Honora said, gesturing toward her next.
“And we hail from the Island,” the two of them uttered in unison.
“Harborough, Nova Scotia, is where I come from,” said Cressida.
“Harborough!” cried Nell. “Why, I was born in that place.”
“Are you actually being serious? Well, that means you are a Bluenose when all is said and done.”
“No, it doesn’t,” Nell fired back. “Wasn’t Dan O’Connell the one who said that a man being born in a stable didn't turn him into a horse? I’m Island through and through.”

“Anyway, I am happy that Harborough was your birthplace. It renders us somewhat like neighbors, does it not? I am pleased by that, for I will not feel like I am revealing secrets to an unknown person when I share them with you. Expressing them is something I must do. Keeping secrets is impossible for me—trying to do so is futile. That is my greatest flaw—that one, along with my previously mentioned indecisiveness. Can you imagine?—deciding which hat to put on when I was preparing to come here took me thirty minutes—here, to a cemetery! Initially, my preference was my brown hat featuring the feather; however, the moment it was on my head, I felt this pink hat possessing the floppy brim would prove more flattering. Once I had it secured with pins, the brown hat appealed to me more. Eventually, I positioned the two of them side by side upon the bed, closed my eyes, and thrust a hat pin at them. The pin pierced the pink hat, which led to me wearing it. It suits me, does it not? Express your opinion, how do my looks strike you?”
Upon hearing this innocent request, uttered with utter gravity, Honora chuckled once more. Nell, however, spontaneously pressed Cressida's hand and spoke,
“It seemed to us earlier today that you were the most attractive girl we came across in Wexcombe.”
A captivating, uneven grin showed on Cressida’s asymmetrical mouth, revealing tiny, exceptionally white teeth.

“That was my own thought,” she surprisingly declared next, “yet I needed the viewpoint of another person to reinforce my own. Even regarding how I look, I cannot make up my mind. The moment I have concluded that I am attractive, a miserable feeling comes over me that I am not. On top of that, there is a dreadful old great-aunt of mine who constantly tells me, while sighing mournfully, ‘You were such a pretty baby. It’s strange how children change when they grow up.’ Aunts I love, but great-aunts I hate. If it is not a bother, please assure me frequently that I am attractive. Believing that I am attractive makes me feel far more at ease. Furthermore, I will willingly do the same for you if you desire—which I can do with a clean conscience.”
“Thanks,” Nell laughed, “however Honora and I believe so strongly in our own beauty that we require no reassurance regarding it, so you do not have to bother.”

“Ah, you are poking fun at me. You believe I am dreadfully conceited, I am aware, yet that is untrue. Truly, not a single trace of conceit exists within me. Furthermore, I am always quite generous with offering praise to different girls if it is earned. Knowing you people brings me such happiness. My arrival was on Saturday, and homesickness has almost killed me ever since. That sensation is dreadful, wouldn't you say? Within Harborough, my status is that of a notable figure, whereas within Portmaris, I am merely a nobody! Certain moments occurred where I imagined my very spirit transforming into a pale shade of blue. What is your dwelling place?”
“Thirty-eight St. John’s Street.”

“Things are improving. Indeed, my location is right nearby on Wallace Street. However, I am not fond of my boardinghouse. The place feels desolate and solitary, and the view from my window shows a truly hideous rear yard. No other spot on earth is as unattractive. Regarding cats—it seems impossible that every cat in Portmaris gathers there after dark, yet fifty percent of them surely do. It delights me when cats lounge on hearth rugs, napping in front of pleasant, welcoming fires, whereas cats in rear yards in the middle of the night transform into completely distinct creatures. During my initial night in this place, I wept throughout the entire night, and those cats wailed just the same. My nose presented a sight the next morning. I longed deeply to have stayed at home!”
“If your indecision is truly so great, I am at a loss to understand how you ever brought yourself to travel to Wexcombe,” remarked an entertained Honora.

“May God bless your soul, my dear, I was not the one. My presence here was desired by my father instead. He had completely fixed his mind on this outcome—for what reason, I am uncertain. Is it not entirely absurd to imagine myself working toward a Bachelor of Arts degree? That is not to say I am incapable of achieving it, naturally. My intellect is quite abundant.”
“Oh!” Honora uttered in an absentminded manner.

“Indeed. However, employing them requires such strenuous effort. Furthermore, B.A.’s are bound to be such scholarly, stately, sagacious, and serious beings. No, traveling to Wexcombe was not my desire. My sole reason for doing so was to accommodate father. He is truly a darling. Additionally, I recognized that remaining at home would force me into matrimony. Mother desired that—desired it unequivocally. Mother possesses a great deal of firmness. Yet the prospect of marriage for another few years was something I truly detested. I wish to enjoy an abundance of amusement prior to settling down. Moreover, as preposterous as the notion of me holding a B.A. sounds, the notion of me becoming an elderly married woman is even more comical, wouldn’t you say? My age is merely eighteen. No, my decision was that I preferred traveling to Wexcombe over getting married. On top of that, in what way could I have ever decided upon which suitor to wed?”
“Was the number truly that large?” Nell chuckled.

“Loads. I am liked tremendously by the lads—they truly do like me. However, merely two of them were of any importance. The others lacked both sufficient age and wealth. A wealthy man is a necessity for my marriage, as you are aware.”
“Why do you have to?”

“Darling, you are unable to picture me as the spouse of a destitute man, aren’t you? Not one helpful task can be performed by me, plus I waste vast amounts of money. Ah, negative, my spouse is required to possess mountains of wealth. Thus my choices were reduced to a pair. However, making a choice between a pair was not a bit simpler than selecting among two hundred. It was entirely clear to me that no matter which single one was chosen by me, my entire existence would be filled with remorse that the alternative had not been wedded.”
“Wasn't either—of them—loved by you?” Nell inquired, somewhat tentatively. Speaking to an unfamiliar person about life's supreme secret and metamorphosis did not come easily to her.

“Heavens, no. Loving anyone is impossible for me. I lack that capacity. Furthermore, I have no desire to. In my opinion, falling in love turns a person into a total slave. Additionally, it would grant a man immense power to inflict pain on you. Fear would take hold of me. No, no, Hector and Orlando are a pair of darling boys, and my fondness for the two of them is so great that determining which one I prefer is truly beyond me. There lies the problem. Naturally, Hector possesses the finest looks, and marrying a man who lacked handsome features is something I just couldn't do. His disposition is pleasant as well, and his dark, curly hair is lovely. He borders on being overly flawless—having a flawless husband doesn't appeal to me, I think—someone in whom I could never discover a flaw.”
“Then why not marry Orlando?” asked Honora gravely.

“Imagine being wedded to a name such as Orlando!” Cressy stated mournfully. “Enduring it seems beyond my ability. Nevertheless, his nose possesses a classic shape, and having a reliable nose in our family would bring relief. Mine cannot be trusted. Up to this point, it resembles the Lindsay style, yet my great fear is that it will display Byrne inclinations as time passes. Daily I inspect it with concern to ensure it remains Lindsay. Mother belonged to the Byrnes and features the Byrne nose to the utmost extent. Just hold on until it comes into your view. Splendid noses are my passion. Nell Harcourt, the nose you have is extraordinarily lovely. His nose almost tipped the scales toward Orlando. Still, Orlando! No, making up my mind proved impossible. Had I been able to handle it like the hats—setting the pair up side by side, closing my eyes, and thrusting with a hatpin—the matter would have been simple.”
“In what manner were Hector and Orlando feeling at the moment you departed?” asked Honora.

“Oh, their hope remains. Having informed them that waiting was required until my decision was reached, I found them entirely agreeable to doing so. You see, I am adored by both of them. My plan in the meantime is to enjoy myself thoroughly. At Wexcombe, my expectation is to be surrounded by a multitude of suitors, as my happiness depends on having them, you know. Yet, is it not your opinion that the first-year students are terribly plain? A single truly good-looking guy was all I noticed in their group, and he departed prior to your arrival. Hugh was the name his friend used when speaking to him, as I overheard. That friend possessed eyes that bulged out to here. Must you leave already, girls? Please stay a while longer.”
“We must, I think,” Nell remarked, somewhat icily. “The hour is growing late, and I have certain tasks to attend to.”

“However, the two of you will visit me, isn’t that right?” inquired Cressida, standing up while placing an arm around both of them. “And allow me to visit you. I wish to be friendly with you. I have become so fond of you two. Furthermore, my silliness hasn’t completely repulsed you, has it?”
“Not quite,” Nell laughed, answering the squeeze from Cressy with a renewed warmth.

“Since I am far less foolish than I appear on the outside, you see. If you merely take Cressida Lindsay as God created her, despite her shortcomings, I think you will grow fond of her in time. Is not this cemetery a charming spot? Being laid to rest here would be wonderful to me. I missed this tomb earlier—the one inside the iron enclosure—oh, girls, come see—the marker states it contains a midshipman who died during the battle between the Shannon and the Chesapeake. Imagine that!”

Stopping beside the balustrade, Nell gazed upon the eroded masonry, her blood surging with abrupt exhilaration. The ancient burial ground, featuring its canopy of foliage and extended corridors of shade, dissolved before her eyes. In its place, she envisioned Portmaris Harbor as it appeared almost one hundred years prior. Emerging gradually from the fog was a grand warship, resplendent with “the meteor flag of England.” Following her came a second vessel, carrying on its quarterdeck a motionless, noble figure enfolded in his own star-adorned banner—the brave Lawrence. The hand of Time had reversed its leaf, revealing the Shannon navigating victoriously into the inlet carrying the Chesapeake as her trophy.
“Return to us, Nell Harcourt—return,” Cressida giggled, tugging at her sleeve. “A century separates you from us. Return.”
Nell returned, letting out a sigh, while a soft shine gleamed in her eyes.

“That ancient tale has always been a favorite of mine,” she remarked, “and even though the English emerged victorious, my affection for it stems from the valiant, vanquished commander. It feels so close and vividly genuine beside this tomb. Just eighteen years old was this unfortunate young midshipman. His inscription states that he ‘died of desperate wounds received in gallant action.’ A warrior could ask for nothing better.”
Prior to turning around, Nell unfastened the small bundle of violet pansies pinned to her and let it fall gently onto the burial site of the youth who had died during the massive naval battle.
“Well, how do you regard our latest acquaintance?” Honora inquired, once Cressy had departed from their presence.

“She appeals to me. Despite every bit of her foolishness, she possesses a truly endearing quality. I think she speaks the truth when she claims she is not nearly as foolish as she appears. She is a sweet, kissable child—and whether she will ever truly mature remains uncertain to me.”

“I am fond of her as well,” Honora stated firmly. “Her conversation involves boys just as frequently as Opal Pettigrew’s does. However, listening to Opal constantly makes me furious or disgusted, while Cressy simply made me want to indulge in a kindly laugh. Now, what is the reason for that difference?”

“There is a distinction,” Nell remarked thoughtfully. “In my view, it stems from Opal being truly so aware of males. She merely pretends at romance and courting. Furthermore, whenever she brags about her suitors, one gets the impression that her motive is to thoroughly impress upon you that your own fall far short in number. On the other hand, whenever Cressy discusses her suitors, her tone suggests she is merely referring to friends. She genuinely regards males as fine companions, and having scores of them following her around brings her joy solely because she enjoys being well-liked and perceived as well-liked. Even Alex and Orlando—after this, I shall be incapable of considering those two names apart—represent nothing more to her than a pair of companions eager for her to join in their games forever. Meeting her brings me happiness, as does our trip to Old St. John’s. This afternoon, I trust I have extended a small soul-root into the earth of Portmaris. It is my desire, at least. Being transplanted is something I detest.”

During the subsequent three weeks, Nell and Honora persisted in feeling like strangers in an unfamiliar territory. Subsequently, all at once, every element appeared to align—Wexcombe, professors, classes, students, studies, and social activities. Rather than consisting of isolated pieces, life grew unified once more. The Freshmen, no longer an assemblage of disconnected people, realized they were a class, possessing a class spirit, a class yell, class interests, class antipathies, and class ambitions. Victory belonged to them in the yearly “Arts Rush” against the Sophomores, through which they acquired the esteem of every class, alongside a huge, confidence-instilling self-image. The Sophomores had emerged victorious in the “rush” for three years; the fact that this year's triumph rested on the Freshmen's banner was credited to the tactical leadership of Hugh Carrow, who organized the operation and devised particular novel methods, which disrupted the Sophs and propelled the Freshmen to success. Due to his recognized merit, he was chosen as president of the Freshman Class, a prestigious and responsible office—at minimum, from a Fresh perspective—desired by numerous individuals. Furthermore, he received an invitation to enter the “Lambs”—Redmondese denoting Lamba Theta—an honor seldom offered to a Freshman. Before the initiation, as a trial, he was required to march through the primary commercial thoroughfares of Portmaris throughout an entire day while dressed in a sunbonnet and a large kitchen apron made of brightly patterned calico. He performed this gladly, tipping his sunbonnet with polite elegance whenever he encountered women he knew. Wilfred Mott, who had failed to receive an invitation to join the Lambs, remarked to Nell that he could not understand how Carrow was able to perform such an act, and that he himself could never degrade himself in that manner.

“Envisioning Wilfred Mott adorned in a calico apron together with a sunbonnet makes me giggle,” Honora giggled. “He would bear a total resemblance to his aged Grandmother Mott. Hugh, by contrast, appeared just as manly wearing those items as he did dressed in his own suitable attire.”

Nell and Honora became deeply involved in the social scene of Wexcombe. Cressida Lindsay was largely responsible for this happening so quickly. As the daughter of a wealthy and prominent man, Cressida hailed from an established and elite “Bluenose” lineage. Because of this, as well as her beauty and charm—a charm recognized by everyone who crossed her path—the doors to every clique, club, and class in Wexcombe were instantly thrown open to her; and Nell and Honora accompanied her wherever she went. Cressy “adored” Nell and Honora, particularly Nell. Possessing a loyal nature, she was entirely free from any sort of snobbery. “Love me, love my friends” appeared to be her implicit rule. Effortlessly, she brought them along into her constantly expanding realm of acquaintances, making the social journey at Wexcombe extremely smooth and enjoyable for the two Brierley girls, which sparked the envy and amazement of the other freshettes who, missing Cressida’s backing, were destined to stay mostly on the sidelines during their initial year at college.

For Nell and Honora, who held graver outlooks on existence, Cressy was still the entertaining, endearing infant she appeared to be when they initially met. Nevertheless, as she declared on her own behalf, she possessed “heaps” of intellect. The moment or location in which she discovered opportunity to read was an enigma, because she appeared constantly sought after for a variety of “fun,” and her domestic nights were packed with visitors. She possessed every one of the “beaux” that a soul might wish for, because nine-tenths of the Freshmen alongside a large portion of every other class competed for her favor. She felt innocently thrilled about this state of affairs, and joyfully detailed every additional triumph to Nell and Honora, offering remarks that could have caused the unfortunate suitor’s ears to sting intensely.
“It appears that Hector and Orlando have no major competitor so far,” Nell observed playfully.

“Not a single one,” Cressida concurred. “Every week I send letters to both of them, sharing all the details regarding my local young men. It undoubtedly amuses them, I feel certain. Nevertheless, naturally, the single one I favor most is unattainable for me. Hugh Carrow ignores me completely, save for gazing at me like I am an agreeable little kitten he wants to stroke. I am all too aware of the cause. Queen Nell, I hold a grievance against you. Truthfully, hating you is what I should be doing, yet I adore you passionately instead, and failing to behold you daily leaves me wretched. No other girl I ever met previously compares to you. Whenever your eyes meet mine in a particular manner, I sense just how unimportant, silly, and little a creature I am, inspiring me to become superior, more intelligent, and stouter of heart. Following that, I form firm intentions; however, the very first handsome chap who crosses my path shatters every one of them from my mind. Isn’t the life at college splendid? It is quite comical reflecting on how I loathed it during that initial day. Yet had I not, my friendship with you might never have truly formed. Nell, do repeat once more that I am liked by you even a small amount. Hearing it is my deep longing.”

“I adore you quite a lot—and to me you seem like a precious, gentle, delightful, soft, harmless, tiny—feline,” Nell chuckled, “yet I fail to understand how you ever manage to find the hours for studying your schoolwork.”

Cressy must have discovered the time, because she maintained her standing in all her year's classes. Even the ill-tempered, elderly Mathematics professor, who hated female students and had fiercely fought their entry into Wexcombe, was unable to stump her. She guided the freshettes in all areas, apart from English, in which Nell Harcourt surpassed her by a wide margin. Nell herself discovered that the coursework of her Freshman year was quite simple, largely owing to the consistent labor she and Hugh had performed over those prior two years in Brierley. Consequently, she had additional time for a social life that she immensely appreciated. Yet she never forgot Brierley and her friends there for a single instant. For her, the most joyful times of every week were the ones when mail arrived from home. Only after receiving her initial letters did she start believing she might ever enjoy Portmaris or feel comfortable there. Prior to their arrival, Brierley had appeared thousands of miles distant; those letters brought it close and bound the past life to the present one so intimately that they started to appear as a single continuous existence, rather than two completely isolated lives. That initial group comprised six letters, written by Odette Pullen, Opal Pettigrew, Isolde Pembroke, Thirza, Mrs. Sowerby, and Robin. The letter from Odette was a copperplate piece of penmanship, featuring every “t” carefully crossed and every “i” accurately dotted, yet it lacked a single captivating sentence. She made no reference to the school, about which Nell was desperate to learn; she responded to none of the inquiries Nell had posed in her correspondence. Instead, she informed Nell about the number of yards of lace she had lately crocheted, as well as the local weather in Brierley, her plans for the construction of her new dress, and her sensations whenever her head throbbed. Opal Pettigrew composed an effusive letter grieving over Nell’s departure, promising her that she was terribly missed in all activities, inquiring about the nature of the Wexcombe “fellows,” and occupying the remainder with stories of her own distressing encounters with her many suitors. It was a foolish, innocent letter, and Nell would have found it amusing if not for the postscript. “Hugh seems to be enjoying Wexcombe, judging from his letters,” wrote Opal. “I don’t think Wilfred is so stuck on it.”

Hugh was corresponding with Opal, then! That was fine. Naturally, he possessed every right to do so. Except—!! Nell was unaware that the initial letter had been sent by Opal and that Hugh’s reply was prompted by plain politeness. Disdainfully, she threw Opal’s note to the side. However, erasing the sharpness of Opal’s postscript required the entirety of Isolde’s lively, informative, and charming communication. Although Isolde’s page mentioned Gideon slightly too often, it was otherwise packed and overwritten with engaging news, making Nell feel nearly returned to Brierley as she perused it. Thirza provided a somewhat formal and muted message, strictly devoid of any rumors or sentiment. Nevertheless, it somehow brought to Nell a breath of the pure, unpretentious existence at Grey Shutters, carrying its hint of old-world quiet and the constant, enduring affection waiting for her there. Mrs. Sowerby’s communication proved packed with parish updates. Because she had disbanded her home, Mrs. Sowerby enjoyed extra leisure to give to religious matters, throwing her whole heart and soul into them. Currently, she felt quite agitated regarding the inferior “supplies” filling the empty Brierley pulpit.

“Only blockheads join the clergy these days, in my opinion,” was her resentful inscription. “The applicants provided to us are terrible, and their sermons are total nonsense! A good portion is false, and even more concerning, it strays from orthodox teaching. Our current minister represents the absolute lowest point. His usual habit is selecting a scripture only to speak on an unrelated topic. Furthermore, he claims a disbelief in the everlasting damnation of every pagan. Imagine that! Should they escape perdition, all of our financial contributions toward Foreign Missions are utterly thrown away, mark my words! During the previous Sunday evening service, he made an announcement that his upcoming sermon would focus on the swimming iron axe-head. My view is that he ought to stick strictly to the Scriptures and refrain from choosing theatrical topics. Conditions are truly shameful when a preacher fails to discover sufficient material within Sacred Scripture to discuss, mark my words. Which place of worship do you frequent, Nell? It is my desire that your attendance is consistent. Individuals frequently become indifferent regarding religious services when distant from their households, and my knowledge is that university pupils commit major offenses regarding this matter. Information has reached me that a large number of them truly complete their schoolwork on the Lord's Day. May you never fall to such a disgraceful level, Nell. Keep your upbringing in mind. Additionally, exercise extreme caution regarding the companions you select. One cannot determine what kinds of beasts inhabit those educational institutions. Externally they could resemble whitewashed tombs while internally behaving like predatory wolves, mark my words. It would be wisest for you to completely avoid speaking with any youth who fails to originate from the Island.”

“I neglected to mention to you what occurred on the day the minister paid a visit here. It was the most amusing sight I have ever witnessed. I remarked to Thirza, ‘If Nell had been here wouldn’t she have had a laugh?’ Thirza herself even laughed. You are aware that he is an extremely short, chubby small man with bow legs.
