Well, that old pig belonging to Mr. Pettifer—the large, tall one—had strayed over here once more that day and forced its way into the yard, and it had entered the back porch, without our knowledge, and it was located there when the minister showed up in the doorway. It executed one frantic charge to escape, but there was no place to charge toward except right between those bow legs. Therefore it went right there, and, since it was so large and the minister so small, it swept him entirely off his feet and bore him off. His hat flew in one direction and his cane in another, right as Thirza and I reached the door. I will never erase the sight of him from my memory. And that unfortunate pig was almost frightened to death. I will never manage to read that narrative in the Bible regarding the swine that charged furiously down the steep slope into the sea without picturing Mr. Pettifer’s pig galloping down the hill bearing that minister. I imagine the pig believed he was carrying the Old Boy on his back rather than within him. I felt grateful the twins were not around. It would not have been proper for them to witness a minister in such an embarrassing plight. Right before they reached the brook the minister leaped off or tumbled off. The pig dashed through the brook like a lunatic and onward through the woods. Thirza and I hurried down and assisted the minister in getting up and dusting his coat. He suffered no injury, but he was furious. He appeared to consider Thirza and me accountable for the entire incident, even though we informed him that the pig was not ours, and had been bothering us the whole summer. Furthermore, why did he approach the back door? You would never have caught Mr. Wace doing such a thing. A considerable amount of time will pass before we find a man like Mr. Wace. Nevertheless, it is an ill wind that blows nobody good. We have not spotted hoof or hair of that pig from that moment on, and I hold the conviction that we never shall.

“Affairs are rather still in Brierley. Grey Shutters does not seem as lonely to me as I anticipated. It is my intention to begin a different cotton warp quilt during this winter. A lovely new apple-leaf design belongs to Mrs. Silas Mott.

“Whenever I need a bit of a thrill, I peruse the murder court cases in the Boston newspaper my niece mails to me. It wasn't my habit past, yet I find them genuinely fascinating. The States has got to be a dreadful region. It is my wish that you won't ever travel there, Nell. However, the manner in which young women wander about the globe these days is truly horrifying. It constantly reminds me of Satan within the Book of Job, traveling back and forth and walking back and forth. I am convinced the Lord never designed it to be so, and that is a fact.”

“Robin has behaved quite well since your departure. He misbehaved one day, so Thirza disciplined him by forcing him to put on Lucy’s apron for the entire day, whereupon he proceeded to chop up every single one of Lucy’s aprons. After I gave him a spanking for doing that, he went off and ran my rooster until it died.

“My residence has become the new home of the MacPhersons. Being a very particular person, she is a wonderful housekeeper. All my June lilies were yanked up by her on the grounds that a garden is made to appear terribly messy by them. At the time of our marriage, Thomas planted those lilies. A pleasant enough fellow describes her husband, yet she is unable to move past having been an old maid, and that is the truth.

“Avoid working too much at your studies, and make certain that you dress in your winter undergarments the moment the temperature drops. Thirza experiences much anxiety regarding you, yet I inform her that you possess considerably more wisdom than I previously anticipated you would acquire, and that you will manage just fine.”
At the very beginning, Robin’s letter descended into a complaint.

“Dearest anne, kindly send a note asking marilla to refrain from fastening me to the bridge rail during my fishing trips since the other boys tease me on those occasions. Living here in your absence feels terribly lonely, though school provides wonderful entertainment. Odette andrews exhibits a nastier disposition than yours. Yesterday evening, I frightened mrs. lynde using a jack-o'-lantern. Her anger was intense, and she became equally enraged because I pursued her elderly rooster throughout the farmyard until he collapsed and perished. Causing his sudden death was not my intention. Nell, what caused his life to end, I am eager to learn. mrs. lynde tossed his body to the pigs when she could have traded him to mr. blair instead. Currently, mr. blair pays 50 cents each for fine deceased roosters. I overheard mrs. lynde requesting the minister's prayers on her behalf. Nell, what dreadful deed did she commit, I am eager to learn. A kite possessing a splendid tail now belongs to me, anne. During class yesterday, Milty bolter shared a marvelous tale with me. The account is accurate. Late one evening last week, old Joe Mosey and Leon engaged in a card game out in the forest. Their playing cards rested upon a tree stump when a colossal dark figure taller than the forest canopy arrived, snatched both cards and stump, and vanished accompanied by a booming sound resembling thunder. They must have been terrified, I am certain. According to Milty, that dark figure was the devil himself. Was it truly him, anne, I am eager to learn. Mr. kimball, who resides in spenservale, suffers from severe illness and must be admitted to the hospitable. Allow me a moment to inquire of marilla whether my spelling is correct. Thirza claims the silem represents his actual destination rather than that first location. He believes a serpent resides within his body. What feeling does housing a serpent in your body produce, anne, I am eager to learn. mrs. lawrence bell has also fallen ill. mrs. lynde asserts that her sole ailment stems from obsessing excessively over her internal organs.”
“What Mrs. Sowerby would make of Cressida,” Nell remarked, putting her letters away, “is something I wonder about.”
“Girls, what do you plan to do with yourselves today?” inquired Cressida, entering Nell’s room suddenly one Saturday afternoon.

“We are taking a stroll through the park,” replied Nell. “I should remain indoors and complete my blouse. However, sewing is impossible for me on such a day. Something within the atmosphere penetrates my blood and creates a kind of magnificence in my soul. My fingers would jerk and I would stitch an uneven seam. Consequently, it is off to the park and the pines.”
“Is anyone besides Honora and you included in 'we'?”
“Indeed, Hugh and Wilfred are part of it, and it would bring us great pleasure to have you join as well.”
"However," Cressida uttered sorrowfully, "going means I must play third wheel, a role Cressida Lindsay has never experienced before."

“Indeed, novel occurrences expand one’s horizons. Join me, and you will find yourself capable of empathizing with every unfortunate individual forced to play third wheel frequently. However, where have all the sufferers gone?”

“Oh, I was weary of the lot of them and just could not be troubled with a single one today. Furthermore, I have been experiencing a slight sadness—merely a faint, fleeting light blue. My mood is not grave enough to warrant a deeper shade. Last week, I penned letters to Hector and Orlando. I placed the notes inside envelopes and wrote their addresses, yet I left them unsealed. Later that night, a peculiar event occurred. Namely, Hector would consider it amusing, whereas Orlando probably would not. Since I was in a rush, I grabbed what I assumed was Hector’s letter from its envelope and hastily added a postscript. Afterward, I posted both of the letters. Orlando’s response arrived for me this morning. Girls, I had written that postscript on his letter instead, and he was enraged. Naturally, he will recover from it—and it matters not to me if he fails to—yet it ruined my day. Consequently, I decided I would visit you darlings so you could brighten my spirits. Once the football season commences, I will not possess any free Saturday afternoons. Football is something I adore. I have acquired the most magnificent cap and sweater featuring stripes in the Wexcombe colors to don for the matches. Admittedly, from a slight distance I will resemble a moving barber’s pole. Are you aware that that Hugh of yours was chosen as Captain of the Freshman football team?”

“Indeed, he mentioned that to us yesterday night,” remarked Honora, noticing that a furious Nell refused to respond. “He visited alongside Wilfred. Having anticipated their arrival, we meticulously hid or removed all the cushions belonging to Miss Ada. The extremely intricate one featuring raised embroidery was dumped onto the ground in the corner behind its chair by me. I assumed its safety was guaranteed there. Yet, can you imagine? Wilfred Mott headed straight to that seat, spotted the cushion lying behind it, gravely pulled it out, and remained seated on it for the entire night. It became an absolute disaster of a cushion! Today, poor Miss Ada inquired of me, her expression remaining polite, yet expressing deep disappointment, why I had permitted someone to sit on it. My response to her was that I hadn’t—it resulted from fate joined with persistent Sloanish behavior, and I lacked the ability to defeat both together.”

“Miss Ada’s cushions are truly irritating me,” Nell remarked. “Seven days ago she completed a pair of new ones, packed tight and covered with embroidery to the extreme limits. Because there was no remaining spot lacking a cushion to place them, she lined them up against the wall on the landing of the stairs. They fall down during fifty percent of the time, and we trip on them whenever we navigate the stairs in pitch-blackness. Last Sunday, while Dr. Twiss offered a prayer for everyone subject to the dangers of the ocean, I privately inserted ‘and for everyone residing in homes where cushions receive an affection that is unwise and excessive!’ There! our preparations are complete, and I spot the boys approaching by way of Old St. John’s. Are you joining your fate with ours, Cressy?”

“Provided I am able to stroll alongside Honora and Wilfred, I will attend. Such an arrangement will render the chaperone role tolerable. Your Hugh is genuinely wonderful, Nell, yet what prompts his frequent company with Goggle-eyes?”
Nell went rigid. Wilfred Mott was not someone she particularly cared for; nevertheless, he belonged to Brierley, which meant no stranger had the right to mock him.
“Wilfred and Hugh have constantly been friends,” she stated distantly. “Wilfred is a good boy. His eyes are not his fault.”

“Forbidden to say so! Indeed he is! To receive the penalty of those very eyes, his past life must have contained a terrible deed. Today’s afternoon will bring Nonie and me great amusement through him. In his presence, we are going to mock him, completely beyond his awareness.”

Unquestionably, “the abandoned P’s,” to use Nell’s phrase, fulfilled their pleasant plans. Mott, however, remained happily unaware; he considered himself quite a dashing chap for strolling alongside a pair of such coeds, particularly Cressida Lindsay, who was the belle and beauty of the class. Nell would certainly be impressed by it. She was bound to realize that certain individuals recognized his true worth.

Hugh and Nell lagged slightly behind the rest of the group, taking pleasure in the quiet, peaceful charm of the autumn afternoon beneath the park's pine trees, along the ascending and winding path that encircled the harbor coast.

“Doesn’t the quietness in this place resemble a prayer?” asked Nell, looking up toward the luminous sky. “My affection for the pine trees is so great! The way they anchor their roots appears to reach into the ancient romance of every era. Finding solace in sneaking off occasionally to have a deep conversation with them brings such comfort. Being out in these woods continually fills me with joy.”
“‘Thus, captured within secluded peaks as if touched by a holy enchantment, their worries slip away from them just like needles brushed from a windy pine tree,’”
quoted Hugh.
“Our small aspirations appear quite insignificant by comparison, do they not, Nell?”
“If I were ever visited by a profound grief, I believe I would seek solace among the pine trees,” Nell remarked in a daydreamy tone.

“I wish that you are never visited by any severe grief, Nell,” uttered Hugh, unable to associate the concept of grief with the lively, happy girl at his side, ignorant that individuals capable of ascending to the loftiest peaks can likewise sink to the lowest abysses, and that those personalities that experience joy most intensely are the very ones that endure pain most acutely.

“However, there has to be—at some point,” Nell reflected. “Right now, life feels like a goblet of triumph pressed to my mouth. Nevertheless, it must contain a degree of gall—all cups do. One day, I will drink my share. Ah, I trust I will possess the strength and courage to face it. Furthermore, I pray it does not arrive as a result of my own wrongdoing. Are you mindful of Dr. Twiss’s remarks this past Sunday night—how the griefs bestowed by God brought consolation and power alongside them, whereas the griefs we inflicted upon ourselves, via foolishness or sinfulness, were immensely more difficult to endure? Still, we should not discuss grief on such an afternoon. It was created for the pure delight of existence, wasn’t it?”
“Nell, I would exclude all things except joy and delight from your existence if it were up to me,” Hugh stated with the particular voice that signaled “danger ahead.”

“If so, your choice would be most foolish,” Nell quickly retorted. “In my view, an existence cannot achieve true growth and completeness if it lacks all hardship and grief—even if we likely acknowledge this fact solely during times of relative ease. Hurry—our companions have reached the pavilion and are waving for us to join them.”

They gathered and sat in the small pavilion so they could observe a fall sunset composed of faint gold and intense crimson fire. Portmaris was situated to their left, with its spires and roofs appearing faint beneath a covering of violet smoke. The harbor was located to their right, acquiring shades of copper and rose while it spread outward toward the sunset. The water sparkled in front of them, silver gray and smooth as satin, and past it, clean shaven William’s Island emerged from the fog, protecting the town in the manner of a resolute bulldog. The signal of its lighthouse shone through the fog resembling a menacing star, which received a reply from a different one on the distant horizon.

“Have you ever beheld a location that appeared so formidable?” Cressida inquired. “I do not particularly desire William’s Island, yet I am certain that it would be unobtainable for me even if I wished for it. Observe the sentry positioned upon the peak of the fortification, directly next to the flag. Is he not the very image of a character who has emerged from a tale of romance?”
“Apropos of romance,” Honora remarked, “we’ve been searching for heather—though, naturally, we weren't able to locate any. I imagine the season is too far advanced.”
“Heather!” cried out Nell. “Does heather grow in America, then?”

“Across the entire continent, only two spots of it exist,” Cressy remarked, “this single one inside the park, and another located in Nova Scotia, though the exact place escapes my memory. A year saw the Black Watch, the renowned Highland Regiment, pitch camp on this site, and as the soldiers beat out their mattress straw during spring, heather seeds caught hold and grew.”
“Oh, how delightful!” said enchanted Nell.

“We could head back via Linden Avenue,” Hugh proposed. “It will allow us to view ‘the grand residences of the rich elite.’ Portmaris has no better street for living than Linden Avenue. Building there is restricted solely to millionaires.”

“Oh, do,” Cressy remarked. “Nell, I want to display a completely delightful small property to you. A millionaire did not construct it. Positioned as the initial site upon exiting the park, its development surely occurred when Linden Avenue remained a rural lane. Developed it was—never constructed! The residences along the Avenue fail to appeal to me. Their condition is overly new and full of plate glass. Yet this tiny location is divine—and as for its title—you must simply wait to behold it.”

As they strolled up the pine-fringed hill from the park, they spotted it. Situated right on the crest, at the point where Linden Avenue tapered off into an ordinary road, stood a small white frame house flanked by clusters of pines that extended their limbs in a protective manner over its low roof. Red and gold vines clad the home, with its green-shuttered windows peering out through them. A miniature garden, encircled by a low stone wall, lay in front of it. Even though it was October, the garden remained deeply fragrant with beloved, old-fashioned, unworldly flowers and shrubs—sweet may, southern-wood, lemon verbena, alyssum, petunias, marigolds and chrysanthemums. Leading from the gate to the front porch was a small brick walk arranged in a herring-bone pattern. The entire property appeared as if it could have been uprooted from a distant rural village; nevertheless, it possessed a quality that rendered its closest neighbor, the grand lawn-surrounded mansion of a tobacco king, remarkably unrefined, ostentatious, and vulgar in comparison. As Cressy said, it was the difference between being born and being made.

“It’s the most precious spot I’ve ever laid eyes on,” Nell stated with joy. “It causes one of my familiar, wonderfully strange pangs. It’s even sweeter and more unusual than the stone home belonging to Miss Rosalind.”

“I want you to pay particular attention to the name,” Cressy said. “See—encircling the archway above the gate, written in white lettering. ‘Tabby’s Place.’ Isn’t that hilarious? Particularly along this Avenue filled with Pinehursts, Elmwolds, and Cedarcrofts? ‘Tabby’s Place,’ no less! I absolutely love it.”
“Do you know who Tabby might be?” inquired Honora.

“I have learned that Tabby Linden is the name of the elderly woman who possesses it,” I remarked. “She resides in that place alongside her niece, and their residence there has spanned hundreds of years, give or take a few—perhaps slightly fewer, Nell. Overstatement is simply a creative surge of poetry. It has come to my knowledge that affluent people have attempted to purchase the property repeatedly—indeed, it commands a great sum today, as you are aware—yet ‘Tabby’ refuses to sell for any price whatsoever. Furthermore, a real apple orchard occupies the space behind the residence instead of a rear lawn—you will spot it once we move slightly further along—an actual apple orchard situated on Linden Avenue!”

“To-night my dreams will be of ‘Tabby’s Place,’” Nell remarked. “Why, it feels to me as though I were a part of it. I am curious whether there is any possibility that we will ever get a view of its interior.”
“It is not probable,” Honora remarked.
Nell gave a mysterious smile.

“No, the likelihood is low. Nevertheless, I hold the belief that it shall occur. A peculiar, eerie, unsettling sensation—term it a presentiment, should you wish—possesses me that ‘Tabby’s Place’ and my person will become even more familiar.”

Those initial three weeks at Wexcombe had appeared lengthy; nevertheless, the remainder of the term sped past on the wings of the wind. Prior to their realizing it, the Wexcombe students found themselves engulfed in the labor of Christmas examinations, coming out of them with varying degrees of triumph. The distinction of topping the Freshman classes shifted among Nell, Hugh and Cressida; Honora performed exceedingly well; Wilfred Mott managed a respectable pass, and conducted himself with as much self-satisfaction as though he were first in every subject.

“I am unable to fully accept that by this hour tomorrow Grey Shutters will be my location,” Nell stated as the final evening prior to leaving arrived. “Yet that is where I will be. Meanwhile, Cressy, your destination will be Harborough alongside Hector and Orlando.”

“I am eager to view them,” confessed Cressy, in the middle of eating her piece of chocolate. “It’s true that they are exceptionally sweet boys, you know. An abundance of dances, drives, and overall festivities is planned. For failing to return home alongside me during the break, Queen Nell, you will never have my forgiveness.”

“‘Never’ equals three days when it comes to you, Cressy. Asking me was sweet of you—and I’d be thrilled to visit Harborough eventually. However, I am unable to attend this year—returning home is a necessity for me. You cannot fathom the degree to which my heart yearns for it.”

“Your experience will not be very enjoyable,” Cressy remarked with contempt. “I imagine a couple of quilting bees will take place; additionally, every old busybody will discuss you, both directly and in your absence. My dear, boredom will be the death of you.”
“In Brierley?” asked Nell, thoroughly entertained.

“Now, a completely magnificent time would be yours if you would accompany me. Harborough would be crazy about you, Queen Nell—the way you look, your hair, and, well, all of it! So distinct are you. A huge hit is what you would be—with me soaking up the borrowed fame—‘near the rose, though not the rose itself.’ Please reconsider and come, Nell.”

“Cressy, your depiction of social successes is very intriguing, but I will create a contrasting image. My destination is a former green, currently somewhat weathered rural farmhouse surrounded by apple trees without leaves. Further down lies a stream, and past that is a fir forest in December where I have listened to rain and wind play upon harps. A neighboring pond will currently appear gray and melancholic. Inside the home, two elderly women will be present, with one being lean and tall, while the other is stout and short; additionally, two twins will be there, with one serving as an ideal example, whereas the other is referred to by Mrs. Sowerby as a ‘holy terror.’ An upper small chamber above the veranda will exist, dense with old memories, alongside a large, plump, wonderful feather mattress that will feel like ultimate comfort following a boardinghouse bed. Cressy, what is your opinion of my image?”
“It appears to be a rather dreary piece,” Cressy remarked, pulling a face.

“Oh, but I omitted the element that changes everything,” Nell uttered gently. “Love will exist there, Cressy—devoted, gentle affection, the kind I will not ever discover anywhere else in the universe—affection that is holding out for me. That turns my painting into a work of art, does it not, even though the hues are somewhat lacking in brightness?”
Without a word, Cressy stood up, threw her chocolate box aside, approached Nell, and embraced her.
“Nell, I desire to be such as you are,” she remarked with gravity.

Isolde came to the Delford station to meet Nell on the following evening, and the pair traveled back to their house beneath quiet skies filled with stars. Grey Shutters seemed extremely celebratory while they made their way up the lane. Illumination shone from all the windows, the brightness bursting forth into the night like fire-red flowers hanging before the black backdrop of the Whispering Wood. Furthermore, a bold bonfire burned in the yard, accompanied by two joyful small figures leaping about it, one of whom uttered a bloodcurdling scream when the buggy pulled in beneath the poplar trees.

“Robin intends that to be an Indian war-whoop,” Isolde stated. “The hired boy of Mr. Pettifer instructed him in it, and he has been refining it to greet you. Mrs. Sowerby claims her nerves have been worn to a frazzle by it. You see, he sneaks behind her, and then releases it. Furthermore, he was set on having a bonfire to celebrate your arrival. For two weeks he has been stacking branches and harassing Thirza to allow him to douse it with kerosene oil prior to lighting it. Judging by the odor, I believe she permitted it, even though Mrs. Sowerby maintained until the end that Robin would destroy himself and all the others if he were allowed.”
By this time, Nell had stepped down from the buggy, and Robin was enthusiastically throwing his arms around her knees, while even Lucy held fast to her hand.
“Is that not a splendid bonfire, Nell? Allow me to demonstrate how to prod it—do you see those sparks? I made it for your benefit, Nell, because your return home made me so happy.”

Thirza’s lean figure appeared in the open kitchen doorway, silhouetted against the light inside. Because she feared greatly that joy would make her weep—she, a rigid, restrained Thirza, who considered any showing of intense feeling improper—she chose to encounter Nell in the dimness. Standing behind her was Mrs. Sowerby, cheerful, gentle, and motherly, just as she used to be. The affection that Nell had assured Cressy was anticipating her encompassed her and wrapped her in its grace and gentleness. Indeed, no new thing could equal former bonds, former companions, and former Grey Shutters! Sitting at the well-filled supper table, Nell had such shining eyes, such rosy cheeks, such silvery, bright laughter! Moreover, Isolde intended to spend the entire night there as well. It mirrored the cherished past so closely! Furthermore, the table was adorned with the rose-bud tea-set! For Thirza, this was the absolute limit of her natural capacity.

“I expect that you and Isolde will go on chatting until morning,” Thirza uttered mockingly while the girls headed up the stairs. Thirza invariably spoke with sarcasm whenever she exposed her true feelings.
“Indeed,” Nell assented cheerfully, “though putting Robin to sleep comes first for me. That is his firm demand.”
“You bet,” Robin said, while they proceeded down the corridor. “I wish for someone to hear my prayers once more. Saying them by myself is no fun.”
“You do not speak those words by yourself, Robin. God remains alongside you continuously to listen to you.”
“Indeed, I am unable to perceive Him,” Robin argued. “My desire is to offer prayers to a person visible to me, yet I refuse to recite them to Thirza or Mrs. Sowerby, so there!”

All the same, as soon as Robin was dressed in his gray flannel nighty, starting did not appear to be his top priority. Shifting one unclad foot against the other, he remained in front of Nell with a hesitant expression.
“Come along, my sweet, drop to your knees,” Nell requested.
Robin approached and pressed his head against the lap of Nell, though he refrained from kneeling.
“Nell,” he uttered, his words suppressed. “I do not want to pray anymore. It has been a week since I last felt like doing so. I—I failed to pray yesterday evening as well as the evening prior.”
“Why wouldn’t you, Robin?” Nell inquired softly.
“If I reveal it to you, you won't get angry, will you?” Robin pleaded.
Nell picked up the small figure clad in gray flannel onto her knee, nestling his head against her arm.
“Is it ever my reaction to become ‘mad’ upon hearing what you have to say, Robin?”

“Na-a-ay, it never happens with you. Yet you become apologetic, and that is more unpleasant. It will make you terribly sorry when I share this with you, Nell—and I imagine you will feel ashamed on my account.”
“Did you do a bad thing, Robin, and does that prevent you from saying your prayers?”
“No, up to this point I have not behaved badly. Nevertheless, committing a misdeed is my desire.”
“What’s the matter, Robin?”

“Nell, I—I feel the need to utter a profane word,” Robin uttered abruptly, straining himself to speak. “A week ago, I caught Mr. Pettifer’s hired boy using it, and from that moment on, the urge to speak it has possessed me constantly—including the moments I recite my prayers.”
“Speak the words then, Robin.”
In astonishment, Robin raised his reddened face.
“However, Nell, the word is terribly bad.”
“Speak the words!”
Robin offered her a second disbelieving glance, after which he uttered the terrible word in a quiet tone. Within moments, he was burying his face into her.
“Oh, Nell, I won't ever repeat it—not ever. I won't ever desire to repeat it. That it was bad I was aware, but I didn't think it was this—this—I didn't think it was of that nature.”
“No, I doubt you will ever wish to utter those words again, Robin—or even ponder them. Also, if I were in your place, I would not associate frequently with the boy hired by Mr. Pettifer.”
“He is capable of producing splendid battle-cries,” Robin remarked with a slight tinge of regret.
“However, you would prefer not to have your mind crammed with vile language, wouldn't you, Robin—terms that are going to corrupt it and expel everything that is virtuous and noble?”
“No,” Robin stated, staring with the wide-eyed intensity of an owl while lost in thought.
“In that case, refrain from accompanying the individuals who employ them. Now, do you believe you are capable of offering your prayers, Robin?”

“Oh, yes,” said Robin, eagerly squirming lower on his knees, “I am able to say them fine now. I am not afraid now to say ‘if I should die before I wake,’ the way I was when I was wishing to say that word.”

Likely Nell and Isolde opened up their hearts completely to one another during that night, yet not a single trace of those shared secrets remains. At the morning meal, the pair appeared as luminous and clear-eyed as merely young people are able to look following illicit hours spent feasting and confiding. Prior to this moment, snow had not fallen, yet when Isolde went over the ancient log bridge heading toward home, light white flakes commenced drifting down upon the fields and forests, which lay russet and gray within their deep slumber. Before long, the distant hillsides and high places grew faint and ghost-like behind their thin wrapping, resembling a pale autumn that had tossed a hazy wedding veil across her tresses while awaiting her winter groom. Thus, they enjoyed a white Christmas when all was said and done, and it proved to be a most agreeable day. During the morning hours, correspondence and presents arrived from Miss Rosalind and Cedric; Nell unsealed them inside the inviting Grey Shutters kitchen, an area brimming with what Robin, inhaling with delight, termed “pretty smells.”

“Miss Rosalind and Mr. Stanhope have taken up residence in their new home now,” Nell reported. “I feel certain Miss Rosalind is completely happy—I can tell from the overall impression of her letter—yet there is a line from Belinda the Fourth. She dislikes Boston immensely, and she is terribly homesick. Miss Rosalind wishes for me to travel to Echo Cottage on some day during my stay at home to burn a fire for ventilation, as well as ensure the cushions are not becoming moldy. I believe I will have Isolde accompany me next week, so we may pass the evening alongside Theodora Dix. I desire to visit Theodora. Incidentally, is Ludovic Speed continuing to visit her?”
“That is what people claim,” Thirza remarked, “and it is probable he will keep doing so. Everyone has stopped anticipating that this wooing will ever lead to anything.”
“If I were Theodora, I would make him move faster,” Mrs. Sowerby remarked. And she unquestionably would have done so.
A typical scribble from Cressida arrived as well, packed with Hector and Orlando, the things they stated, the actions they performed, and the expressions on their faces upon catching sight of her.

Cressy penned, “However, deciding which one to wed is something I am unable to do yet. My wish is that you had accompanied me so you could choose on my behalf. A decision will need to be made by somebody. My heart pounded heavily upon seeing Hector, making me think, ‘The right man could be him.’ Then, Orlando arrived, causing my heart to pound once more. That offers no direction, even if it ought to based on every novel I have read in my life. Nell, wouldn’t your heart refrain from pounding for anyone other than the true Prince Charming? A fundamental flaw must exist within my own heart. Nevertheless, my time here is absolutely wonderful. I desire so much for you to be present! Snow is falling on this day, bringing me sheer delight. Having a green Christmas was a great fear of mine, as I despise them. When Christmas turns into a filthy grayish-brownish thing that appears as though it was forgotten a century back and soaked continuously from then on, you are aware that it receives the name of a green Christmas! Request no explanation from me as to why. To quote Lord Dundreary, ‘there are thome thingth no fellow can underthtand.’”

“Nell, have you ever boarded a street car only to find out that you had no money on you to pay the fare? I experienced that recently. It feels terrible. Upon boarding the car, I possessed a nickel. I believed it was located in my coat's left pocket. After I was settled comfortably, I searched for it. It was absent. A cold chill ran through me. I searched inside the opposite pocket. Still absent. A second chill hit me. Subsequently, I searched inside a small interior pocket. It was entirely useless. I suffered two chills at the same time.

“Removing my gloves, I placed them upon the seat, and I searched through every one of my pockets once more. There was no sign of it. I got to my feet, shook my clothing, and subsequently inspected the floor. A crowd of individuals returning home from the opera packed the car, and every person gazed at me, though I no longer concerned myself with a minor matter of that nature.
“However, my fare was nowhere to be found. My conclusion was that I had likely placed it inside my mouth and accidentally gulped it down.

“Uncertainty overwhelmed me. I pondered whether the conductor would bring the streetcar to a halt and force me off in disgrace and humiliation. Could I perhaps persuade him that my situation stemmed purely from my own forgetfulness, rather than an attempt by a dishonest person to steal a ride under fraudulent claims? I longed desperately for the presence of Hector or Orlando. They were absent, however, precisely because I desired them to be there. Had I possessed no wish for them, they would have appeared in great numbers. Meanwhile, I remained unable to choose what I ought to tell the conductor upon his approach. The moment I formulated a single explanatory statement in my thoughts, I doubted anyone would accept it, forcing me to draft a different one. Relying on Providence appeared to be the sole option left, though it offered me no more reassurance than it gave the elderly woman who, upon being instructed by the captain amid a tempest to place her faith in God, cried out, ‘Oh, Captain, is it as bad as that?’”

“Precisely at the expected instant, after all expectation was gone, and while the ticket collector was presenting his container to the rider beside me, the location where I had placed that miserable piece of money abruptly came back to my mind. It had not been consumed by me in the end. Quietly, I extracted it from my glove's forefinger and thrust it inside the container. I beamed at all the people and experienced a sense that the world was lovely.”

Going to Echo Cottage proved to be just as delightful as numerous other enjoyable vacation excursions. Nell and Isolde returned there via the familiar path through the beech woods, taking along a lunch basket. Echo Cottage, having remained shut continuously from the time of Miss Rosalind’s wedding, was temporarily opened wide to the breeze and light of the sun again, and the glow of firelight shone once more within the tiny rooms. The fragrance from Miss Rosalind’s rose bowl continued to saturate the atmosphere. One could scarcely credit that Miss Rosalind would not enter briskly in a moment, her brown eyes sparkling with welcome, and that Belinda the Fourth, wearing a blue bow and a broad smile, would not appear suddenly at the doorway. Cedric, as well, appeared to linger nearby, accompanied by his magical imaginations.

“It truly causes me to feel somewhat like a phantom returning to see the moon’s ancient glimpses,” Nell chuckled. “Let us step outside to discover whether the echoes remain present. Fetch the aged horn. You can still find it stationed in back of the door to the kitchen.”

Across the pale stream, the echoes remained in their usual place, just as bright as silver and as abundant as they had always been; and once they no longer replied, the girls secured Echo Cottage once more and departed during the flawless thirty minutes that come after the pink and yellow hues of a winter sunset.

No pinky-yellow sunset or green twilight marked the quiet departure of the old year. Rather, its end arrived amid a wild, white bluster and blow. On that night, the storm-wind sped across the black hollows and frozen meadows, groaned around the eaves resembling a lost creature, and slammed the snow hard against the rattling panes.

“Precisely the type of evening folks enjoy snuggling under their bedclothes and enumerating their blessings,” Nell remarked to Odette Pullen, who had arrived to pass the afternoon and remain until morning. However, once they were snuggled under their bedclothes, inside Nell’s small porch chamber, Odette was contemplating something other than her blessings.
“Nell,” she stated in an exceedingly serious manner, “there is a matter I wish to share with you. Will you allow me”

Following the previous evening's party hosted by Opal Pettigrew, Nell felt quite tired. Instead of hearing Odette’s disclosures, which she felt certain would prove uninteresting, she preferred by far to fall asleep. What lay ahead was something she had no intuitive forewarning of. Odette had likely become engaged as well; according to local gossip, Opal Pettigrew had agreed to marry the Tullyvale schoolteacher, a man over whom every girl was reportedly mad.
“It won’t be long before I’m the sole unattached young woman remaining from our former group of four,” Nell mused, feeling sleepy. Speaking out loud, she uttered, “Of course.”
“Nell,” Odette inquired, with even greater gravity, “how do you feel about my brother Barney?”

This unlooked-for query caused Nell to draw her breath in sharply, her mind grasping about in vain. What was her opinion of Barney Pullen, for pity's sake? Round-faced, foolish, endlessly grinning, kindly Barney Pullen was someone she had never harbored a single thought about. Was Barney Pullen ever in anyone's thoughts?
“I—I fail to comprehend, Odette,” she faltered. “What are you trying to say—precisely?”
“Is Barney to your liking?” Odette inquired directly.

“Why—why—yes, I like him, of course,” gasped Nell, questioning whether she was speaking the absolute truth. Indubitably, Barney was not someone she disliked. Yet could her feeling of unconcerned tolerance toward him whenever he chanced to fall within her field of sight truly be counted as liking? What point was Odette attempting to make clear?
“Is it your wish to have him as a husband?” inquired Odette in a serene manner.

“A husband!” Nell, who had been sitting up in bed to better contend with the issue of how she truly felt about Barney Pullen, now collapsed flatly onto her pillows, the breath completely knocked out of her. “Whose husband?”

“Yours, naturally,” Odette replied. “Barney desires to make you his wife. He has perpetually been mad about you—and currently father has bestowed the upper farm upon him under his own name, so there is no obstacle to stop him from taking a bride. However, he is so bashful that he was unable to inquire directly whether you would take him, which led him to persuade me to act on his behalf. I would have preferred not to, but he harassed me incessantly until I promised that I would, provided a suitable opportunity arose. What is your opinion on the matter, Nell?”

Could this be a dream? Was it akin to those horrific nightmares where you discover you are betrothed or wedded to a person you despise or are unacquainted with, having no clue how it occurred? No, she—Nell Harcourt—was resting right there, fully awake, inside her own bed, while Odette Pullen sat next to her, composedly making a marriage proposal on behalf of her brother Barney. Nell was uncertain if she felt like squirming or laughing; however, neither reaction was possible, because she had to avoid injuring Odette’s feelings.
“I—I was unable to wed Bill, don't you see, Odette,” she succeeded in breathing out. “Indeed, a thought like that was never in my mind—not once!”

“It probably didn't,” concurred Odette. “Courting is something Barney has constantly been much too timid to consider. Even so, you could reflect upon it, Nell. My brother Barney is a fine man, which I am obligated to state. He lacks any negative vices, works extremely hard, and is someone you can count on. ‘A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.’ He instructed me to inform you that he would be entirely agreeable to waiting until your college education is finished, should you demand it, even if his preference is a wedding this spring prior to the start of planting. I feel certain he would constantly treat you with great kindness, and, Nell, you are aware of how delighted I would be to gain you as a sister.”

“I cannot marry Barney,” Nell stated firmly. Having regained her composure, she was now experiencing a touch of annoyance. The entire situation was utterly absurd. “It is pointless to consider it, Odette. My feelings for him are not of that nature, and you need to inform him of this.”

“Indeed, I never anticipated your agreement,” Odette uttered with a weary exhale, believing she had given her utmost effort. “Though I informed Barney that requesting this of you seemed completely futile, he urged me anyway. So, Nell, your choice has been finalized, and I trust you will not rue it.”

Odette’s tone was somewhat icy. It had been her firm conviction that the infatuated Barney stood zero prospect of persuading Nell into marriage. Even so, a slight bitterness touched her that Nell Harcourt, a person who was ultimately just a taken-in orphan lacking any family whatsoever, would reject her brother—a member of the Brierley Pullen. Ah well, self-importance occasionally precedes a collapse, Odette brooded darkly.
Nell allowed a smile to cross her face in the dark at the thought of ever being sorry for failing to wed Barney Pullen.
“I hope Barney won’t take it too hard,” she said kindly.
Odette shifted as though she was flinging her head back against her pillow.

“Oh, he won’t break his heart. Barney possesses far too much good sense for that to happen. He likes Nettie Scobie fairly well, too, and mother would prefer him to marry her over anyone else. She is a very capable manager and saver. I believe that as soon as Barney is certain you refuse to have him, he will choose Nettie. Please do not speak of this to anybody, will you, Nell?”

“Certainly not,” said Nell, who lacked any wish at all to broadcast to the world that Barney Pullen sought her hand in marriage, choosing her, when everything was taken into account, over Nettie Scobie. Nettie Scobie!
“And now I think we should try to get some sleep,” Odette proposed.

Slumber came effortlessly and promptly to Odette; yet, despite being extremely dissimilar to MacBeth in the majority of ways, she had undoubtedly managed to slay sleep for Nell. That proposed-to damsel remained upon an insomniac pillow until the wee sma’s, though her thoughts were distant from being romantic. Nevertheless, it was not before the following morning that she possessed a chance to enjoy a hearty laugh about the entire business. Once Odette had departed for home—bearing a trace of frost in her tone and demeanor still, owing to Nell having refused the distinction of a union with the House of Pullen so thanklessly and firmly—Nell withdrew to the porch room, closed the door, and finally enjoyed her full laugh.

“If only there were someone to share this humor with!” was her thought. “However, that is impossible. Isolde is the sole person I would wish to confide in, yet, setting aside my oath of secrecy to Odette, I am unable to share anything with Isolde anymore. Every detail gets passed on to Gideon—of that I am certain. At any rate, my initial proposal of marriage has happened. While I anticipated its eventual arrival—it never occurred to me that it would arrive through an intermediary. Though it is immensely amusing—it nevertheless carries a certain sharp pain.”

Nell was fully aware of what made it hurt so much, even if she refrained from expressing it in words. She had cherished her own private fantasies regarding the initial occasion when a person might pose that momentous query to her. Furthermore, within those fantasies, the moment had invariably been immensely romantic and lovely: while the “some one” was required to be exceedingly handsome, dark-eyed, distinguished in appearance, and articulate, regardless of whether he turned out to be Prince Charming, destined to be overjoyed by a “yes,” or a suitor who had to receive a sorrowful, exquisitely phrased, yet firm rejection. In the case of the second option, the rejection was meant to be conveyed with such finesse that it would closely resemble an acceptance, whereupon he would depart, having kissed her hand, guaranteeing her his unchangeable, lifelong allegiance. Additionally, the event was bound to remain a lovely recollection, serving as a source of pride while carrying a slight tinge of sadness, too.

And at present, this exciting event had proven to be nothing more than ridiculous. Barney Pullen had coaxed his sister into making the offer on his behalf since he had been granted the upper farm by his father; and provided that Nell did not desire to “have him”, he could take Nettie Scobie instead. There was romanticism for you, indeed! Nell gave a laugh—and subsequently a sigh. The freshness had been wiped away from a single youthful fantasy. Was this distressing sequence destined to continue till all things turned ordinary and dull?

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: The initial term at Wexcombe had passed rapidly, and the second went by just as fast—“actually whizzed away,” Cressida remarked. Every aspect of it brought complete enjoyment to Nell—the invigorating competition in class, the formation and strengthening of fresh, beneficial bonds, the cheerful, small-scale social gatherings, the activities of the several clubs to which she belonged, and the broadening of her outlook and pursuits. Her studies were pursued diligently because she was resolved to secure the Thorburn Scholarship in English. Obtaining this award signified that her return to Wexcombe for the following year would not require dipping into Thirza’s modest savings—an outcome Nell was steadfastly set against permitting.

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: Hugh was likewise pursuing a scholarship with all his might, yet he discovered abundant leisure to drop by Thirty-eight, St. John’s quite often. Nearly every college function saw him serving as Nell’s escort, and she was aware that gossip in Wexcombe joined their names together. This enraged Nell, but she was powerless; throwing off an old friend such as Hugh was impossible, particularly since he had abruptly become prudent and cautious, as was necessary given the perilous closeness of several Wexcombe youths who would eagerly have filled his spot beside the slim, red-haired coed, whose gray eyes possessed the allure of evening stars. Nell never drew the throng of eager sufferers that accompanied Cressida’s triumphant progress during her Freshman year; nevertheless, a lanky, intelligent Freshie, a cheerful, small, plump Sophomore, and a tall, scholarly Junior all enjoyed visiting Thirty-eight, St. John’s to discuss ’ologies and ’isms, along with merrier topics, with Nell inside the cushioned parlor of that residence. Hugh harbored no affection for any of these rivals, and he exercised extreme caution not to grant any of them an upper hand over him through an ill-timed exhibition of his genuine emotions toward Nell. In her eyes, he had transformed back into the boy-companion from Brierley times, and in that role he could maintain his position against any infatuated suitor who had thus far joined the competition against him. Nell candidly admitted to herself that no one made a more pleasant associate than Hugh; she felt very pleased, as she informed herself, that he had clearly abandoned all foolish notions—even if she devoted a good deal of time to privately pondering the reason.

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: Just a single unpleasant event ruined that winter. Sitting completely straight on the cushion Miss Ada cherished most, Wilfred Mott queried Nell one evening whether she would give her word “to become Mrs. Wilfred Mott some day.” Following Barney Pullen’ proxy attempt, this failed to startle Nell’s romantic feelings as severely as it might have under different circumstances; nevertheless, it undoubtedly served as another agonizing disappointment. She felt furious as well, believing she had refrained from offering Wilfred any reason to think such an outcome might occur. Yet what else could be anticipated from a Mott, as Mrs. Agatha Sowerby was accustomed to inquire with contempt? Everything about Wilfred’s posture, pitch, demeanor, and language absolutely dripped with Sloanishness. “He was conferring a great honor—no doubt whatever about that. Furthermore, when Nell, entirely unappreciative of the honor, declined his proposal, handling it with as much tact and thoughtfulness as possible—since even a Mott possessed emotions that shouldn't be excessively hurt—Sloanishness revealed itself even more clearly. Wilfred definitely failed to accept his rejection in the manner of Nell’s fictional refused suitors. On the contrary, he grew enraged, and made his feelings obvious; he uttered a couple or three distinctly spiteful remarks; Nell’s own anger flared rebelliously, prompting her to strike back with a sharp, brief reply whose edge penetrated through even Wilfred’s defensive Sloanishness to hit a sensitive spot; he snatched his hat and stormed out of the residence displaying a bright red face; Nell hurried to the upper floor, tripping two times over Miss Ada’s cushions as she went, and dropped onto her bed, weeping from embarrassment and anger. Could she really have lowered herself to argue with a Mott? Was it conceivable that anything uttered by Wilfred Mott possessed the capability to infuriate her? Oh, this represented true humiliation—worse by far than competing against Nettie Scobie!

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “I wish I would never have to lay eyes on the dreadful beast again,” she wept maliciously against her pillows.

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: She was unable to prevent encountering him once more, yet the deeply offended Wilfred made sure that such meetings did not occur at a very short distance. From that point on, Miss Ada’s cushions were protected from his raids, and whenever he passed Nell in the street, or within the hallways of Wexcombe, he offered a bow that was cold in the highest degree. For almost a year, the connection between these two former classmates remained so tense! Subsequently, Wilfred shifted his shattered devotion to a small, plump, pink-cheeked, snub-nosed, blue-eyed Sophomore who valued his feelings properly, after which he pardoned Nell and stooped to being polite to her once more; he did so with a condescending demeanor designed to demonstrate to her precisely what she had forfeited.

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: A single day, Nell rushed with excitement into the room belonging to Honora.

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “Peruse this,” she exclaimed, throwing a letter to Honora. “It is from Mabel—and her arrival at Wexcombe takes place next year—and how does her proposal strike you? My opinion is that it is absolutely marvelous, provided we are able to execute it. Is it your belief that we are capable of it, Nonie?”

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “When I discover what it is, I will be in a better position to inform you,” stated Honora, putting down a Greek lexicon and picking up the missive from Mabel. Mabel Colby was among their friends at Regent’s Academy and had served as a schoolteacher continually from that time onward.

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “However, Nell dear, I intend to abandon it,” she communicated, “and attend college the coming year. Since I completed the third year at Regent’s, I am eligible to join the Sophomore class. I am weary of instructing in an isolated rural school. At some point, I will compose a paper concerning ‘The Trials of a Country Schoolmarm.’ A agonizing piece of realism is what it will be. People generally seem to believe that our existence is effortless and that our sole responsibility is to collect our quarterly earnings. The reality regarding us will be revealed in my paper. Really, should seven days go by without somebody informing me that my labor is light and my wage is high, I would decide I ought to request my ascension garment ‘immediately and to onct.’ ‘Well, your pay comes easily,’ a certain tax-payer will remark to me patronizingly. ‘Your sole task is sitting there and listening to recitations.’ Initially, I was accustomed to debating the point, yet I possess more wisdom today. Facts are unyielding entities, though as an individual cleverly remarked, they are far less unyielding than misconceptions. Consequently, I merely offer a haughty smile nowadays in meaningful quiet. Really, nine grades exist within my schoolhouse, forcing me to instruct on a bit of every subject, ranging from examining the internal anatomy of earthworms to analyzing the solar system. Four years old is my youngest scholar—whose mother dispatches him to class in order to ‘get him out of the way’—while my eldest is twenty—having been ‘suddenly struck’ by the notion that attending school and gaining a learning would prove less difficult than continuing behind the plough. During the frantic attempt to pack every variety of study into a daily six hours, I would not be surprised if the youngsters experience what the young lad did upon being taken to view the biograph. ‘Before I understand what passed previously, I must watch for what approaches next,’ he voiced his grievance. That is precisely how I feel.”

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “And the mail I receive, Nell! The mother of Tommy writes to me that Tommy does not make progress in arithmetic as quickly as she desires. He remains merely in simple reduction, whereas Johnny Johnson has reached fractions, and Johnny possesses not even half the intelligence of her Tommy, so she finds it incomprehensible. Furthermore, the father of Susy desires to learn why Susy is unable to compose a letter without incorrectly spelling half of the words, and the aunt of Rufus wishes for me to move his seat, since the wicked Brown boy beside whom he sits is instructing him in speaking naughty words.

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “Regarding the monetary aspect—however, I shall not start with that. The gods first transform into country schoolmarms those whom they desire to ruin!

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “Having let out that complaint, I now feel relieved. When all is said and done, these previous two years have been enjoyable for me. Even so, Wexcombe is where I am heading.

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “And now, Nell, I have a small scheme. You are aware of how much I hate boarding. Having boarded for four years, I am utterly sick of it. I am not in the mood to put up with another three years of it.

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “Now, why can’t you and Honora and I pool our resources, lease a small home in Portmaris, and manage our own meals? It would cost less than any alternative. Naturally, a housekeeper would be necessary, and I already have someone suitable. You’ve heard me talk about Aunt Euphemia? She is the most wonderful aunt in existence, regardless of her name. That wasn't her fault! Her name became Jamesina since James, her father, perished in a drowning accident at sea one month prior to her birth. My usual name for her is Aunt Phemie. Well, her single daughter just got married and departed for the foreign mission field. Left by herself in a huge residence, Aunt Euphemia experiences terrible loneliness. She will relocate to Portmaris to manage our home if we desire it, and I am certain you will both adore her. This scheme appeals to me increasingly as I ponder it. We could enjoy such pleasant, autonomous days.

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “Now, provided you and Honora are in agreement, wouldn't it make sense for you, being right here, to search the area and attempt to locate an appropriate residence during this spring season? Doing so would prove superior to waiting until autumn. It would be even more advantageous if you were able to secure a place that is furnished, but should that fail, we can manage to gather some pieces of furniture amongst ourselves and long-time family friends who have attics. In any case, make a decision at your earliest convenience and send me a letter, which will allow Aunt Euphemia to determine her arrangements for the coming year.”

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “I believe that is a wise plan,” Honora remarked.

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “I feel the same way,” Nell concurred with enthusiasm. “Naturally, our lodging here is pleasant, but no matter how you look at it, a place like this cannot replace a home. Therefore, we should start searching for a house right away, prior to the arrival of examinations.”

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “I am concerned that finding an truly appropriate home will prove difficult,” cautioned Honora. “Do not hold high hopes, Nell. Pleasant dwellings in pleasant neighborhoods are bound to exceed our budget. It is probable that we must settle for a worn small residence along a road inhabited by folks whose acquaintance brings obscurity, and let our interior living make up for the exterior.”

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: Consequently, house-hunting became their pursuit, yet discovering precisely what suited them turned out to be more difficult than Honora had anticipated. A abundance of dwellings existed, both with furniture and without; nevertheless, a particular one was excessively large, whereas another was excessively small; a certain one cost too much, while another was located at too great a distance from Wexcombe. Examinations occurred and concluded; the final week of the term arrived and yet their “house o’dreams,” to use Nell’s phrase, continued to be a castle in the air.

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “I guess we will be forced to yield and delay until autumn,” Honora stated exhausted, while they strolled about the park during a most lovely April day filled with wind and azure, at a time when the harbor churned white and glinted below the pearly fogs drifting above it. “Perhaps we will locate a hovel to house us at that time; and should we fail, we will forever possess boardinghouses.”

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “At any rate, I won’t fret over that at the present moment and ruin such a wonderful afternoon,” Nell declared, looking about herself joyfully. Pine balsam gave a subtle scent to the brisk, cold atmosphere, while an immense upside-down bowl of favor—the sky overhead—was entirely clear and blue. “My blood is filled with the song of spring today, and April’s call can be felt throughout the air. Nonie, I am experiencing visions and indulging in dreams. The westerly origin of the wind accounts for that. The west wind is something I truly adore. Doesn't it chant about joy and hope? Whenever an easterly breeze blows, my thoughts invariably turn to doleful waves washing a slate-colored coastline and mournful rain falling on the roof eaves. Should the wind come from the east once I grow elderly, I am going to suffer from rheumatism.”

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “And isn’t it wonderful when you shed furs and heavy winter clothes for the first time and step out, like this, in spring clothes?” asked a laughing Honora. “Don’t you feel as though you have been transformed into someone brand new?”

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “Spring makes all things new,” remarked Nell. “Furthermore, springs themselves are constantly so fresh. Not a single spring ever mirrors another spring precisely. Each one possesses a unique quality that creates its own distinctive charm. Look at the grass’s deep green color encircling that small pond, and observe the willow buds opening up.”

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “And tests are finished and past—the period of Convocation approaches shortly—on coming Wednesday. Seven days from now we shall be back home.”

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “I’m glad,” Nell said dreamily. “So many things exist that I want to do. Sitting on the steps of the back porch and feeling the wind blow down across the fields of Mr. Pettifer is something I want. Hunting ferns within the Whispering Wood and gathering violets inside Primrose Dell are things I want. Honora, do you remember the day when we had our golden picnic? Hearing the singing of the frogs and the whispering of the poplars is what I want. However, I have also learned to love Portmaris, and returning next fall makes me glad. Had I not won the Thorburn, I do not believe I could have. Taking any part of the little hoard belonging to Thirza is something I couldn’t do.”

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “If we were just able to discover a home!” Honora uttered with a sigh. “Direct your gaze over to Portmaris, Nell—there are houses all around, yet none available for us.”

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “Cease, Nonie. ‘The best is yet to be.’ In the manner of the ancient Roman, we will discover a home or construct one. On an occasion such as this, fail is not a word present in my luminous lexicon.”

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: Remaining in the park until the sun went down, they existed within the astonishing miracle, glory, and wonder of the spring season; and, taking their customary route back by way of Linden Avenue, they traveled so that they could experience the joy of viewing Tabby’s Place.

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “I have a sensation like a strange occurrence is about to take place immediately—‘by the pricking of my thumbs,’” Nell remarked while they climbed the incline. “It is a pleasant, tale-like sensation. Oh—oh—oh! Honora Hollis, glance in that direction and inform me whether it is real, or if I am imagining it?”

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: Honora directed her gaze to the spot. The thumbs and eyes of Nell had spoken the truth. Above the arched entrance to Tabby’s Place, a modest, small sign hung loosely. The words read, “To Let, Furnished. Inquire Within.”

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “Honora,” Nell murmured softly, “is there any chance, do you think, that Tabby’s Place could be rented by us?”

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “No, I don’t,” Honora stated. “That would be far too good to be real. Modern life doesn't feature fairy tales. Nell, I refuse to hope. Facing the disappointment would be utterly unbearable. Their asking price is bound to exceed our budget. Keep in mind its location on Linden Avenue.”

chapter_title: Chapter IX An Unwelcome Lover and a Welcome Friend
text: “Anyhow, we have to discover it,” Nell stated with determination. “Calling tonight is out of the question because it is too late, but our visit will be tomorrow. Oh, Nonie, if acquiring this lovely location is possible! Ever since my initial sight of Tabby’s Place, I’ve constantly had the feeling that my destiny was connected to it.”

The following evening, they were walking with determination along the herringbone path that crossed the small garden. The April wind was causing the pines to sing their song, while the grove teemed with robins—large, fat, bold creatures, swaggering on the walkways. The girls pressed the doorbell with some hesitation, and a stern, elderly maid let them in. Entering through the door brought them straight into a spacious living room, in which two additional ladies, both equally stern and elderly, were seated beside a bright, small fire. Aside from the fact that one appeared to be roughly seventy and the other fifty, there appeared to be small variation between the two. Both possessed remarkably large, pale-blue eyes behind steel-framed glasses; both were wearing a cap and a gray shawl; both were knitting continuously at an unhurried pace; both were rocking calmly and eyeing the girls in silence; and positioned directly behind both was a big white china dog, covered in circular green spots, with a green nose and green ears. Those dogs instantly caught Nell’s imagination; to her, they appeared to be the dual protective spirits of Tabby’s Place.

Silence reigned among everyone for a brief period. Speech eluded the girls because of their anxiety, while the old ladies and the china dogs appeared equally uncommunicative. Nell looked around at her surroundings. How charming the place was! From it, a second door led straight to the pine grove, where robins fearlessly approached the actual step. Scattered across the floor were circular braided rugs, identical to those Thirza constructed at Grey Shutters, though such items were deemed obsolete anywhere else, Brierley included. Nevertheless, they were present right here on Linden Avenue! Positioned in a corner, a large, gleaming grandfather’s clock made loud, solemn ticking sounds. Above the mantelpiece sat charming small cupboards, their glass doors revealing shiny, curious pieces of china. Old prints together with silhouettes adorned the walls. The staircase ascended in a corner, featuring a wide window paired with an attractive seat at its initial low landing. Everything corresponded precisely to what Nell was certain it would be.
At this point the quiet had become exceedingly unbearable, so Honora gave Nell a nudge to signify that she ought to talk.
“By your notice, we—we—observed that this dwelling is available for rent,” Nell uttered weakly to the senior woman, who clearly was Miss Tabby Linden.
“Oh, yes,” Miss Tabby stated. “It was my intention to remove that sign today.”
“Then—in that case we are late,” Nell said mournfully. “Has it been let to another person?”
“No, but we have made a decision that it will not be let under any circumstances.”
“Oh, I’m so sorry,” Nell blurted out spontaneously. “I love this place so much. I really hoped we might have secured it.”

At that moment, Miss Tabby set her knitting aside, removed her spectacles, wiped them clean, placed them back on, and peered at Nell as a fellow person for the very first time. The second woman mirrored her actions with such exactness that she could easily have passed for an image in a looking glass.

“You love it,” Miss Tabby stated forcefully. “Does that signify that your affection for it is genuine? Or does it simply imply that its appearance pleases you? Young women these days make such extravagant assertions that a person can never determine what they actually intend to say. Things were different when I was young. Back then, a girl would not declare her love for turnips using the exact same tone she could have employed to declare her love for her mother or her Savior.”
Her conscience gave Nell strength.

“I truly do adore it,” she spoke softly. “Ever since I spotted it previous autumn, I have adored it. Next year, my two college buddies and I wish to manage a home rather than live in a boarding house, which is why we are searching for a small property to lease; and I felt so joyful upon seeing that this residence was available to rent.”

“You are welcome to take it, provided you love it,” Miss Tabby stated. “Maria and I made up our minds today against renting it after all, since none of the individuals who desired it appealed to us. Renting it is not something we are forced to do. Our trip to Europe remains affordable for us even without leasing it. Although it would assist us financially, no amount of money could convince me to surrender my home to the kinds of people who have visited and viewed it. Your case is not the same. It is my belief that you truly love it and will treat it well. It is yours to have.”
“If—if we are able to pay the price you demand,” Nell faltered.
The necessary sum was stated by Miss Tabby. A mutual look was exchanged between Nell and Honora. A shake of her head came from Honora.
“I fear we are unable to pay that high a price,” Nell remarked, suppressing her letdown. “You see, we happen to be merely college girls, and our funds are limited.”
“How much did you imagine you were able to pay?” asked Miss Tabby, without pausing in her knitting.
Nell stated how much she wanted. Miss Tabby gave a serious nod.

“That will suffice. As I previously mentioned to you, renting it out is not absolutely required for us. Though we lack wealth, our means are sufficient for a trip to Europe. I myself have never set foot in Europe, nor did I ever anticipate or desire such a journey. However, my niece over there, Maria Linden, has developed a desire to travel there. Surely you understand that a youth such as Maria is unable to travel the world by herself.”
“No—I—I suppose not,” muttered Nell, observing that Miss Tabby was completely and seriously sincere.

“Certainly not. Therefore, I must accompany her to take care of her. I anticipate liking it as well; my age is seventy years, yet I am not weary of life so far. It is likely I would have traveled to Europe earlier had I thought of it. Our absence will last for two years, maybe three. Our departure by ship is in June, at which time we will mail you the key and arrange everything so you can move in whenever you decide. A few items that we value particularly will be packed up by us, but everything else is going to remain.”
“Are you going to leave the china dogs behind?” Nell inquired with hesitation.
“Do you want me to?”
“Oh, truly, yes. They are charming.”
Miss Tabby’s face took on a satisfied look.

“Those dogs mean a lot to me,” she boasted. “Their age exceeds one hundred years, and their positions on both flanks of this hearth have remained unchanged from the time my brother Aaron fetched them from London half a century back. My brother Aaron was the namesake for Linden Avenue.”
“He was a fine man,” Miss Maria stated, offering her initial remark. “Ah, his equal cannot be found these days.”
“Maria, to you he was a good uncle,” Miss Tabby said, showing clear emotion. “Remembering him is the right thing for you to do.”

“I will never forget him,” Miss Maria remarked with gravity. “In my mind's eye, I see him right now, positioned in front of the hearth with his hands tucked beneath his coat-tails, smiling warmly at us.”
Miss Maria produced her handkerchief to dry her eyes, yet Miss Tabby returned with determination from sentimental matters to those of a practical nature.

“Provided you pledge to take great care of the dogs, I am going to leave them in their current spots,” she stated. “They are named Gog and Magog. Gog’s gaze goes toward the right, whereas Magog’s goes toward the left. Furthermore, I have a final query. It isn't a problem for you, I trust, if this house goes by the name of Tabby’s Place?”
“No, truly. It seems to us that this represents one of its most delightful aspects.”

“I observe that you possess good sense,” Miss Tabby remarked with an air of deep gratification. “Can you imagine? Every single person who arrived to lease this residence inquired whether removing the gate’s name while they resided here was permissible. I informed them firmly that the property and its name were inseparable. From the moment my brother Aaron bequeathed this property to me, it has been known as Tabby’s Place, and Tabby’s Place it will continue to be called until my death and Maria’s death. Once those occur, whoever inherits it next is free to give it whatever absurd title pleases him,” Miss Tabby finished, in a manner quite similar to saying, “After that—the deluge.” “Now, prior to treating our agreement as finalized, would you care to tour the residence and inspect everything?”

Continued searching brought the girls even more joy. A kitchen and a little bedroom were located on the lower floor, in addition to the spacious living-room. Three bedrooms were situated on the upper floor, consisting of one big room and two little ones. A particular small room, which looked out toward the massive pines, captivated Nell, and she wished for it to belong to her. Its walls were covered in light blue wallpaper, and it contained a tiny, vintage vanity table equipped with candle sconces. A window with diamond-shaped panes featured a bench beneath its light blue muslin drapes, offering an ideal place to study or daydream.
“Everything is so wonderful that I am certain we will awaken to discover it was merely a passing dream,” Honora stated while they departed.
“Miss Tabby and Miss Maria do not seem like the material that dreams are created from,” Nell chuckled. “Could you imagine them traveling around the world—particularly wearing those caps and shawls?”

“I imagine that once they start moving at a genuine trot, they will set them down,” remarked Honora, “yet I am certain that they will carry their knitting wherever they go. It would be impossible for them to leave it behind. I am convinced they will wander around Westminster Abbey while continuing to knit. In the time between, Nell, we will reside in Tabby’s Place—as well as on Linden Avenue. Already, I feel as if I were a millionairess.”
“I feel as though I am a morning star singing with delight,” Nell declared.
Cressy Lindsay tiptoed into Thirty-eight, St. John’s, during that night and threw herself onto the bed belonging to Nell.

“My darlings, I am utterly exhausted. My situation brings to mind the person who lacked a homeland—or perhaps he lacked a shadow? I cannot recall which one. At any rate, my time has been spent packing.”
“And I assume your exhaustion comes from being unable to choose what to pack first, or deciding where to place them,” Honora laughed.

“Precisely. Furthermore, once I had managed to stuff all my belongings inside, and both my landlady and her maid sat atop it as I secured the lock, I realized that numerous items needed for Convocation were stowed at the absolute bottom. Unlocking the ancient trunk became necessary, requiring an hour of rummaging and probing to retrieve the desired objects. I would grasp an item that seemed to be the right one, pull it out, and find it was a different article entirely. Indeed, Nell, I refrained from swearing.”
“I never claimed that you had done so.”

“Indeed, your appearance reflected it. Yet I confess that my own reflections bordered on the blasphemous. Furthermore, my head cold is so severe that my actions are limited entirely to sniffling, sighing, and sneezing. Does that not strike you as alliterative torment? Queen Nell, I beg you to utter something that might raise my spirits.”
“Bear in mind that on the coming Thursday evening, you will return to the realm of Hector and Orlando,” Nell proposed.
Cressy gave a sorrowful shake of her head.

“Further use of alliteration. No, Hector and Orlando are not what I desire when my head is stuffed with a cold. However, what has occurred with the pair of you? Now that my gaze is fixed upon you attentively, you appear entirely illuminated by an inner radiance. Why, you are literally glowing! What is going on?”

“In the coming winter, we will be residing at Tabby’s Place,” Nell declared with a triumphant air. “Take note, we will actually live there rather than board! It has been rented by us, with Mabel Colby joining our household and her aunt taking on the housekeeping duties for us.”
Jumping up, Cressy dried her nose, after which she dropped to her knees in front of Nell.

“Girls—girls—allow me to accompany you, too. Oh, my behavior will be so wonderful. Should you lack space for me, my bed will be the small kennel situated in the orchard—I have observed it. Just permit me to join.”
“Rise, you goose.”
“I will not rise from my knees until you assure me that I may reside with you during the coming winter.”

Nell exchanged a glance with Honora. After that, Nell spoke deliberately, “We would be delighted to host you, Cressy dear. However, it is best to be honest with one another. My means are limited—Nonie lacks money too—and Mabel Colby has little wealth—consequently, our home management must be extremely modest and our food unpretentious. Your lifestyle would need to match ours. As it stands, you possess fortune, and your boardinghouse meals prove it.”

“Oh, why should that matter to me?” asked Cressy dramatically. “It is far superior to share a simple meal of herbs alongside your friends than to eat a fattened ox in an isolated boardinghouse. Do not assume that I care only for my belly, girls. I would happily survive on mere bread and water—accompanied by just a tiny bit of jam—provided you allow me to join you.”
“And after that,” Nell went on, “a lot of labor will need to be accomplished. The aunt of Mabel is unable to handle everything. Each of us anticipates having tasks to perform. As for you—”

“Neither do I spin, nor do I toil,” Cressida concluded. “However, I will get the hang of tasks. Demonstrating them to me a single time will be sufficient. Starting off, making my own bed is within my ability. Moreover, keep in mind that even if cooking is beyond me, holding my temper is not. That counts for something. Furthermore, complaining about the weather is something I never do. That counts for even more. Oh, I beg you, I beg you! My desire for anything has never been this strong in all my days—and how terribly hard this floor feels.”

“There is only one additional matter,” stated Honora with determination. “As the whole of Wexcombe is aware, you, Cressy, receive visitors nearly every night. However, at Tabby’s Place that will not be permitted for us. It has been settled that Friday nights are the sole times we will receive our acquaintances. Should you join us, you must conform to that regulation.”

“Well, you surely don't imagine I'll object to that, do you? Why, it pleases me. I was aware that I ought to have established a similar regulation on my own, but I lacked sufficient resolve to create it or adhere to it. Being able to shift this burden onto your shoulders will provide genuine comfort.
