Should you refuse to allow me to share your fate, the sorrow will kill me, and subsequently I shall return to disturb you. I shall make my home right upon the threshold of Tabby’s Place, making it impossible for you to enter or leave without tripping across my ghost.”
Once more, expressive glances passed between Nell and Honora.

“Well,” Nell remarked, “naturally, our ability to bring you along depends on speaking with Mabel first; nevertheless, I doubt she will have any objections, and speaking for ourselves, you are free to join us with a warm reception.”
“If you grow weary of our humble existence you are free to depart from us, without being questioned,” Honora appended.
Cressy leapt to her feet, gave a joyful hug to the pair, and continued on her path with delight.
“I wish that everything turns out well,” Honora remarked with gravity.
“We have to force them to head right,” declared Nell. “It seems to me that Cressy is going to suit our ’appy little ’ome extremely well.”

“Oh, Cressy is wonderful to hang out with and be good friends. And, naturally, having more people in our group will lighten the burden on our small budgets. However, what will it be like sharing a home with her? A person must be experienced through summer and winter before you can determine whether she is agreeable to live with or not.”

“Oh, well, every one of us will be put to the test, for that matter. And we need to conduct ourselves like reasonable people, living and letting live. Cressy is not selfish, even if she is somewhat thoughtless, and I think that all of us will get along wonderfully in Tabby’s Place.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: Nell had returned to Brierley, bearing the prestige of the Thorburn Scholarship upon her forehead. She was informed by locals that she was largely unaltered, spoken with an inflection implying astonishment and mild chagrin that she remained the same. Brierley itself had likewise undergone no transformation. Such was her initial impression, at any rate. Yet, as Nell occupied the Grey Shutters pew during the initial Sunday following her arrival and surveyed the gathered people, she noticed various small alterations that, striking her simultaneously, forced her to understand that time was not entirely frozen, even within Brierley. The pulpit was occupied by a different minister. Within the pews, several accustomed faces had vanished permanently. Aged “Uncle Zeb,” whose predictions were now ended, Mrs. Peter Mott, who had uttered her final sigh, one hoped, Timothy Cotton, who, according to Mrs. Agatha Sowerby “had actually managed to die at last after practicing at it for twenty years,” alongside aged Josiah Mott, unrecognizable to everyone in his casket owing to his neatly groomed whiskers, were all buried in the small churchyard behind the building. Furthermore, Barney Pullen had taken Nettie Scobie as his wife! Their “appearing out” occurred that very Sunday. As Barney, glowing with satisfaction and joy, escorted his bride, dressed in feathers and silk, into the Gorham Pullen pew, Nell lowered her eyes to conceal her amused gaze. Her memory returned to the tempestuous winter evening during the Christmas vacation when Odette had made the marriage proposal on Barney’s behalf. His heart had clearly not been shattered by that refusal. Nell questioned whether Odette had likewise proposed to Nettie on his behalf, or whether he had summoned sufficient courage to pose the decisive question on his own. Every member of the Pullen family appeared to participate in his satisfaction and joy, extending from Mrs. Gorham seated in the pew to Odette singing in the choir. Odette had surrendered her position at the Brierley school and planned to travel West during the autumn.

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Is unable to secure a suitor in Brierley, that is the reason,” stated Mrs. Agatha Sowerby with disdain. “Claims she believes her wellbeing will improve out West. It was never my understanding that her wellbeing was frail previously.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “A sweet girl, Odette,” Nell had faithfully remarked. “Unlike certain others, she did not ever seek to draw eyes to herself.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Oh, if you are asking whether she pursued the boys, she certainly did not,” Mrs. Agatha remarked. “However, she harbored a desire to get married, precisely like anyone else, and that is the truth. What other reason could drive her to the West to a deserted spot that possesses no merit except a high population of men and a shortage of women? Do not attempt to convince me otherwise!”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: However, it was not toward Odette that Nell looked with distress and astonishment on that occasion. Instead, her eyes were fixed on Opal Pettigrew, who was seated next to her among the singers. What could have occurred to Opal? Although she had grown still more beautiful, her blue eyes shone with an overly vivid radiance, and her cheeks bore a feverishly intense flush; furthermore, she had become extremely slender, and the hands gripping her hymnal appeared nearly see-through in their fragility.

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Has Opal Pettigrew taken sick?” inquired Nell to Mrs. Sowerby while the pair returned from the chapel.

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Opal Pettigrew is dying of galloping consumption,” Mrs. Sowerby stated without preamble. “All the townspeople are aware of it, apart from her and her own kin. They refuse to admit it. According to them, her health is completely fine. Ever since her bout of congestion during the winter, she has been unable to instruct her classes, yet she claims she will resume teaching come autumn, and she is trying to secure the position at Pale Sands school. By the time the Pale Sands school term begins, that unfortunate girl will be lying in her grave, mark my words.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: Nell stood frozen in mute astonishment upon hearing the news. Was it really true that her former classmate, Opal Pettigrew, was on her deathbed? Though time had weakened their connection in recent years, the former bond of childhood friendship remained, striking Nell with a sudden, poignant ache. How could someone as radiant, lively, and teasing as Opal be linked to the grim reality of dying? Just after the church service, she had warmly and cheerfully welcomed Nell, insisting that she visit her the following night.

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “I will not be here Tuesday or Wednesday nights,” she had uttered in triumph. “A concert is taking place in Delford, followed by a gathering at Pale Sands. Herb Tranter is escorting me. He is my newest flame. Do not fail to visit me tomorrow. I am eager to have a proper conversation with you. I wish to know everything regarding your activities in Wexcombe.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: Nell was aware that Opal intended to inform Nell completely regarding her personal recent flirtations, yet she agreed to attend, and Isolde volunteered to accompany her.

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “For a long time I’ve been wishing to visit Opal,” she remarked to Nell, as they departed Grey Shutters the following evening, “yet I truly was unable to go by myself. Listening to Opal talk endlessly in that way of hers is so terrible, and her acting like she isn’t ill, even though coughing makes it nearly impossible for her to talk. She is striving so desperately to survive, and still, people claim she stands no possibility whatsoever.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: In silence, the girls journeyed along the red road at twilight. High up in the crowns of the trees, robins sang their evening prayers, pouring their joyous songs into the golden air. From the ponds and marshes, the silver piping of frogs drifted across the fields, where underground seeds started to awaken and react to the rain and sunlight that had passed above. A wild, sweet, and healthy scent wafted from patches of young raspberries, perfoming the air. Above quiet hollows, white fogs drifted, while blue-glowing violet stars illuminated the land around the brook.

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “What a lovely sunset,” Isolde remarked. “Look, Nell, it resembles a country all on its own, doesn’t it? That extended, low strip of purple cloud represents the coastline, and the bright sky beyond it is akin to a golden sea.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “How wonderful it would be if we could journey there aboard the moonshine boat that Cedric mentioned in his former essay—do you recall it?” asked Nell, awakening from her musings. “Isolde, do you suppose all our yesterdays might be discovered in that place—every one of our former springs and blooms? Could the floral beds Cedric witnessed over there be the very roses that blossomed for us in days gone by?”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Stop!” Isolde said. “You cause me to feel as though we are elderly women with all of life already past.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Ever since I learned about poor Opal, I’ve felt nearly as though we were,” Nell said. “Any other mournful event could also be real if her impending death is indeed true.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Is it all right if we stop by Elisha Duckett’s briefly?” Isolde inquired. “I was requested by Mother to drop off this small bowl of jelly for Aunt Drusilla.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Which person is Aunt Drusilla?”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Ah, is this news to you? She is Tullyvale’s Mrs. Samson Coates, who happens to be Mrs. Elisha Duckett’s aunt. Furthermore, she is also my father’s aunt. Following the death of her husband this past winter, which left her in great poverty and solitude, the Ducketts welcomed her into their home. Although mother believed it was our duty to house her, father firmly refused. Under no circumstances would he reside alongside Aunt Drusilla.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Is she that awful?” Nell asked distractedly.

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “It is likely you will observe her true nature prior to our departure,” Isolde remarked meaningfully. “According to Father, her face resembles a hatchet that slices through the air. Nevertheless, her tongue possesses an even greater sharpness.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: Even though it was late, Aunt Drusilla sat in the Duckett kitchen cutting potato sets. Wearing a washed-out old wrapper, she had hair that was gray and unmistakably messy. Because Aunt Drusilla disliked being “caught in a kilter,” she made a special effort to be unpleasant.

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Oh, so you’re Nell Harcourt?” she remarked, as Isolde presented Nell to her. “I’ve heard of you.” Her manner suggested that what she had heard was far from favorable. “Mrs. Pullen mentioned to me that you were back. She noted that you had gotten much better.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: It was beyond question that Aunt Drusilla believed there remained ample space for additional refinement. Without pause, she continued to sever acquaintanceships with great vigor.

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Would there be any point in inviting you to take a seat?” she asked with sarcasm. “Naturally, you won't find much to amuse you here. Everyone else has gone out.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “You were sent this small jar of rhubarb jelly by Mother,” Isolde remarked in an agreeable manner. “Having prepared it today, she believed you could enjoy a bit.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Oh, thank you,” Aunt Drusilla remarked with bitterness. “Your mother’s jelly has never appealed to me, as her recipe is always overly sweet. All the same, I shall attempt to force a little of it down. This spring, my eating has been terribly poor. My health is quite poor,” Aunt Drusilla added with gravity, “yet I carry on regardless. This world has no place for those who are unable to labor. Should it not prove overly burdensome, would you deign to place the jelly inside the pantry? Finishing these potatoes this evening is an urgent matter for me. I imagine that a pair of ladies such as yourselves would never engage in such tasks. The risk of ruining your hands would surely terrify you.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Prior to us renting the farm, I would slice potato sets,” Nell stated with a smile.

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “I still do that,” Isolde said with a laugh. “Last week, I skipped sets three days. Naturally,” she remarked in a teasing manner, “I put lemon juice and kid gloves on my hands every night following it.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: Aunt Drusilla let out a sniff.

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “My guess is that you derived that idea from one of those foolish periodicals you spend so much time reading. It surprises me that your mother permits it. However, you were always indulged by her. At the time Laurence wed her, every one of us believed she would prove to be an inappropriate spouse for him.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: Aunt Drusilla let out a deep sigh, as though every ominous prediction regarding Laurence Pembroke’s wedding had come to pass completely and gloomily.

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Are you leaving?” she asked when the girls got up. “Well, talking to an old woman such as myself probably doesn't offer you much entertainment, I reckon. It is a shame that the boys are not at home.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “We desire to pop inside and visit with Opal Pettigrew for a short time,” Isolde clarified.

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Oh, naturally, any reason will suffice,” Aunt Drusilla remarked pleasantly. “Merely darting inside and darting back out prior to having a moment to offer a proper greeting. I reckon it is college pretentiousness. Staying clear of Opal Pettigrew would be more prudent for you. According to the doctors, consumption is contagious. I was certain Opal would contract a disease, running around visiting Boston this past autumn. Individuals who lack the contentment to remain at home invariably contract a disease.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Individuals who refrain from making calls contract illnesses as well. On occasion, they even perish,” Isolde remarked gravely.

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “They cannot hold themselves responsible for it in that case,” Aunt Drusilla answered with a victorious air. “Word has reached me that your wedding will take place in June, Isolde.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “That rumor is completely false,” Isolde said, turning red.

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Well, do not delay it for too long,” Aunt Drusilla remarked meaningfully. “You will lose your looks shortly—you consist entirely of complexion and hair. Furthermore, the Ducketts are exceedingly changeable. A hat should be worn by you, Miss Harcourt. Your nose is becoming scandalously freckled. My, what red hair you have! Ah well, I suppose we are all just as the Lord created us! Pass along my regards to Thirza Abernethy. She has not visited me a single time since I arrived in Brierley, though I imagine I should not protest. The Abernethys constantly believed they were superior to everybody else in these parts.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Oh, isn’t she terrible?” Isolde gasped, while they fled down the lane.

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “She is inferior to Miss Eliza Pullen,” Nell stated. “However, consider spending a lifetime bearing a moniker such as Drusilla! Is there anyone whose disposition it would not embitter? Her effort should have been directed toward conceiving her name to be Lucinda. A vast benefit could have been derived from that. That method assuredly aided me during the time I harbored a dislike for Nell.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Once Flossie Tulk reaches adulthood, she will resemble her completely,” Isolde remarked. “You are aware that Aunt Drusilla and Flossie’s mother are cousins, aren’t you? Ah, me, I am relieved that it has ended. She possesses such malice—a bitter taste seems to be added to everything by her. A remarkably amusing tale concerning her is told by Father. At one point, a clergyman who was exceptionally pious and decent, yet exceedingly hard of hearing, served in Tullyvale. No normal speech could be perceived by him whatsoever. Now, a prayer gathering was customarily held on Sunday nights, during which every member of the congregation in attendance would stand up to offer a prayer one by one, or speak briefly regarding a passage of scripture. On one particular night, however, Aunt Drusilla sprang to her feet. Neither a prayer nor a sermon was delivered by her. Rather, she attacked all the other people in the congregation and subjected them to a terrible tongue-lashing, identifying them explicitly by name, detailing the way every one of them had acted, and bringing back up every single feud and disgrace from the preceding decade. At last, she concluded by declaring that she felt revulsion toward the congregation at Tullyvale, that entering its portal ever again was far from her intentions, and that she trusted a terrible punishment would fall upon it. Exhausted, she then resumed her seat, and the clergyman, who had failed to catch a single statement she uttered, promptly observed, using a most pious tone, ‘amen! May the prayer of our beloved sister be granted by the Lord!’ The tale should be heard as told by Father.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Talking about tales, Isolde,” observed Nell, using a meaningful, secretive voice, “are you aware that recently I have been asking myself whether I might compose a short piece of fiction—a tale that would possess sufficient quality to get into print?”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Why, to be sure you were able to,” Isolde uttered, once she had comprehended the astonishing proposal. “You were accustomed to composing entirely exciting tales a long time back in our former Story Club.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Well, I scarcely intended that sort of tale,” Nell smiled. “I have pondered it somewhat recently, yet I am nearly fearful of attempting it, because, were I to be unsuccessful, the shame would be unbearable.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Honora mentioned to me on one occasion that every initial tale by Mrs. Varley was turned down. Nevertheless, I am certain that yours would avoid such a fate, Nell, since it is probable that modern editors possess greater judgment.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “A story was written last winter by Margaret Burton, a Junior girl at Wexcombe, and Canadian Woman published it. Writing one that is at least as good is something I truly believe I could do.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “And do you intend to publish it within the Canadian Woman?”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “First, I could attempt to send it to a larger magazine. It hinges entirely on the type of story I produce.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “What will the subject be?”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “I am not sure so far. My goal is to secure a strong plot. From the perspective of an editor, I consider this extremely essential. The heroine’s name represents the single element I have determined. Evadne Garth shall be her name. Is it not quite lovely, in your opinion? Keep this secret from everyone, Isolde. Besides you and Mr. Pettifer, I have informed no one else. His reaction lacked encouragement—he claimed that an excess of rubbish was being produced these days already, and that he had anticipated a superior effort from me, following one year of college.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “How can Mr. Pettifer know anything regarding that?” Isolde asked in a contemptuous tone.

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: They discovered that the Pettigrew house was bright with illumination and visitors. From opposite sides of the parlor, Leonard Kimball, coming from Tullyvale, and Varley Bell, hailing from Delford, exchanged fierce looks. A number of cheerful young women had stopped by. Opal wore a white dress, and a strong luster marked both her eyes and her cheeks. She giggled and talked without stopping, and when the remaining girls departed, she escorted Nell to the upper floor so she could show off her recent summer gowns.

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “I still have a blue silk that needs to be made up, though it is rather heavy for the summer months, so I believe I will hold off on it until autumn. As you are aware, I am planning to teach at Pale Sands. What is your opinion of my hat? The one you wore to church yesterday was truly cute, but my preference is for something more vibrant. Have you seen those two foolish boys on the ground floor? Both of them arrived resolved to outstay the other. You know, I do not care even a little about any of them. Herb Tranter is the person I actually favor, and on occasion, I honestly believe he is the one for me. Back at Christmas, I believed the Tullyvale schoolmaster was that man, but I discovered something regarding him that made me lose interest. When I rejected him, he almost lost his mind. I really wish those two boys had stayed away tonight, because I was hoping we could have a wonderful, long conversation, Nell, so I could share so many things with you. The two of us have always been great friends, haven’t we?”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: With a slight, quiet chuckle, Opal encircled Nell’s waist with her arm. Yet their gaze locked for merely an instant, and within the depth of Opal’s shining eyes, Nell perceived a look that grieved her heart.

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Will you come up frequently, Nell?” Opal murmured. “Make sure to come by yourself—I need you.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Is your health completely fine, Opal?”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: “Me! Well, I am completely fine. Never in my entire existence have I felt superior to this. To be sure, I was somewhat weakened by that congestion during the previous winter. However, simply look at my complexion. Surely, I do not appear at all like a sick person.”

chapter_title: Chapter XI The Round of Life
text: With a tone that bordered on harshness, Opal spoke. Resentfully, it seemed, she jerked her arm from Nell and dashed down the stairs, becoming even more exuberant there, seemingly so captivated by teasing her pair of suitors that Nell and Isolde felt somewhat excluded and departed before long.
“What are you daydreaming about, Nell?”

One dusk, the pair of young females was lingering beside a enchanted glen belonging to the stream. Within it, fronds dipped, and tiny blades of turf showed vivid green, while wild pear trees draped sweetly-fragranced, pale drapes about the spot.
With a contented sigh, Nell shook off her daydreaming.
“I was developing my tale in my mind, Isolde.”
“Oh, is it true that you’ve started it?” Isolde exclaimed, instantly glowing with enthusiastic curiosity.

“Yes, I have composed merely a couple of pages, yet the whole thing is mapped out quite thoroughly in my mind. Finding an appropriate plot has been an enormous struggle for me. Every single plot I came up with seemed ill-fitted for a girl called Evadne.”
“Was it not possible for you to have given her a different name?”

“No, it was an impossible thing. Although I attempted to, I was unable to accomplish it, just as I could not alter yours. Evadne possessed such reality for me that regardless of any alternative name I attempted to assign to her, I simply considered her to be Evadne beneath everything. Eventually, however, I obtained a storyline that suited her. After that, the thrill of selecting names for every one of my characters arrived. How captivating that process is, you cannot imagine. For hours I have stayed awake contemplating those names. Perceval Dalrymple is the name of the hero.”

“Are all the characters named by you?” Isolde inquired longing. “I was planning to request that you allow me to give a name to one if you hadn’t—simply an insignificant individual. It would make me feel like I possessed a part of the tale in that case.”
“The small hired lad residing alongside the Lesters can be named by you,” Nell granted. “While his significance is minimal, no one else remains without a name.”

“Name him Raymond Fitzosborne,” Isolde proposed, as she possessed a supply of those names stored in her mind, remnants from the former “Story Club,” an association that she, Nell, Odette Pullen, and Opal Pettigrew had kept during their school years.
With a shake of her head, Nell expressed her doubt.
“I fear such a name possesses too much nobility for a farmhand, Isolde. Could you envision a Fitzosborne tending to swine and gathering kindling?”

If one possessed any imagination whatsoever, Isolde failed to understand why it could not be expanded to such a degree; yet Nell likely possessed superior judgment, and ultimately the chore boy was named Robert Ray, with the option of being referred to as Bobby if the situation demanded it.
“What amount do you think you’ll receive for it?” Isolde inquired.
However, this had not crossed Nell’s mind whatsoever. Her quest was for renown rather than vile money, and financial motives had not yet corrupted her writerly ambitions.
“Won’t you permit me to read it?” begged Isolde.
“Once it is completed, I will share it with you and Mr. Pettifer by reading it aloud, and I will require your rigorous critique. Before its publication, no other person will be permitted to view it.”
“In what manner will you conclude it—with a happy ending or an unhappy one?”

“I am uncertain. Ending it unhappily is my preference, since that would be far more romantic. However, I am aware that editors are prejudiced against tragic conclusions. I once overheard Professor Hamilton remark that writing a sad ending should only be attempted by a genius. And,” Nell added with modesty, “a genius is the last thing I am.”

“Oh, happy endings are my favourite. Allowing him to wed her would be best,” uttered Isolde, who believed that all tales ought to conclude in this manner, particularly after becoming betrothed to Gideon.
“Yet you enjoy weeping when tales are told?”
“Oh, yes, right in the center of them. However, I prefer for all things to end well eventually.”
“There has to be a single touching scene included,” Nell remarked in a reflective manner. “It’s possible I could cause Robert Ray to get hurt in a mishap and incorporate a deathbed scene.”
“No, Bobby must not be killed off,” Isolde declared, with a laugh. “I claim him, so it is my wish for him to stay alive and thrive. If a character must die, let it be another.”

During the following two weeks, Nell suffered or delighted, depending on her frame of mind, in her writing endeavors. At times she became overjoyed by a fantastic notion, and at other times she felt hopeless when a stubborn character refused to conduct themselves correctly. Isolde was unable to comprehend this.
“Force them to act according to your desires,” she said.

“I am unable to,” Nell lamented. “Evadne proves to be a heroine who is so difficult to control. She persists in acting and speaking in ways I did not intend for her. Subsequently, that ruins all the preceding material, forcing me to rewrite the entire thing.”

At last, nevertheless, the tale reached its completion, and Nell recited it to Isolde within the privacy of the porch gable. She had managed to include her “pathetic scene” while keeping Robert Ray alive, and she observed Isolde attentively throughout her reading. Isolde met her expectations by weeping appropriately; yet, as the conclusion arrived, she appeared somewhat dissatisfied.
“What made you murder Marcel Lennox?” she inquired in a tone of blame.
“The villain was who he was,” Nell argued. “Punishment had to be given to him.”
“Of everyone, he is my favorite,” declared irrational Isolde.
“Indeed, he is deceased, and he must remain so,” Nell remarked, with a touch of resentment. “Had I allowed him to survive, he would have continued his harassment of Evadne and Perceval.”
“Yes—unless he had been reformed by you.”
“It wouldn’t have been romantic, and, what’s more, the story would have been made too long.”
“At any rate, it is a thoroughly delightful tale, Nell, and I am certain it will bring you fame. Have you thought of a name for it?”

“Oh, the title was chosen by me a long time back. Evadne’s atonement is what I name it. Isn't that pleasing and alliterative in sound? Now, Isolde, speak to me honestly, are there any flaws you perceive in my tale?”

“Well,” Isolde wavered, “the section in which Evadne bakes the cake appears to my mind not entirely romantic enough for the remainder. Anyone could do precisely that. I am of the opinion that heroines ought not to engage in cooking.”
“Why, that is the source of the humor, and it represents one of the finest elements of the entire tale,” Nell stated. And it can be affirmed that regarding this point she was entirely correct.

Isolde wisely held back from making any additional critiques, though Mr. Pettifer proved far more difficult to satisfy. To begin with, he informed her that the narrative contained far too much description.
“Omit all those ornate sections,” he stated callously.

Nell possessed an uneasy belief that Mr. Pettifer was correct, and she compelled herself to remove the majority of her cherished descriptions, even though the tale required three rewrites until it could be trimmed sufficiently to satisfy the exacting Mr. Pettifer.
“Except for the sunset, I have omitted every description,” she finally remarked. “It was impossible for me to part with it. None of the others were as good.”

“It is completely unrelated to the tale,” Mr. Pettifer said, “and you ought not to have set the action amidst wealthy city folk. What acquaintance do you have with such individuals? Why did you not set it directly here in Brierley—altering the name, naturally, or otherwise Mrs. Agatha Sowerby would likely imagine herself to be the main character.”
“Oh, such an idea would not have worked at all,” Nell objected. “Although Brierley is the most cherished location on earth, it lacks sufficient romance to serve as a tale's setting.”

“I imagine quite a few romances have occurred in Brierley—along with quite a few tragedies as well,” Mr. Pettifer observed dryly. “However, the people you write about are unlike actual people in any location. Their speech is overly abundant, and they employ excessively elaborate phrasing. In one particular spot, that Dalrymple fellow speaks continuously across two whole pages without allowing the young woman to insert a single remark. Had he behaved like that in reality, she would have thrown him over.”

“I do not credit it,” declared Nell plainly. Deep within her hidden spirit, she believed that the lovely, poetic statements uttered to Evadne would entirely capture the heart of any young woman. Furthermore, it was horrifying to listen to reports of Evadne, the grand, regal Evadne, “pitching” somebody. Evadne “rejected her suitors.”

“Be that as it may,” Mr. Pettifer relentlessly continued, “it is a mystery to me how Marcel Lennox failed to win her. Compared to the other, he was double the man. His actions were wicked, yet he took action. Mooning was all Perceval ever found the time to do.”
“Mooning.” The term proved to be far more disagreeable than “pitching!”
“The bad guy was Marcel Lennox,” Nell stated with indignation. “It makes no sense to me that Perceval is less popular with everyone than he is.”
“Perceval is excessively righteous. He is infuriating. The next time you compose a story featuring a hero, include a small dash of human imperfection in his character.”
“Marcel couldn’t have been married by Evadne. Bad was what he was.”

“She would have changed him for the better. A man can be changed; naturally, a jelly-fish cannot be changed. The tale you told is not poor—I must allow that it holds some interest. However, your youth prevents you from composing a tale that would have genuine value. Allow ten years to pass.”

Nell resolved that she would not request anyone's feedback the next time she authored a tale. The process proved excessively disheartening. Even though she informed Hugh regarding the narrative, she refused to read it to him.
“If it turns out well you will get to read it upon publication, Hugh, though if it proves a disappointment no one will ever lay eyes on it.”

Thirza was completely unaware of the project. Within her mind, Nell pictured herself reading a magazine story aloud to Thirza, tricking her into complimenting the piece—since within the imagination every outcome can occur—before victoriously revealing that she was the writer.

Nell brought a lengthy, thick envelope to the Post Office on a certain day, directed to the absolute largest among the “big” periodicals with the charming trust typical of young, inexperienced people. Isolde felt just as much excitement about this as Nell did.
“How much time do you think will pass prior to receiving word from it?” she inquired.
“It ought not to take more than two weeks. Oh, I will be so delighted and filled with pride if they accept it!”

“Naturally it is going to be accepted, and they are probable to request that you forward additional work to them. A day might come when you are as well-known as Mrs. Varley, Nell, and I will be so proud to be your acquaintance,” said Isolde, who had, if nothing else, the remarkable quality of selflessly appreciating her friends’ talents and virtues.

Seven days of wonderful reverie ensued, after which a painful realization arrived. During a certain evening, Isolde discovered Nell inside the porch gable, her eyes appearing doubtful. Positioned upon the table were a lengthy envelope alongside a creased manuscript.
“Nell, hasn’t your story come back?” Isolde cried in disbelief.
“Yes, it has,” Nell answered abruptly.
“Indeed, that editor has to be insane. What justification did he offer?”
“There is no reason whatsoever. A printed piece of paper simply states that it was not deemed acceptable.”

“I never held a high opinion of that magazine, regardless,” Isolde stated with heat. “Its tales are not nearly as captivating as the ones in the Canadian Woman, despite its significantly higher price. I imagine the editor holds a bias against anyone who is not a Yankee. Do not lose heart, Nell. Recall how the stories of Mrs. Varley were returned. Submit yours to the Canadian Woman.”

“I think I shall,” Nell said, taking courage. “And I will mail a marked issue to that editor from America if it gets printed. However, I am going to remove the sunset. Mr. Pettifer was correct, I believe.”

The sunset came out; nevertheless, despite this valiant cutting, the Canadian Woman’s editor returned Evadne’s Atonement with such speed that an angry Isolde insisted it had not been read whatsoever, swearing she would cancel her subscription at once. Nell received this second refusal with the composure that accompanies hopelessness. She placed the manuscript under lock and key inside the attic trunk containing the former Story Club stories; however, she initially acceded to Isolde’s pleas and provided her with a duplicate.
“My literary ambitions have come to an end,” she declared with bitterness.
Although she never brought up the subject with Mr. Pettifer, he directly inquired of her one evening whether her story had been accepted.
“No, the editor wouldn’t accept it,” she replied laconically.
Mr. Pettifer glanced laterally toward the reddened, frail side of the face.
“Well, I imagine you will continue to write them,” he remarked in a supportive tone.
“No, I shall never try to write a story again,” announced Nell, exhibiting the despairing decisiveness of a nineteen-year-old facing a closed door.

“I wouldn’t throw in the towel completely,” Mr. Pettifer said musingly. “I’d compose a story every now and then, but I wouldn’t bother editors with it. I’d write about people and places such as I was familiar with, and I’d have my characters speak ordinary English; and I’d permit the sun to rise and set in the customary tranquil manner without making a big deal out of the occurrence. If it was necessary for me to include villains, I’d afford them an opportunity, Nell—I’d afford them an opportunity. I guess there exist some awfully wicked men in the world, but you’d need to travel a great distance to locate them—even if Mrs. Sowerby thinks we are all wicked. However, the majority of us possess a bit of goodness somewhere inside. Continue writing, Nell.”
“No. Attempting it was a big mistake on my part. Once my time at Wexcombe is finished, I will confine myself to teaching. Teaching is something I can do. Writing stories is not.”
“Once you have finished Wexcombe, it will be time for you to find a husband,” Mr. Pettifer said. “I do not believe in delaying marriage for too long—as I did.”
Nell stood up and walked briskly back to her house. Mr. Pettifer was truly unbearable on certain occasions. “Pitching,” “mooning,” and “getting a husband.” Ow!!

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: Robin and Lucy had gotten prepared to attend Sunday School. They were making the trip by themselves, a circumstance that occurred infrequently, because Mrs. Sowerby invariably went to Sunday School. However, Mrs. Sowerby had injured her ankle by twisting it and could not walk easily, which meant she was remaining at home on this particular morning. The twins were additionally expected to serve as the family's representatives at church, since Nell had departed the previous evening to pass Sunday alongside friends residing in Delford, while Thirza was suffering from a headache.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: Robin descended the stairs with slow steps. Lucy, whom Mrs. Sowerby had gotten prepared, was in the hall waiting for him. Robin had taken care of his own preparations. A cent was in his pocket for the collection at Sunday School, along with a five-cent piece for the church collection; one of his hands held his Bible while the other held his Sunday School quarterly; his lesson, his Golden Text, and his catechism question were known by him perfectly. Had he not been forced to study them in the kitchen of Mrs. Sowerby, during the entirety of the previous Sunday afternoon? Robin ought to have possessed a placid state of mind, consequently. In reality, text and catechism notwithstanding, his inner self resembled a ravening wolf.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: As he went to Lucy, Mrs. Sowerby came limping out from her kitchen.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “Are you clean?” she asked with severity.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “Yes—every part of me that is visible,” answered Robin, scowling in defiance.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: A sigh escaped Mrs. Agatha. Regarding the neck and ears of Robin, she harbored her doubts. She was aware, however, that Robin would probably run off if she tried to inspect him herself, and giving chase was beyond her today.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “Well, make certain you conduct yourselves properly,” she cautioned them. “Avoid walking through dust. Avoid halting on the porch to converse with additional children. Avoid squirming or wriggling in your seats. Avoid forgetting the Golden Text. Avoid losing your collection money or failing to deposit it. Avoid whispering while prayers are said, and avoid failing to focus on the sermon.”

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: Robin did not condescend to answer. With the submissive Lucy trailing behind, he stepped off down the path. Yet his inner spirit raged. Robin had endured, or believed he had endured, numerous grievances from the actions and words of Mrs. Agatha Sowerby ever since her arrival at Grey Shutters, because Mrs. Sowerby was incapable of sharing a home with anyone, regardless of whether they were nine or ninety, without attempting to train them correctly. Furthermore, it was merely the prior afternoon when she had stepped in to persuade Thirza not to permit Robin to go angling alongside the Timothy Cottons. Robin remained furious about this.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: The moment he cleared the lane, Robin halted and contorted his face into an expression so unearthly and terrifying that Lucy, despite being familiar with his talents for doing so, felt genuine panic that he might remain stuck like that forever.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “Darn her,” Robin exploded.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “Oh, Robin, don’t swear,” Lucy gasped in dismay.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “‘Darn’ is not a swear word—at least not a genuine one. Even if it were, it wouldn't matter to me,” Robin shot back impetuously.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “Well, if you have to utter terrible words, please refrain from doing so on Sunday,” begged Lucy.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: Although Robin remained quite distant from feeling remorse, within his hidden heart he sensed that his actions might have slightly exceeded the proper limits.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “I will create a curse word for myself,” he stated.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “God will penalize you should you perform that,” Lucy stated in a serious manner.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “In that case, I believe God is a cruel old rascal,” Robin shot back. “Is He unaware that a guy needs a method for ’spressing his emotions?”

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “Robin!!!” exclaimed Lucy, anticipating that he would be instantly struck down dead where he stood; however, no such thing occurred.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “At any rate, I am not going to endure another bit of Mrs. Sowerby’s bossing,” sputtered Robin. “Nell and Thirza might possess the right to order me around, but she lacks it. I intend to perform every last thing that she instructed me not to do. Just watch me.”

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: In severe, quiet intentness, as Lucy observed him with horrified enchantment, Robin walked off the green roadside turf, sinking to his ankles in the powdery dust that a month without rain had created on the highway, and proceeded forward through it, stamping his feet fiercely until a murky fog shrouded him.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “That is the start,” he declared with victory. “And I intend to delay in the entryway and chat for as long as there is anyone present to converse with. I plan to twist and fidget and murmur, and I intend to state that I am ignorant of the Golden Text. And I am about to discard each of my collections at this very moment.”

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: And with intense pleasure, Robin flung the cent and nickel across the fence belonging to Mr. Pembroke.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “It was Satan who drove you to do that,” Lucy said in a reproachful tone.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “He didn’t,” Robin exclaimed with indignation. “I merely figured it out on my own. Furthermore, I’ve come up with another idea. I will not be attending Sunday School or church whatsoever. Instead, I’m heading up to play with the Cottons. Yesterday, they mentioned to me that they wouldn't be going to Sunday School today, since their mother was out of town and no one was forcing them to go. Come on, Lucy, we’re going to have a wonderful time.”

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “I do not wish to go,” Lucy objected.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “You must,” Robin said. “I will inform Thirza that you were kissed by Frank Bell at school this past Monday if you fail to come.”

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “I was unable to prevent it. His actions were unknown to me in advance,” exclaimed Lucy, turning bright red.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “Well, you failed to slap him or appear even slightly annoyed,” Robin snapped back. “If you refuse to come, I will report that to her as well. We will use the short cut across this field.”

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “I am terrified of those cows,” poor Lucy objected, perceiving a chance to get away.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “To think that you would be afraid of those cows,” Robin mocked. “After all, you are older than either of them.”

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “They are larger,” Lucy remarked.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “They will not harm you. Come on, right now. It is fantastic. I am not going to take the trouble to attend church whatsoever when I am older. I reckon that I am able to reach heaven on my own.”

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “Violating the Sabbath day will send you to the other place,” remarked miserable Lucy, who trailed behind him extremely reluctantly.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: However, Robin felt no fear—so far. The torments of hell remained exceedingly distant, whereas the pleasures of going fishing alongside the Cottons were extremely close at hand. He desired that Lucy possessed greater courage. She continuously glanced behind her as though she might burst into tears at any second, which ruined a boy's enjoyment. Girls were a nuisance, regardless. On this occasion, Robin refrained from thinking "darn", even mentally. He felt no regret—so far—for having uttered the word a single time, though he reasoned it was wise not to push the Unknown Powers excessively in a single day.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors

Oh, if that detestable Frank Bell had simply not kissed her! Robin could have been defied by her then, and she could have attended her cherished Sunday School.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: Naturally, they did not dare to fish upon the pond, since folks traveling to church would spot them there. It swarmed with trout, however, and they enjoyed a wonderful morning—or at least the Cottons definitely did, and Robin appeared to as well. Retaining a small measure of caution, he had removed his stockings and boots to put on a pair of Tommy Cotton’s overalls. Clad in this manner, he feared neither marsh, bog, nor brushwood. Lucy was openly and obviously wretched. As she trailed behind the rest of the group from one pool to another, she held her Bible and quarterly close to her chest, bitterly pondering her cherished class where she ought to be seated at that exact minute, in front of a beloved teacher. Instead of that, she found herself wandering through the forest alongside those semi-savage Cottons, attempting to shield her pretty white frock from tears and smudges while keeping her boots spotless. Mirabel had proposed lending her an apron, but Lucy had rejected the offer with disdain.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: The trout took the bait just like they always do on Sundays. Within an hour, all the fish they desired had been caught by the transgressors, who then went back to the house, which was a great relief to Lucy. As the rest engaged in a noisy game of tag, she sat in a proper manner on a hencoop in the yard; and after that, every one of them went up to the roof of the pig-house and carved their initials into the saddleboard. Robin received yet another idea from the henhouse with its flat roof and a heap of straw under it. They had a marvelous thirty minutes going up onto the roof and leaping down into the straw while uttering whoops and yells.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: Yet even illicit enjoyments cannot last forever. Ditching Tommy's overalls and putting his own proper clothes back on, he turned from his line of trout and sighed. Taking them back to the house was out of the question.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “Well, didn’t we have a wonderful time?” he asked in a challenging way, while they walked down the field on the hill.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “The Cottons are fine,” Robin replied. “Moreover, their lives are much more enjoyable than ours. They act precisely as they wish and speak their minds openly in front of anyone. From now on, I intend to do the same.”

text: “You wouldn’t have the courage to mention many of those matters in front of the whole group,” Lucy declared.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: This came as a complete shock. Robin had not anticipated a demonstration of free speech that was quite so tangible. However, consistency was unnecessary when dealing with Lucy.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors

Mrs. Sowerby could be domineering; nevertheless, a container of biscuits remained in her kitchen pantry and she lacked any meanness. chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: However, the limit of Robin’s wrongdoing had still not been reached. He would soon learn that concealing a single misdeed requires committing a second one. That afternoon, they dined alongside Mrs. Sowerby, who began by inquiring of Robin,

text: Sleepily, Nell sat upright.

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors

text: “Yet Robin, He was aware regardless.”

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “I fled from Sunday School—and I went angling alongside the Cottons—and I uttered ever so many falsehoods to Mrs. Sowerby—oh! nearly six—and—and—I—I uttered a profanity, Nell—or something almost like a profanity, at least—and I hurled insults at God.”

text: Quietness descended. Robin was uncertain how to interpret this. Could Nell be in such state of shock that she would refrain from talking to him ever again?

text: “I want to understand what my conscience is.”

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “There is a quality inside you, Robin, which invariably informs you whenever you act improperly and causes you to feel miserable if you continue doing so. Have you not observed that?”

chapter_title: Chapter XIII The Way of Transgressors
text: “Indeed, though I was unaware of its nature. I would rather be without it. My enjoyment would be much greater. In what place is my conscience, Nell? My desire is to find out. Does it reside within my stomach?”

text: “I reckon I can’t escape it, in that case,” Robin uttered with a sigh. “Will you inform Thirza and Mrs. Sowerby about my actions, Nell?”

Opal Pettigrew and Nell were seated in the Pettigrews’ garden when the day, having dragged itself slowly across the space, finally vanished. A warm, smoky afternoon of summer had just passed. Outbursts of blooms covered the earth in magnificence. Hazes filled the lazy valleys. Shadows decorated the paths through the woods, while purple asters adorned the fields.

Nell had sacrificed a night excursion under the moon to the Pale Sands beach so that Opal could have her company for the evening. Throughout that summer, she had passed numerous evenings in the same manner, even though she frequently questioned the benefit it brought to anybody, and occasionally returned home resolved never to return.

As the summer drew to a close, Opal’s complexion became paler; she surrendered the Pale Sands school—“till New Year’s, her father believed she ought not to teach”—and the fancy work she cherished slipped from her hands with increasing frequency as they became too tired to hold it. Nevertheless, she remained perpetually cheerful, ever optimistic, constantly talking and whispering about her suitors, alongside their conflicts and heartbreaks. Because of this, Nell found her visits difficult to endure. What previously appeared foolish or entertaining had turned macabre; it resembled death gazing out from behind a deliberate facade of vitality. Even so, Opal appeared to hold fast to her, refusing to allow her to depart without a pledge to return shortly. Mrs. Sowerby complained regarding how often Nell visited, asserting that she would contract consumption, and even Thirza felt uncertain.
“Each time you visit Opal you return looking exhausted,” she said.

“It is extremely mournful and terrible,” Nell stated quietly. “Opal appears completely unaware of her state. Even so, I somehow sense her need for assistance—her longing for it—and I wish to provide it to her but am unable to. Whenever I am beside her, I feel just like I am observing her battle an unseen enemy—attempting to repel it using what little strength she possesses. This reason explains why I return home exhausted.”

However, Nell was not as acutely aware of this on this particular night. Opal remained unusually silent. Not a single word escaped her lips regarding dresses, drives, parties, and “fellows.” With her untouched work lying next to her, she rested in the hammock, a white shawl enveloped around her thin shoulders. Her lengthy yellow hair braids—those gorgeous braids that Nell used to envy so much during their former schooldays!—were positioned on both sides of her. She had removed the pins because they caused her head to ache, according to her. For the moment, the hectic flush had faded, causing her to appear pale and childlike.

Ascending into the silver-hued sky, the moon gave a pearly luster to the surrounding clouds. Beneath it, the pond gleamed within that misty glow. Located a short distance past the Pettigrew homestead stood the church, accompanied by the ancient graveyard adjacent to it. Beaming upon the white stones, the moonlight rendered them vividly distinct against the backdrop of dark trees.

“The cemetery appears so peculiar under the moon’s light!” Opal uttered abruptly. “So spectral!” she trembled. “Nell, the time is drawing near when I will be resting in that place. You, Isolde, and everyone else will be moving around, brimming with vitality—while I will be situated there—within the ancient cemetery—deceased!”
Nell was thrown into confusion by the suddenness of the event. Speech eluded her for a brief period of time.
“You are aware that it is true, aren’t you?” Opal urged.
“Yes, I know,” Nell replied softly. “Dear Opal, I know.”

“Everyone is aware of it,” Opal stated with bitterness. “It is known to me—it has been known to me the entire summer, even if I refused to admit it. And, oh, Nell”—she stretched her hand forth and grasped the hand of Nell in a pleading, impulsive manner—“dying is not what I want. The thought of dying frightens me.”
“Opal, what is the reason for your fear?” Nell inquired in a soft voice.

“Because—because—oh, Nell, I am not scared that I will fail to get into heaven. I belong to the church. But—everything there is going to be so unfamiliar. I ponder—and ponder—and it makes me so scared—and—and—homesick. Of course, heaven has to be extremely beautiful, as the Bible states—however, Nell, it will not be like what I am accustomed to.”

A unwelcome memory floated into Nell’s mind of an amusing tale she had listened to Cressida Lindsay recount—the narrative of a certain elderly man who had uttered almost the identical remark regarding the afterlife. At the time, it had struck her as comical—she recalled the way she and Honora had giggled about it. Yet, emanating from Opal’s wan, quivering lips, it did not appear the least bit funny anymore. It felt sorrowful, disastrous—and accurate! The celestial realm could not resemble what Opal was accustomed to. Absolutely nothing in her merry, lighthearted existence, nor her superficial principles and desires, had prepared her for that monumental transition, or rendered the next life as anything to her except foreign, imaginary, and unwanted. Powerlessly, Nell pondered what words of assistance she might offer her. Was there anything she could voice? “I think, Opal,” she initiated with uncertainty—since Nell found it challenging to converse with anyone about the profoundest reflections in her soul, or the fresh notions regarding the vast enigmas of existence in this world and the next that had indistinctly started forming in her thoughts, replacing her previous youthful beliefs, and talking about them to someone like Opal Pettigrew was the most difficult of all—“I think, perhaps, we have very mistaken ideas about heaven—what it is and what it holds for us. I don’t think it can be so very different from life here as most people seem to think. I believe we’ll just go on living, a good deal as we live here—and be ourselves just the same—only it will be easier to be good and to—follow the highest. All the hindrances and perplexities will be taken away, and we shall see clearly. Don’t be afraid, Opal.”

“I can’t help it,” Opal said in a pitiful manner. “Even if what you say about heaven is true—and you can’t be sure—it may be only that imagination of yours—it won’t be just the same. It can’t be. I want to go on living here. I’m so young, Nell. I haven’t had my life. I’ve fought so hard to live—and it isn’t any use—I have to die—and leave everything I care for.” Nell remained seated, experiencing an agony that was nearly unbearable. She was unable to utter soothing lies; and every word Opal spoke was so dreadfully accurate. She was departing from all she held dear. It was on earth alone that she had stored her treasures; she had existed entirely for the small matters of life—the things that fade away—neglecting the grand matters that proceed into eternity, spanning the chasm between the two existences and turning death into a simple transition from a single abode to another—from dusk to clear daylight. There, God would mind her—Nell believed—she would come to understand—yet at present it was not surprising that her soul held fast, with unseeing helplessness, to the sole items she understood and cherished.
Prop scene on her arm, Opal elevated her luminous, lovely blue eyes toward the heavens bathed in moonlight.

“I want to live,” she said, her voice shaking. “I want to live the way other girls do. I—I desire to get married, Nell—and—and—possess tiny children. You are aware that babies were always something I loved, Nell. To nobody else except you could I admit this. That you comprehend, I know. Furthermore, poor Herb—he—he cares for me and my love belongs to him, Nell. Nothing was meant to me by the others, yet he matters—and provided I could remain alive, I would become his wife and experience such happiness. Oh, Nell, this is difficult.”

Reclining once more upon her pillows, Opal wept uncontrollably. Nell squeezed her hand with immense, anguished empathy—a voiceless compassion that may have comforted Opal better than fragmented, flawed speech ever could; consequently, her agitation soon waned and her weeping stopped.

“I am pleased that I have shared this with you, Nell,” she murmured. “Simply expressing everything has brought me relief. Throughout the entire summer—with each of your visits—I desired to do so. I wished to discuss it with you—yet it was impossible for me. Admitting my impending demise, or having another person utter or imply it, felt as though it would render death absolute. I refused to speak it, or allow myself to contemplate it. During daylight hours, surrounded by others and amidst bright surroundings, avoiding such thoughts proved less difficult. However, during sleepless nights—Nell, it was utterly terrible. Escape from it was impossible at those times. Death merely arrived and gazed directly at me, terrifying me to the point where I felt ready to shriek.
“However, Opal, you will not feel scared from now on, will you? You are going to be courageous, and have faith that everything will turn out fine for you.”
“I will endeavor to do so. What you told me will be weighed in my mind, and I will attempt to hold it as true. Also, your visits will be as frequent as possible, will they not, Nell?”
“Certainly, my love.”

“It—it will not take much time now, Nell. I am certain of that. And I would prefer to have you over anybody else. Of all the girls I attended school alongside, I always favored you the most. You never showed jealousy, or malice, as a few of them did. Poor Em White came by to visit me yesterday. Do you recall that Em and I were great friends for three years while attending school? And subsequently we fell out at the time of the school concert. Ever since, we have not uttered a word to one another. Was it not foolish? Any occurrence of that sort appears foolish at present. However, Em and I resolved the former dispute yesterday. She mentioned that she would have conversed years back, except she believed I would refuse to. And I refrained from ever conversing with her since I was convinced she would refuse to converse with me. Is it not peculiar the way folks misjudge one another, Nell?”

“It seems to me that the majority of life’s difficulties arise from a lack of understanding,” Nell stated. “I have to leave at this moment, Opal. The hour is growing late—and staying out in this moisture is bad for you.”
“It will not be long before you ascend once more.”
“Yes, extremely shortly. And I will be delighted if I can assist you in any way.”
“I am aware. Already, you have provided aid to me. At present, nothing appears entirely so terrible. Good night, Nell.”
“Good night, my love.”

Nell made her way back home with great deliberation under the light of the moon. Something within her had been altered by the evening. The significance of life was now different, its intention more profound. Externally, everything would proceed as before; nevertheless, her innermost depths had been moved. Her fate could not resemble that of poor butterfly Opal. Arriving at the conclusion of one existence could not mean encountering the subsequent one with the recoil of fear toward an entirely alien realm—a realm for which habitual ideas, thoughts, and ambitions had left her unready. The minor details of existence, while pleasant and fine in their proper context, could not become her reasons for living; she had to seek out and pursue the ultimate; the existence of heaven had to commence right here in this earthly world.

That lovely evening in the garden was forever. Opal was never again seen alive by Nell. The following night a send-off party was held by the B.V.I.S. for Odette Pullen prior to her leaving for the West. And, as light feet were dancing and bright eyes were laughing and merry tongues were chattering, a call came to a soul in Brierley that could neither be ignored nor avoided. The following morning news spread from one house to another that Opal Pettigrew had passed away. She had passed away in her sleep, without pain and peacefully, bearing a smile on her face—as though, in the end, death had arrived like a gentle friend guiding her across the doorway, rather than the horrific specter she had feared.

Following the burial, Mrs. Agatha Sowerby stated with conviction that Opal Pettigrew was the most beautiful deceased person she had ever beheld. Dressed in white amidst the fragile blossoms Nell had arranged around her, her physical grace while resting was recalled and discussed in Brierley for a long time. Opal’s attractiveness had been constant; however, her charm had possessed a worldly, grounded nature that carried a specific arrogant air, seeming to display itself boldly to any viewer, unilluminated by soul and unpolished by mind. Yet the touch of death had hallowed her features, revealing subtle contours and a faultless silhouette hitherto invisible—achieving what living, loving, profound grief, and the intense happiness of womanhood might have accomplished for Opal. Gazing through her blurred weeping at her former companion, Nell believed she observed the countenance God had intended for Opal, keeping that image in her mind forever.
Prior to the departure of the funeral procession from the house, Mrs. Pettigrew drew Nell into an empty room and handed her a small package.

“Take this, I want it to be yours,” she wept. “Having you possess it is what Opal would have wanted. This embroidered centerpiece was a project she was making. A little work remains—where her poor small fingers left it when she set it aside for the final time, during the afternoon preceding her death, the needle still pierces the fabric.”
“A portion of incomplete labor is perpetually remaining,” Mrs. Sowerby remarked, her eyes filled with tears. “Yet I imagine an individual is constantly present to complete it.”

“It is so hard to truly grasp that someone we have known forever is actually gone,” Nell remarked while she and Isolde made their way back home. “Opal is the very first among our schoolmates to pass away. Eventually, one after another, every single one of us will have to follow.”

“Yes, I suppose so,” Isolde stated with discomfort. Talking about that was not what she desired. Discussing the particulars of the funeral—the magnificent white velvet coffin Mr. Pettigrew had demanded for Opal—“the Gillises must always make a splurge, even at funerals,” Mrs. Agatha Sowerby had remarked—the sorrowful countenance of Herb Tranter, the uninhibited, hysterical sorrow of a sister of Opal's—would have been her preference, yet Nell refused to converse about those matters. A daydream appeared to envelop her, one in which Isolde felt with loneliness that she shared no portion or role.
“A great girl to laugh was Opal Pettigrew,” Robin remarked all at once. “Is she going to laugh in heaven as frequently as she did in Brierley, Nell? I wish to know.”
“Indeed, I believe she is going to,” Nell remarked.
“Oh, Nell,” Isolde objected, smiling in a somewhat scandalized way.
“Well, why not, Isolde?” Nell inquired with gravity. “Is it your belief that we will never laugh in heaven?”
“Oh—I—I do not know” stumbled Isolde. “It appears not quite proper, in some way. You are aware that it is quite terrible to giggle inside a church.”
“However, church is not what heaven will resemble—continuously,” Nell stated.

“I trust it isn’t,” Robin stated with force. “Should it be, I have no desire to attend. Church is terribly boring. Regardless, I do not intend on going for a very long time. My intention is to reach one hundred years of age, similar to Mr. Thomas Scobie of Pale Sands. He claims his longevity is due to always smoking tobacco, which destroyed every germ. Will I be allowed to smoke tobacco fairly soon, Nell?”
“No, Robin, my wish is that tobacco will never be used by you,” Nell remarked in a distracted manner.
“How will it make you feel if I end up dying from the germs, in that case?” Robin asked.
