“It’s the homiest spot I ever saw—it’s homier than home,” declared Cressida Lindsay, scanning her surroundings with eyes full of delight. Everyone was gathered as dusk fell in the large living-room at Tabby’s Place—Nell and Honora, Cressy and Mabel, Aunt Euphemia, Smudge, Joseph, the Sarah-Cat, and Gog and Magog. Across the walls, flickering shadows cast by the fire were dancing; purrs came from the cats; and, glowing through the golden dusk like creamy moons, stood a grand bowl of hothouse chrysanthemums that had been sent to Cressy by a victim.

Twenty-one days had passed since they thought of themselves as established, and everyone was currently convinced that the trial would prove successful. A agreeable level of excitement had filled the initial fourteen days following their homecoming; they had kept themselves occupied placing their domestic possessions, arranging their modest home, and reconciling various viewpoints.

Nell did not feel excessively grieved about departing from Brierley once it was time for her to go back to college. The final days of her holiday had been far from enjoyable. Island newspapers had printed her prize story; moreover, on his store counter, Mr. William Blair maintained a massive stack of pamphlets in pink, green, and yellow that held the tale, handing a copy to each buyer. After he dispatched a complimentary pack to Nell, she immediately threw every single one into the kitchen stove. Her feelings of shame stemmed solely from her personal standards, because the people of Brierley considered her winning the prize to be utterly grand. Honest admiration was felt for her by her numerous friends, whereas her small number of enemies viewed her with disdainful jealousy. Flossie Tulk remarked that she suspected Nell Harcourt had simply stolen the story, claiming certainty that she recalled seeing it in a publication years earlier. Having discovered or surmised that Wilfred had been rejected, the Motts remarked that they felt it was hardly a matter for pride, as nearly anyone could accomplish the same thing if she made an effort. Aunt Drusilla informed Nell that learning she had resorted to composing novels brought her great regret, adding that no person native to Brierley would engage in such a thing, and that this served as the result of taking in orphans from heaven knows where, whose parents possessed heaven knows what background. Even Mrs. Agatha Sowerby harbored gloomy doubts regarding the moral fitness of authoring fiction, even if that twenty-five dollar check nearly brought her around to accepting it.
“The amount of money given for those falsehoods is truly astonishing, it really is,” she remarked, displaying a mixture of pride and sternness.

Taking everything into account, the arrival of departure time brought a sense of relief. Furthermore, returning to Wexcombe felt delightful, being a knowledgeable, seasoned Soph surrounded by numerous companions welcoming one another on the lively first day. Nonie, Mabel, Hugh, and Wilfred Mott—who appeared more pompous than any Sophomore ever had previously—were present, alongside Cressy, whose Hector-and-Orlando debate remained unresolved, and Elias Purdy MacKinnon. Ever since departing Regent’s, Elias Purdy had worked as a schoolteacher, yet his mother decided that he ought to cease teaching at last and focus on studying for the ministry. Unfortunate Elias Purdy encountered misfortune right at the start of his university journey. A team of six merciless Sophs, living in the same boarding house, descended upon his room one evening and clipped the hair from one side of his head. The unfortunate Elias Purdy was forced to attend classes looking like this until his hair regenerated. He remarked to Nell with resentment that occasionally he questioned whether he actually possessed a true calling to become a minister.

Aunt Euphemia delayed her arrival until the girls had prepared Tabby’s Place for her. A letter accompanied the key that Miss Tabby sent to Nell, stating that Gog and Magog were stored in a box beneath the spare-room bed, though they could be removed whenever desired; she appended a postscript expressing her hope that the girls would exercise care when hanging pictures. Five years prior, the living room had received new wallpaper, and she and Miss Maria desired that no more holes than were strictly required be punched into that fresh paper. Otherwise, she left all matters in Nell’s hands.

What pleasure those girls derived from arranging their home! In the words of Cressy, it was nearly as delightful as a wedding. A person experienced the joy of creating a home minus the trouble of a spouse. Everyone carried an item along to decorate or add comfort to the small dwelling. Nonie and Cressy and Mabel possessed an abundance of ornaments and artwork, which they then hung based on their preferences, completely ignoring the new wallpaper of Miss Tabby.
“We will fill the openings with putty upon our departure, dear—it will remain completely unknown to her,” they remarked to Nell, who was objecting.

Nell was given a pine needle cushion by Isolde, while a fearfully and wonderfully embroidered cushion was presented to both her and Honora by Miss Ada. A large box of preserves had been sent by Thirza, who also made dark hints about a Thanksgiving hamper, and a patchwork quilt was given to Nell by Mrs. Sowerby, who additionally lent her five others.
“You take them,” she instructed with authority. “There is no reason for them to be stored in that garret trunk for moths to chew when they could be utilized instead.”

Moths would not have dared approach those quilts, because the smell of mothballs on them was so strong that two whole weeks hanging in the orchard at Tabby’s Place were required before anyone could bear them inside the house. Indeed, the refined Linden Avenue had seldom seen a sight quite like it. The stern elderly millionaire residing "next door" walked over with the desire to purchase the magnificent red and yellow "tulip-pattern" quilt that Mrs. Agatha had bestowed upon Nell. He explained that his mother used to create similar quilts, and by Jove, he desired one so he could remember her. Nell refused to sell her quilt, which disappointed him greatly, but she penned a full account of the incident to Mrs. Sowerby. Upon hearing this, the delighted lady sent a reply stating she possessed an identical extra quilt, allowing the tobacco king to obtain his quilt in the end, and he demanded that it be placed upon his bed, which appalled his stylish wife.

Mrs. Sowerby’s quilts proved extremely helpful during that winter. Despite possessing numerous virtues, Tabby’s Place was not without its defects. It was actually quite a chilly residence; thus, as the freezing nights arrived, the girls felt extremely happy to nestle beneath Mrs. Sowerby’s quilts, wishing that lending them would be remembered as a virtuous deed. Nell occupied the blue room she had desired from the moment she saw it. Honora and Mabel were in the big room. Cressy felt completely delighted with the small room situated above the kitchen; while Aunt Euphemia was designated to occupy the ground-floor room adjacent to the living-room. Initially, Smudge made his bed on the doorstep.

Returning from Wexcombe several days later, Nell, as she walked toward her house, noticed that she was receiving secretive, fond grins from the folk she encountered. What could be wrong with her, Nell pondered with apprehension. Had her hat gone askew? Was her belt untied? Twisting her neck to check herself, Nell, finally, caught sight of Smudge.

Trotting along behind her, near her heels, was easily the most miserable example of the cat family she had ever seen. The creature was far beyond kittenhood, gangly, skinny, and scruffy-looking. Portions of its ears were missing, one eye was presently out of order, and its jowl was swollen in a laughable manner. Regarding its shade, had a cat that was formerly black been completely and thoroughly scorched, the outcome would have matched the tone of this stray’s sparse, wet, unattractive coat.

Nell attempted to "shoo" him away, yet the cat refused to "shoo." For as long as she remained standing, he remained seated upon his haunches and stared at her in a reproachful manner using his single functional eye; whenever she started walking again, he trailed behind. Nell accepted his presence beside her right up to the moment she arrived at the entrance of Tabby’s Place, a gate she unkindly closed right in front of him, foolishly assuming she was done with him forever. However, when Cressy held the door open fifteen minutes afterward, the cat of a rusty-brown shade was waiting right on the step. Furthermore, he immediately rushed inside and jumped onto Nell’s lap, uttering a "miaow" that sounded partly begging and partly victorious.
“Nell,” Mabel said in a severe tone, “is that animal yours?”

“No, I do not,” objected revolted Nell. “The beast trailed me back from somewhere. It was impossible for me to shake him off. Ugh, get down. Decent cats are reasonably acceptable to me; however, beasties with your coloring do not appeal to me.”
Pussy, on the other hand, declined to descend. He unconcernedly coiled himself into Nell's lap and started purring.
“It is clear he has chosen you as his own,” Honora chuckled.
“I will NOT be adopted,” Nell declared with insistence.
“The poor creature is starving,” Cressy said with pity. “Why, his skin is nearly pierced by his bones.”
“Indeed, I will provide him with a full meal, after which he has to go back to his original location,” Nell declared with determination.

The cat received food and was placed outside. Upon the arrival of morning, he remained located on the doorstep. He persisted in sitting on the doorstep, rushing inside every time someone opened the door. Not even the slightest chilly reception impacted him; he paid no attention to anyone except Nell. Driven by pity, the girls gave him food; however, once seven days went by, they concluded that action needed to be taken. The cat looked better. Normalcy had returned to his eye and cheek; his thinness was slightly reduced; and someone had observed him cleaning his face.

“Even so, we are unable to retain him,” Mabel stated. “Aunt Phemie arrives the following week, bringing along the Sarah-cat. Having two cats is impossible for us; besides, should we attempt it, this Smudge Coat would engage in constant battles with the Sarah-cat. Combat is inherent to his character. Yesterday night, he engaged in a fierce war against the tobacco-king’s cat, completely vanquishing him, horse, foot and artillery.”

“It is necessary that we dispose of him,” concurred Nell, glaring grimly at the topic of their conversation, who was vibrating with a purr on the fireside mat, appearing as gentle as a lamb. “The issue, however, remains—in what manner? By what means can four defenseless women dispose of a feline that refuses to be disposed of?”
“It is necessary that we chloroform him,” Cressy remarked briskly. “That represents the most humane approach.”
“Does any single one of us understand how to give a cat chloroform?” Nell inquired in a dismal tone.

“I truly do, sweetheart. Being able to do this is among my rare—regrettably rare—practical skills. Back home, I have gotten rid of a number of them. In the morning, you collect the cat and feed him a hearty meal. Next, you fetch a former burlap sack—you can find one on the back porch—place the cat upon it, and cover him with an inverted wooden box. After that, obtain a two-ounce container of chloroform, remove its cork, and slide it beneath the box's rim. Place a substantial weight onto the upper part of the box and do not disturb it until nightfall. The cat will have passed away, resting curled up calmly just as though he were sleeping. There is no pain—no fighting.”
“That seems simple,” Nell remarked with doubt.
“There is nothing to it. Simply entrust the matter to me. I will make sure it is handled,” Cressy said in a reassuring tone.

Thus the chloroform was obtained, and Smudge was enticed to his death the following morning. Having eaten his breakfast and licked his chops, he scrambled onto Nell’s lap. Nell felt a pang of doubt. She was loved and trusted by this poor animal. In what way could she participate in this slaughter?
“Take him, here,” she told Cressy hurriedly. “A murderess is what I feel like.”
“You know he won’t suffer,” Cressy offered by way of comfort, yet Nell had already run away.
Within the back porch, the deadly act took place. On that day, no one approached the area. However, as twilight fell, Cressy announced the necessity of burying Smudge.
“The digging of his grave in the orchard must be done by Nonie and Mabel,” stated Cressy, “and I need Nell to accompany me to carry the box away. It is that specific task that I constantly abhor.”

The pair of plotters walked on tiptoe unwillingly toward the rear veranda. With great care, Cressy raised the rock that she had placed upon the crate. At that moment, weak yet clear, an indisputable meow echoed beneath the crate.
“He—he isn’t dead,” Nell gasped, sitting down on the doorstep of the kitchen with a blank look.
“It cannot be otherwise,” Cressy stated, unable to believe it.
A second faint cry confirmed his continued existence. A mutual gaze passed between the pair of young women.
“What steps shall we take?” asked Nell.
“Why on earth aren’t you coming?” asked Mabel, showing up at the entrance. “The grave is prepared by us. ‘What silent still and silent all?’” she mockingly quoted.
“‘Indeed, no, the speech of those who have passed resembles the remote rush of a waterfall,’” Nell immediately replied with a quotation of her own, gesturing with gravity toward the chest.
The strain was dispelled by an eruption of giggles.

“We have to leave him in this place until the morning,” Cressy said, putting the stone back into position. “For five minutes now, he has not made a sound. It could be that those noises we caught were his last dying gasp. Otherwise, beneath the pressure of our remorseful minds, we might have simply fancied them.”

However, upon the removal of the box that morning, Smudge leaped with a single joyful bound onto Nell’s shoulder, whereupon he started lovingly licking her face. No cat had ever been more undeniably full of life.
“There is a knot hole in the box right here,” Cressy groaned. “It escaped my notice. The reason he failed to die is that. Re-doing everything is what we must do now.”
“No, we haven’t,” Nell abruptly proclaimed. “Smudge will not be slain another time. He belongs to me—and you simply must accept it.”
“Oh, well, provided you arrange things with Aunt Phemie and the Sarah-cat,” Mabel said, speaking like someone disclaiming all further responsibility for the matter.

Since that moment Smudge belonged to the household. Nightly, he rested upon the scrubbing cushion located in the rear porch and feasted upon the best food available. When Aunt Euphemia arrived, he had become chubby, shiny, and fairly presentable. Nevertheless, similar to the cat of Kipling, he “walked by himself.” Every cat's paw opposed him, just as his own paw opposed every cat. Gradually, he defeated the high-class cats inhabiting Linden Avenue. Regarding people, his affection belonged exclusively to Nell. No other person attempted to pet him. A furious spit alongside a noise resembling highly inappropriate words met whoever tried it.
“The pretensiousness that cat displays is entirely unbearable,” stated Mabel.
“He was a pleasant old cat, he was,” affirmed Nell, stubbornly hugging her animal.

“Indeed, I am unsure how he and the Sarah-cat will manage to co-exist,” Mabel remarked with pessimism. “Feline battles occurring in the orchard during the night are troublesome enough. However, feline battles right here in the livingroom cannot be tolerated.” Eventually, Aunt Euphemia made her appearance. Nell, Honora, and Cressy had anticipated her coming with some apprehension; yet, once Aunt Euphemia was settled in the rocking chair facing the burning hearth, they metaphorically prostrated themselves and revered her.

Small and elderly, Aunt Euphemia possessed a diminutive face that was gently triangular, along with big, tender blue eyes possessing an irrepressible youthfulness and brimming with as many expectations as those of a young maiden. Her cheeks were rose-colored, and her silver-white hair was arranged in charming, small rolls above her ears.

“It is quite an outmoded method,” she remarked, busily working her needles on an item as delicate and rosy as an evening cloud. “However, I am outmoded myself. My garments are, and naturally my views are as well. Remember, I am not claiming they are superior because of it. Indeed, I suppose they are likely much inferior. Nevertheless, they have proven quite comfortable through use. Fresh footwear looks finer than worn footwear, yet the worn footwear feels more pleasant. I have reached an age where I can pamper myself regarding footwear and views. My intention is to be very relaxed here. I am aware you anticipate that I will supervise you and maintain your propriety, yet I refuse. If you will ever understand how to conduct yourselves, you are at an age to know it now. Therefore, as it pertains to me,” Aunt Euphemia finished, a gleam present in her youthful eyes, “you are all free to ruin yourselves as you see fit.”
“Oh, won't someone divide those cats?” Mabel implored, shuddering.
Not only the Sarah-cat but also Joseph was brought along by Aunt Euphemia. Joseph, as she clarified, used to belong to a cherished friend of hers who had relocated to Vancouver.

“She was unable to bring Joseph along, which led her to entreat me to keep him. Refusing her was truly not an option for me. He is a wonderful cat—or rather, his temperament is wonderful. She gave him the name Joseph owing to his multicolored coat.”

That was undoubtedly true. As Mabel remarked in disgust, Joseph resembled a mobile bag of rags. The base shade of his coat could not be determined. White adorned his legs, which were marked by black spots. A large yellow swatch on one flank and a black one on the opposite side sat upon his gray back. Yellow comprised his tail, except for its gray end. One of his ears was black, whereas the other was yellow. Because a black patch covered one eye, he possessed an intensely devil-may-care appearance. Actually, he possessed a gentle, harmless, and friendly nature. Joseph resembled a lily of the field in a single way, even if in no other. He did not labor, nor did he spin, nor did he hunt mice. Nevertheless, Solomon, despite all his splendor, did not rest upon cushions that were softer, nor did he indulge more completely in rich foods.

Delivered via express, Joseph and the Sarah-cat came in individual crates. Following their uncrating and a meal, Joseph chose the particular cushion and spot that suited his fancy, whereas the Sarah-cat quietly took a seat in front of the hearth and began cleaning her face. A giant, smooth, gray-and-white feline, she possessed a massive self-respect that was in no way diminished by any awareness of her lowborn roots. Aunt Euphemia had received her as a gift from her laundress.

“Because her name was Sarah, puss was always referred to as the Sarah-cat by my husband,” Aunt Euphemia clarified. “Being eight years old, she is an extraordinary mouser. Have no fear, Mabel. Fighting is something the Sarah-cat never does and Joseph seldom.”
“Out of self-defense, they will be forced to fight at this spot,” Mabel remarked.

Right at this point, Smudge came into view. He leaped with glee to the middle of the chamber prior to spotting the unwanted guests. Thereupon he froze instantly; his tail swelled to thrice its normal size. The hair along his spine stood erect in a hostile curve; Smudge dipped his head, let out a terrifying scream of rage and resistance, and hurled himself toward the Sarah-cat.

The grand creature had ceased cleaning her face to observe him with curiosity. A single disdainful swat from her skilled paw countered his charge. Tumbling uncontrollably onto the rug, Smudge gathered himself in a daze. What manner of feline was she to have cuffed his ears? Dubiously, he gazed at the Sarah-cat. Should he try again, or should he refrain? Turning her back on him on purpose, the Sarah-cat restarted her grooming. Smudge chose to refrain. He failed to ever try again. Starting from that moment, the Sarah-cat was in complete control. Smudge did not ever bother her again.

However, Joseph unwisely sat upright and yawned. Smudge, eager to pay back his humiliation, launched himself at him. Though Joseph possessed a peaceful disposition, he was capable of fighting, and fighting effectively, when required. A succession of indecisive clashes followed. Smudge and Joseph engaged in combat whenever they saw one another daily. Nell sided with Smudge and loathed Joseph. Mabel felt hopeless. Aunt Euphemia, on the other hand, merely chuckled.

“Allow them to settle it themselves,” she remarked with indulgence. “They will become friendly before long. Joseph requires some activity—he was becoming excessively overweight. Meanwhile, Smudge must realize that he is not the sole cat in existence.”

In time, Joseph and Smudge resigned themselves to the state of affairs, transforming from bitter foes into devoted companions. Resting upon one shared pillow, they entwined their paws and solemnly licked one another’s faces clean.
“Everyone has become accustomed to one another,” Cressy remarked. “Also, cleaning dishes and sweeping floors are skills I have acquired.”
“However, you do not have to attempt to convince us of your ability to chloroform a cat,” Nell chuckled.
“The knothole was entirely to blame,” Cressy objected.

“That the knothole existed was fortunate,” Aunt Euphemia remarked with a somewhat stern tone. “The drowning of kittens is a necessity, I acknowledge, or else the earth would become overcrowded. However, no respectable, fully grown cat ought to be killed—except if he consumes eggs.”
“If you had witnessed Smudge upon his arrival at this place, you would not have deemed him particularly presentable,” Mabel remarked. “He truly resembled the Old Nick.”

“I do not think the Devil could be quite so unattractive,” Aunt Euphemia remarked thoughtfully. “He would fail to cause as much damage were that the case. My impression of him has always been that of an attractive gentleman.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “Girls, snow is starting to fall,” stated Cressy, entering on an evening in November, “and the path through the garden is covered with the most charming tiny crosses and stars. The fact that snowflakes are such truly exquisite objects had never caught my attention until now. A person possesses the time for observing details of that nature when leading the simple life. I thank you all for allowing me the opportunity to experience it. Feeling anxious over a five-cent increase in the price of a pound of butter is actually wonderful.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “Is that so?” asked Mabel, the one responsible for the family’s financial records.

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “It has—and your butter is right here. I am becoming rather skilled at shopping. It is more enjoyable than flirting,” Cressy stated seriously.

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “Prices are rising at a scandalous rate,” Mabel let out a sigh.

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “Don't worry. Thank goodness we still don't have to pay for air and salvation,” Aunt Euphemia said.

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “Laughter is the same way,” Nell appended. “It isn't taxed yet, which is fortunate, as every one of you will be laughing shortly. Robin’s letter is what I am about to read to you. Over this last year, his spelling has gotten vastly better, even if apostrophes aren't his strong suit, and he undeniably has a talent for composing an engaging letter. Give this a listen and laugh, prior to us getting down to the evening’s study-grind.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “Dear Nell,” Robin’s letter began, “I am writing to let you know that everyone here is doing well enough, and I hope you are also in good health. Snow is falling a bit today, and Thirza tells me the old woman up in the sky is dusting her feather mattresses. Is that old woman in the sky married to God, Nell? I would like to know.

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “Mrs. Sowerby was quite ill, though her health has improved now. The previous week, she tumbled down the steps to the cellar. As she dropped, she clutched the ledge holding every single milk pail and stewpan, causing it to collapse and plummet alongside her, producing a glorious racket. Initially, Thirza believed an earthquake was happening.

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “A stewpan got completely dented, and Mrs. Sowerby strained her ribs. Following the doctor's arrival, he provided her with liniment for her ribs, yet she failed to comprehend his instructions and swallowed the entire dose instead. Although the doctor remarked that it was miraculous she survived, she suffered no fatal effects, her ribs were healed, and Mrs. Sowerby maintains that doctors possess little knowledge regardless. Nevertheless, repairing the stewpan proved impossible. Thirza was forced to discard it. Thanksgiving occurred during the previous week. Classes were canceled, and a grand feast took place. I consumed mince pie, roast turkey, fruit cake, donuts, cheese, jam, and chocolate cake. Thirza predicted that I would perish, yet I survived. Lucy suffered from earache subsequently, except the location was not her ears but rather her stomach. I experienced no earache whatsoever.

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “The male teacher who just started instructs us in a humorous way. A week ago, he assigned every boy in the third class a task to compose an essay about our ideal future wives, while the girls had to write about their preferred husbands. Reading our papers caused him to burst into overwhelming laughter. I wrote this one, which I believed you might enjoy viewing.

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “‘The sort of spouse I’d prefer to Possess.

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “‘She needs to possess good manners, serve my food punctually, obey my instructions, and remain exceptionally polite toward me at all times. She needs to be fifteen yers old. She needs to treat the poor well, maintain a neat home, display a pleasant disposition, and attend church routinely. She needs to be exceedingly handsome with curly hair. Provided I secure a wife who matches my preferences entirely, I will prove to be an extraordinarily fine husband to her. It is my belief that a woman should be exceptionally good to her spouse. Certain unfortunate women possess no husbands whatsoever.

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “‘THE END.’”

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “I attended Mrs. Isaac Ducketts burial at Pale Sands during the previous week. The spouse of the deceased person experienced genuine sorrow. Mrs. Sowerby claims that the grandfather of Mrs. Duckett took a sheep, yet Thirza contends that we ought not talk badly about deceased individuals. Why ought we not, Nell? I wish to understand. It is fairly secure, is it not?

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “The other day, Mrs. Sowerby got terribly angry when I inquired whether she lived during Noah’s era. My intention was not to offend her. I merely desired to find out. Did she, Nell?

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “Mr. Pettifer desired to dispose of his hound. Consequently, he suspended him once, yet he revived and darted toward the barn as Mr. Pettifer dug his grave, which led him to suspend him once more, and he remained deceased on that occasion. Mr. Pettifer employs a new worker. He is extremely clumsy. Mr. Pettifer remarks that he possesses left-handed traits in both of his feet. Mr. Pembroke’s farmhand is slothful. Mrs. Pembroke asserts this, though Mr. Pembroke states that he is not precisely slothful, merely believing it is simpler to supplicate for items than to labor to attain them.

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “The prize pig belonging to Mrs. Gorham Pullen, which she spoke of so frequently, perished from a fit. According to Mrs. Sowerby, it was divine punishment for her vanity. However, my opinion is that the pig suffered unfairly. Milty Gammon was ill recently. A foul-tasting medicine was prescribed to him by the physician. I proposed to swallow it in his place if he paid me twenty-five cents, but those Boulters display such stinginess. Milty stated he preferred swallowing it on his own to keep his cash. When I inquired of Mrs. Gammon regarding the way one should proceed to capture a husband, she became extremely angry and replied that she did not know, as she had never pursued men.

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “The hall will be repainted by the B.V.I.S. They are sick of its blue color.

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “Yesterday evening, the new minister came over for tea. Three slices of pie were eaten by him. Mrs. Sowerby would term me piggy if I performed such an action. Furthermore, his eating was quick with large bites taken, something Thirza constantly instructs me against doing. What allows ministers to perform actions forbidden to boys? That is what I wish to learn.

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “There is no additional news from me. Accept these six kisses. xxxxxx. One is sent by Lucy. This is the one from her. x.

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “Your loving friend DAVID FARROW”

chapter_title: Chapter XVII A Letter from Robin
text: “P.S. Nell, I want to know, who was the father of the devil?”

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: Upon the arrival of the Christmas holidays, the girls belonging to Tabby’s Place departed for their own homes, yet Aunt Euphemia chose to remain right there.

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “I am unable to visit any of those locations where I received invitations while bringing along those three cats,” she stated. “Furthermore, I refuse to abandon the poor animals in this house by themselves for almost three weeks. I might do so if we were blessed with respectable neighbors who could give them food, yet this street contains only millionaires. Therefore, I will remain in this house and ensure Tabby’s Place stays warm until your return.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: Nell returned to her house anticipating her customary joy—expectations that were only partially realized. Upon her arrival, Brierley was locked in an unseasonably early, freezing, and tempestuous winter that surpassed the memories of even the “oldest inhabitant”. Massive snowdrifts practically encircled Grey Shutters. Ferocious storms raged on nearly every single day of that unfortunate break, and continuous drifting persisted even when the weather cleared. Whenever the roads were cleared, they promptly became blocked once more. Venturing outside proved nearly impossible. On three separate nights, the B.V.I.S. attempted to throw a gathering to celebrate the college students, but the gale proved so fierce on every occasion that no one could attend, leading them to abandon the effort in utter frustration. Although Nell cherished and remained devoted to Grey Shutters, she was unable to prevent her thoughts from drifting wistfully toward Tabby’s Place, with its comforting hearth, Aunt Euphemia’s laughing eyes, the trio of cats, the lively banter among the girls, and the delightful Friday nights spent with visiting college friends conversing about serious and lighthearted matters.

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: Nell experienced loneliness; throughout the entirety of the break, Isolde was confined to her house due to a severe bout of bronchitis. Travelling to Grey Shutters was impossible for her, and Nell was seldom able to reach Pear Hill, because snowdrifts blocked the former path through the Whispering Wood, while the lengthy route across the icy Lake of Glassy Waters proved nearly as difficult. Opal Pettigrew lay buried in the snow-covered cemetery; Odette Pullen had taken a job instructing at a school situated on western prairies. Hugh, indeed, remained loyal, slogging through the snow to Grey Shutters on any evening he could. Nevertheless, Hugh’s calls were no longer what they used to be. Nell nearly feared them. Looking up during a abrupt lull in conversation only to discover Hugh’s hazel eyes locked onto her, displaying a completely obvious look in their serious depths, was extremely unsettling; even more unsettling was discovering that she was glowing flushed and uneasy beneath his look, precisely as if—precisely as if—well, the experience caused great embarrassment. Nell longed to be returned to Tabby’s Place, a spot where another person was constantly present to soften the tension of an awkward moment. Whenever Hugh arrived at Grey Shutters, Thirza immediately retired to Mrs. Sowerby’s area and made sure the twins accompanied her. The meaning behind this action could not be misunderstood, leaving Nell in a state of powerless rage about it.

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: Robin, nevertheless, was thoroughly delighted. He delighted in stepping outside during the morning hours and clearing the tracks to the henhouse and well with a shovel. He took great pleasure in the Christmas-season treats that Mrs. Sowerby and Thirza competed to bake for Nell, and he was engrossed in a fascinating story, contained in a school library volume, about an extraordinary protagonist who appeared to possess an uncanny knack for stumbling into predicaments from which he was typically rescued by a volcanic explosion or an earthquake, which blasted him safely clear of his difficulties, dropped him into wealth, and concluded the narrative with suitable éclat.

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “Nell, I am telling you that the tale is fantastic,” he exclaimed with delight. “Reading it pleases me far more than reading the Bible.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “Would you?” Nell smiled.

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: Robin cast a curious glance toward her.

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “Nell, you appear not the least bit startled. When I mentioned it to Mrs. Sowerby, she was tremendously shocked.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “No, Robin, I am not shocked. A nine-year-old child preferring an adventure book over the Bible seems entirely understandable to me. However, once you grow up, it is my hope and belief that you will come to understand how incredible the Bible is.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “Well, I believe certain sections of it are good,” admitted Robin. “Take that tale regarding Joseph—it is great. However, had I been Joseph, forgiving the brothers would not have been my choice. Absolutely not, Nell. Off with all their heads I would have gone. Mrs. Sowerby became terribly angry when I uttered that, closing the Bible and declaring she would not read me another bit of it if I spoke in that manner. Therefore, I remain silent now while she reads it on Sunday afternoons; I merely formulate thoughts and share them with Milty Gammon the following day at school. I related the tale concerning Elisha and the bears to Milty, and it frightened him so much that not once has he mocked Mr. Pettifer’s bald head since. Do any bears exist on St. Brendan’s Island, Nell? I wish to learn.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “No longer,” Nell remarked, her mind elsewhere, while a dusting of snow was hurled by the gust against the glass. “Oh, my, is the storm ever going to end.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “God knows,” Robin remarked blithely, getting ready to go back to his book.

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: This time, Nell felt a wave of shock.

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “Robin!” she cried out in a tone of rebuke.

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “That is what Mrs. Sowerby says,” Robin objected. “Thirza asked, ‘Will Ludovic Speed and Theodora Dix ever get married?’ one evening last week, and Mrs. Sowerby replied, ‘“God knows”’—in precisely that manner.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “Well, she ought not to have said it,” Nell stated, quickly choosing which horn of this dilemma she would impale herself on. “No one should take that name in vain or use it casually, Robin. You must never do it again.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “If I utter it slowly and solemnly, similar to the preacher, would it still not?” Robin asked with seriousness.

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “No, not even then.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “Well, I shall not. Middle Welby is where Ludovic Speed and Theodora Dix reside, and according to Mrs. Agatha, he has courted her for a century. Will they not be getting too old for marriage soon, Nell? It is my hope that Hugh does not court you for such a length of time. Nell, at what time will you be getting married? Mrs. Sowerby states that it is certain.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “Mrs. Sowerby is a—” Nell started with anger; then she paused. “Terrible old gossip,” finished Robin serenely. “Every person refers to her like that. But is it certain, Nell? I wish to know.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “You’re a very silly little boy, Robin,” said Nell, walking out of the room with a haughty air. Nobody was in the kitchen, so she took a seat near the window while the cold winter twilight rapidly deepened. The sun was no longer up, and the wind had ceased. From behind a western ridge of purple clouds, a pale, cold moon peeked through. As the sky lost its color, the ribbon of yellow following the western horizon became sharper and more intense, giving the impression that every scattered ray of light was gathering in that single place; set against it, the far-off hills, bordered by priest-like firs, were sharply defined and dark. Nell gazed over the quiet, snow-covered fields, which appeared cold and dead beneath the unforgiving glow of that bleak sunset, and released a sigh. She felt extremely isolated and deeply sad, as she pondered whether she could go back to Wexcombe the following year. It appeared improbable. The sole scholarship available during the Sophomore year was quite minor. She refused to accept Thirza’s money, and there appeared to be scant chance of gathering sufficient earnings over the summer break.

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “I guess I will simply be forced to leave after this year,” she pondered gloomily, “and go back to teaching at a district school till my earnings cover the rest of my studies. By then, everyone in my former class will already be done with school, making Tabby’s Place an impossibility. Oh well! Cowardice is not for me. Having the ability to pay my own expenses if required is something I appreciate.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “Mr. Pettifer is coming up the lane, wading through,” Robin called out as he ran outside. “My hope is that he has the mail with him. Three days have passed since our last delivery. What those pesky Grits are up to is something I want to see. Nell, I am a Conservative. And let me tell you, keeping your eye on those Grits is necessary.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: The mail was delivered by Mr. Pettifer, and Nell’s sad mood was quickly chased away by cheerful letters from Mabel, Honora, and Cressy. A letter had also arrived from Aunt Euphemia, who wrote that she was maintaining the home fires, and she noted that the cats were all in good health and the house plants were thriving.

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “The climate has been exceedingly freezing,” her letter stated, “which is why the felines were allowed by me to stay overnight inside—Smudge along with Joseph upon the living-room couch, while the Sarah-cat rested at my bed’s end. Hearing her purr offers true companionship whenever I awaken during the night and ponder my unfortunate child over in the foreign field. Were her location any place other than India, anxiety would not plague me, yet the serpents in that region are reported to be dreadful. Driving the idea of those serpents from my mind requires the entirety of the Sarah-cat’s purring. My faith suffices for all matters except for the serpents. Why Providence created them escapes my comprehension. At times I doubt that He was their creator. My inclination is to think that the Old Harry played a role in fashioning them.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: Nell had set aside a slender, typed note for the end, believing it to be of little consequence. After reading its contents, she remained motionless, tears welling in her eyes.

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “What is the problem, Nell?” Thirza inquired.

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “Miss Lavinia Pembroke has passed away,” Nell stated, speaking softly.

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “At length, she passed away,” Thirza remarked. “Indeed, she was ill for more than a year, and her death has been anticipated by the Pembrokes at any moment. Her passing brings a merciful end to her dreadful suffering, Nell. Toward you, she was ever gentle.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “Thirza, she remained good to me until the end. Her attorney sent this letter. In her testament, she bequeathed me one thousand dollars.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “My goodness, isn't that a tremendous amount of cash,” cried Robin. “Isn't she the female you and Isolde landed upon when the pair of you leapt onto the bed in the spare room? Isolde related that tale to me. Did she bequeath you such a large sum for that reason?”

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “Be quiet, Robin,” Nell murmured softly. Her heart overflowing, she stole off to the gable of the porch, permitting Thirza and Mrs. Sowerby to discuss the intelligence as much as they wished.

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “Do you think Nell will ever wed now?” Robin wondered with concern. “When Dorcas Mott got married this past summer she remarked that if she’d possessed sufficient money to support herself she’d never have bothered with a man, though even a widower with eight children beat living with a sister-in-law.”

chapter_title: Chapter XVIII Miss Lavinia Remembers the Nell-girl
text: “Robin Farrow, keep quiet,” Mrs. Agatha stated with severity. “For a young child, your manner of speaking is simply shocking, it really is.”

“It is amazing to realize that I am turning twenty today and have permanently bidden farewell to my teenage years,” remarked Nell, who sat huddled on the hearth-rug holding Smudge on her lap, addressing Aunt Euphemia, who was perusing a book in her favorite chair. Nobody else was present in the living room. Having departed for a committee meeting, Mabel and Honora were absent, while Cressy was in her room above dressing up for a social gathering.
“I imagine you feel a bit regretful,” Aunt Euphemia remarked. “One’s teenage years are a delightful period of existence. Personally, I am pleased that I have remained in them continuously.”
A laugh came from Nell.

“Aunty, you never are going to. You are going to be eighteen when a hundred ought to be your age. Indeed, I regret it, and I am also somewhat discontented. A long time back, Miss Thorne informed me that my character, whether for good or evil, would be shaped once I reached twenty. I do not sense that mine is as it ought to be. Imperfections fill it.”

“So’s everybody’s,” Aunt Euphemia said happily. “Mine has a hundred cracks in it. It is probable that your Miss Thorne was referring to how, by the age of twenty, a person's character has acquired a fixed inclination toward one way or another, after which it keeps evolving along those lines. Nell, do not stress about it. Fulfill what you owe to God, to those around you, and to yourself, while enjoying your life. Such is the doctrine I live by, and it has served me quite effectively. To what place is Cressy going this evening?”
“She is attending a dance, having acquired the most charming attire for the occasion—creamy yellow silk paired with lace like cobwebs. Those brown shades of hers are perfectly complemented by it.”

“‘Silk’ and ‘lace’ are magical terms, wouldn’t you agree?” Aunt Euphemia asked. “I feel like darting away to a ball at their mere utterance. As for yellow silk, it brings a gown made of sunlight to mind. A yellow silk dress was something I perpetually desired, yet my mother initially, and later my husband, refused to countenance it. Obtaining a yellow silk dress is the absolute first action I intend to take upon arriving in heaven.”
Cressy descended the stairs to the sound of Nell laughing heartily, draped in magnificent splendor, and examined her reflection within the wall’s tall oval glass.
“A mirror that flatters fosters a pleasant disposition,” she remarked. “The glass in my own chamber unquestionably gives me a green hue. Am I looking quite nice, Nell?”
“Are you truly aware of how lovely you look, Cressy?” inquired Nell, with genuine appreciation.

“Naturally I do. Why else do mirrors and men exist? That was not my point. Have all my ends been tucked in? Is the alignment of my skirt straight? Also, would a lower position suit this rose better? I am worried it is placed too high—it is going to give me a lopsided appearance. However, I detest having objects tickle my ears.”
“All is completely ideal, and your indentation on the southwest side is charming.”
“Nell, a specific quality I admire in you above all is your generosity—you lack even the smallest trace of envy.”
“What reason does she have to feel envy?” Aunt Euphemia asked. “Perhaps she isn't fully as attractive as yourself, yet the nose she possesses is considerably more handsome.”
“I am aware of that,” Cressy acknowledged.
“A source of immense solace has ever been my nose,” admitted Nell.

“And the manner in which your hair grows on your forehead is something I love, Nell. Also, that single tiny curl, which constantly appears about to fall yet never falls, is delightful. However, regarding noses, my own causes me terrible distress. I am certain that it will be Byrney once I reach forty. How do you imagine I will appear when I turn forty, Nell?”
“As if she were a mature, wedded, settled female,” poked fun Nell.

“I will not,” Cressy stated, making herself comfortable as she awaited her escort. “Joseph, you spotted little creature, stay off my lap. I refuse to attend a dance covered in cat hairs. No, Nell, I am not going to appear matronly. However, I shall certainly end up married.”
“Is it to Hector or Orlando?” Nell inquired.
“I guess it will be to one of those men,” Cressy sighed, “provided I am ever able to choose between them.”
“Deciding ought not to prove difficult,” Aunt Euphemia chided.
“My birth made me an oscillating Aunty, and there is no way I will ever be stopped from swaying.”
“Cressida, you should possess greater composure.”

“Naturally, maintaining composure is preferable,” concurred Cressida, “yet you lose out on a great deal of enjoyment. Regarding Hector and Orlando, being acquainted with them would make you comprehend the challenge in selecting one over the other. Their pleasantness is identical.”
“In that case, choose a person who is kinder,” Aunt Euphemia proposed. “Look at that Senior who is so attached to you—Will Lorna. His eyes are so wonderfully big, pleasant, and gentle.”
“Cruelly, Cressy remarked that they resembled a cow’s, being somewhat excessively big and gentle.”
“What is your opinion regarding Laurence Tibbs?”
“No more can be said regarding him, save that he constantly appears as though he were recently starched and ironed.”
“Then there is Marr Holworthy. No one could possibly fault him.”

“No, he would be acceptable if he were not lacking money. I have to wed a wealthy gentleman, Aunt Euphemia. That requirement—along with handsome features—is essential. I would wed Hugh Carrow were he wealthy.”
“Oh, do you think so?” Nell inquired, speaking with a bite of venom.

“Even though Hugh isn't someone we desire for ourselves, oh, no, we dislike that notion immensely,” Cressy taunted. “However, we should avoid discussing unpleasant topics. Sometime or another, I will likely be forced to wed, yet I intend to delay that unfortunate moment for as long as possible.”
“Ultimately, Cressy, you should not take anyone as a husband unless you love them,” Aunt Euphemia said.
“‘Ah, the affection that once filled devoted souls Has faded from popularity for a very long time.’”
tweeted Cressy tauntingly. “There is the carriage. I am off—Bi-bi, you pair of old-fashioned darlings.”
After Cressy departed, Aunt Euphemia cast a serious gaze upon Nell.
“That girl is lovely, gentle, and kind, but, Nell, do you believe she is fully sane at times?”
“Oh, I doubt anything is wrong with Cressy’s head,” Nell remarked, suppressing a grin. “That is merely how she speaks.”
Her head was shaken by Aunt Euphemia.

“Well, Nell, I do hope that is true, since I am in love with her. However, I fail to comprehend her—she completely baffles me. She differs from every girl I have ever known, as well as every girl that I used to be.”
“Aunt Phemie, how many girls were in your family?”
“Around six of them, my darling.”
“This has been a dull, prosy day,” Cressy yawned, lazily stretching out upon the sofa after first ousting a pair of highly offended cats.
Nell raised her eyes from Pickwick Papers. Having completed her spring examinations, she was indulging in Dickens as a treat.

“This day was mundane for our part,” she uttered reflectively, “yet for others it was extraordinary. Someone experienced blissful joy during it. Maybe a monumental act occurred somewhere today—or an incredible poem was composed—or an important man was brought into the world. And a heart was crushed, Cressy.”
“Honey, why did you ruin your nice idea by adding that final sentence?” complained Cressy. “Broken hearts—or any disagreeable topic—are things I prefer not to think about.”
“Do you believe you will manage to avoid disagreeable matters your whole life, Cressy?”
“Good heavens, no. Aren't I facing them at this moment? Surely you wouldn't consider Hector and Orlando agreeable, would you, when they do nothing but make my life a misery?”
“Cressy, you do not ever treat anything with seriousness.”

“Why ought I to? A sufficient number of people do so. Individuals such as myself are required by the world, Nell, merely to entertain it. Were every person to be intellectual, grave, and profoundly, solemnly serious, it would be an awful place. The purpose I have is, in the words of Josiah Allen, ‘to charm and allure.’ Admit it now. In this previous winter, has not existence at Tabby’s Place actually been far brighter and more agreeable owing to my presence here to lighten all of you?”
“Indeed, it has,” admitted Nell.

“And every one of you loves me—including Aunt Euphemia, who considers me completely insane. For what reason, then, ought I to attempt to change? Oh, goodness, I am terribly drowsy. My eyes were open until one o’clock last night because I was engrossed in a chilling tale about a phantom. I perused it while lying in bed, and once I completed it do you imagine I was able to step out of bed so I could extinguish the light? I was not! Had Mabel not luckily arrived late that lamp would have continued to burn well and brightly right up to the morning. The moment I caught the sound of Mabel I summoned her inside, clarified my dilemma, and persuaded her to extinguish the lamp. Had I stepped out to accomplish it on my own I was certain that something would clutch my feet as I climbed back inside. On another note, Nell, has Aunt Euphemia made up her mind regarding her plans for this summer?”
“Yes, she will remain here. I am aware that she is doing this for those dear cats, despite her claim that unsealing her home is an excessive burden, and her aversion to staying as a guest.”
“What is it that you’re reading?”
“Pickwick.”

“A book like that perpetually stimulates my appetite,” Cressy remarked. “It contains such a abundance of delicious food. It appears the characters are constantly feasting upon ham and eggs alongside milk punch. Reading Pickwick usually prompts me to forage through the cupboard. Just thinking about it makes me realize I am famished. Do we have any delicacy in the pantry, Queen Nell?”
“This morning I baked a pie made of lemon. A slice of it can be yours.”

Cressy rushed away toward the pantry and Nell, alongside Smudge, went off to the orchard. It was a damp, delightfully fragrant night in the beginning of spring. The snow in the park had not completely disappeared; a small, dirty mound of it still remained beneath the pine trees along the harbor road, protected from the warmth of April suns. This sustained the mud on the harbor road and cooled the night air. Nevertheless, green grass was sprouting in protected areas and Hugh had discovered some faint, fragrant arbutus within a concealed location. Carrying a handful of it, he walked up from the park.

Perched upon the large gray rock in the fruit garden, Nell gazed at the poetic sight of a leafless birch branch suspended with complete elegance before the light red dusk. In her imagination, she was constructing a grand structure—a marvelous residence with sun-drenched courtyards and grand chambers filled with the fragrance of Araby, where she held power as ruler and mistress. Seeing Hugh approach across the fruit garden made her scowl. Recently, she had succeeded in avoiding being alone in Hugh's presence. However, he had cornered her completely this time; and even Smudge had abandoned her.
Taking a seat next to her on the rock, Hugh offered his Mayflowers to her.
“Nell, do these not bring back memories of home and the picnics from our former school days?”
Nell accepted them and pressed her face into their depths.
“At this exact instant, I am located within Mr. Silas Mott’s barrens,” she declared with pure delight.
“I take it you will actually arrive there in several days?”
“No, not for two weeks. I am intending to stay with Cressy in Harborough prior to returning home. You will reach Brierley ahead of me.”
“No, Nell, I will not spend any time in Brierley during this summer. Since I have received an offer for a position at the Daily News office, I intend to accept it.”

“Oh,” Nell replied absentmindedly. She pondered how an entire summer at Brierley would feel in Hugh’s absence. For some reason the thought displeased her. “Well,” she finished in a dull tone, “it is certainly beneficial for you.”
“Indeed, I had been wishing to obtain it, as it will prove beneficial to me in the coming year.”

“You ought not to overwork yourself,” uttered Nell, absent-mindedly stating whatever came to mind. Her heart longed for Cressy to emerge. “Your studies have been so continuous during this past winter. Is this night not lovely? Imagine this: beneath that gnarled, ancient tree over there, I chanced upon a bunch of white violets today. It gave me the sensation of unearthing a mine of gold.”
“It is a habit of yours to continually find gold mines,” Hugh remarked—likewise inattentively.
“We should walk over and check whether we are able to discover any others,” Nell enthusiastically proposed. “Cressy will be summoned by me and—”
“Do not concern yourself with Cressy and the violets at this moment, Nell,” Hugh said gently, holding her hand so firmly that she was unable to pull it away. “I have something to tell you.”
“Oh, refrain from saying it,” Nell exclaimed in a pleading manner. “Refrain—please, Hugh.”

“I have to. We cannot continue in this manner anymore. Nell, my love belongs to you. You are aware of that. I—I am unable to express the extent of it. Can you give me your word that you will marry me one day?”
“I—I am unable to,” Nell uttered sorrowfully. “Oh, Hugh—you—you have ruined it all.”
“Are you completely devoid of feelings for me?” was Hugh’s inquiry following a most terrible silence, throughout which Nell had lacked the courage to raise her eyes.
“No—not like that. You mean a lot to me as a friend, certainly. However, Hugh, I am not in love with you.”
“Is there no chance, however, that you might offer me a bit of hope for the future?”
“No, I can’t,” Nell cried out in desperation. “I never, never can love you—in that way—Hugh. This is something you must never mention to me again.”

Another interval occurred—of such great length and terror that Nell was finally forced to raise her eyes. Hugh’s features were drained of colour right to his lips. And his gaze—Nell trembled, however, and turned her sight elsewhere. This contained no romance. Did marriage offers have to be either absurd or—terrible? Would she be able to erase the memory of Hugh’s countenance?
“Is there anyone besides us?” he inquired finally with a quiet tone.

“No—no,” Nell answered with fervor. “I have no affection for anyone of that sort—and my fondness for you surpasses anyone else in the world, Hugh. And it is essential—it is essential that we remain friends, Hugh.”
A small, harsh laugh escaped Hugh.
“Comrades! Nell, I am unable to be fulfilled by your friendship. It is your love that I desire—yet you inform me that it will always be out of my reach.”

“Forgive me, Hugh; I’m sorry,” represented the entirety of what Nell was able to utter. Oh, where, indeed, had gone every one of those elegant and courteous addresses with which she had routinely, in her mind, turned away unwanted suitors?
Hugh softly let go of her hand.
“Forgiveness is not required here. I believed at certain moments that you held genuine affection for me. It was merely my own self-deception. Farewell, Nell.”

Nell made her way to her room, took a seat on her window seat behind the pines, and wept bitterly. A feeling came over her that an incalculably precious element had departed from her life. Naturally, it was Hugh’s friendship. Oh, for what reason did she have to lose it in this manner?
“Honey, what is wrong?” Cressy inquired, stepping inside via the moon-drenched darkness.
Nell offered no reply. Just then, she longed for Cressy to be a thousand miles distant.
“You have probably gone and turned down Hugh Carrow. Nell Harcourt, you are a fool!”
“Is it idiotic to decline marrying someone who holds no place in my heart?” Nell asked with a chilling tone, driven to answer.

“You fail to recognize love when it appears before you. Using your imagination, you have fabricated an idea that you believe to be love, and you anticipate that genuine love will resemble it. Look at that, I have just uttered the initial logical remark of my entire existence. I am curious about how I accomplished it?”
“Cressy,” begged Nell, “do go away and leave me by myself for a short time. My world has collapsed into ruins. I wish to rebuild it.”
“Lacking any Hugh inside?” asked Cressy, departing.

"A world without Hugh!" Nell uttered the phrase mournfully. Might it not turn out to be an extremely desolate, deserted realm? Be that as it may, Hugh was entirely to blame. He had ruined their wonderful friendship. She would simply have to adjust to existing in its absence.

The two weeks that Nell passed in Harborough were extremely enjoyable, though a subtle undertone of obscure ache and discontent coursed through the period whenever Hugh crossed her mind. Still, she had few opportunities to ponder over him. A most lively spot was "Mount Holly," the lovely, historic Lindsay family estate, which swarmed with Cressy’s male and female companions. A almost dizzying sequence of excursions, balls, outings, and rowing gatherings occurred—every one of which Cressy vividly grouped together as "jamborees"; Hector and Orlando were present so incessantly that Nell pondered whether their sole occupation was catering to the whims of that elusive Cressy. Each was a pleasant, honorable young man, yet Nell refused to be persuaded to judge which of the two was preferable.
“And I was relying so heavily on you to assist me in deciding which one I ought to give my pledge of marriage to,” lamented Cressy.
“That is something you have to accomplish on your own. Deciding which spouses are suitable for everyone else is a skill you have truly mastered,” Nell replied, with a somewhat biting tone.
“Ah, that is a completely distinct matter,” Cressy stated, in truth.

Yet the most delightful moment of Nell’s stay in Harborough occurred when she visited where she was born—that small, faded yellow dwelling on a secluded street which had so frequently filled her dreams. Her eyes shone with joy as she gazed upon it, stepping through the gate alongside Cressy.

“It matches my mental image nearly to a tee,” she remarked. “Although honeysuckle does not drape over the windows, a lilac tree stands near the gate, and—indeed, muslin curtains hang in the windows. It brings me such joy that the yellow paint remains.”
The door was opened by a woman who was extremely thin and extremely tall.

“Indeed, two decades back, the Shirleys were residents here,” she remarked, responding to the query from Nell. “The place was leased by them. My memory holds them. Fever claimed both of their lives at the same time. A deeply tragic event occurred. A baby was left behind by them. My assumption is that it passed away a long time back. That child was frail. The child was taken in by Old Thomas and his spouse—just as though they lacked a sufficient number of their own children.”
“It failed to perish,” Nell remarked, grinning, “and I was the infant in question.”

“Is that so! Well, you have gotten bigger,” the woman cried out, appearing greatly astonished that Nell was no longer an infant. “Now that I examine you, I notice the likeness. Your complexion is like your pa’s. Red hair was what he had. However, your eyes and mouth look like your ma’s. A sweet little person was what she was. Her school was attended by my darter, who was almost wild about her. A single grave held both of them when they were buried, and a tombstone was erected for them by the School Board as a recompense for devoted service. Will you step inside?”
“May I be allowed to explore the entire house?” Nell asked with enthusiasm.

“Goodness, certainly, go right ahead if that is your wish. It will be quick—since the place is quite small. My husband gets no peace from me about constructing another kitchen, yet moving fast is not his way. That door leads to the parlor, while a pair of rooms sits on the upper floor. Feel free to wander around on your own. My attention is needed by the baby. Your birth took place in the room facing east. Your mother expressing her fondness for watching the dawn comes back to me; moreover, I recall being told that your arrival occurred exactly as the sun ascended, making its beams upon your countenance the initial sight your mother beheld.”

Nell climbed the tight staircase and stepped into that small east room with her heart overflowing. To her, it resembled a sanctuary. In this place, her mother had envisioned the lovely, joyful visions of awaiting motherhood; in this place, that crimson dawn illumination had washed over the two of them during the holy moment of delivery; in this place, her mother had passed away. Nell gazed around herself with awe, her eyes filled with tears. For her, it represented one of life’s precious moments that shine brilliantly always in recollection.
“Only consider that—when I came into the world, mother was not as old as I currently am,” she murmured.
As Nell descended the stairs, the mistress of the home encountered her in the hallway. A small, dusty bundle secured with a washed-out blue ribbon was extended toward her by the woman.

“In this upstairs closet, I stumbled upon a package of ancient mail after I moved in,” she remarked. “Their contents are unknown to me—as I did not care to examine them, yet ‘Miss Bertha Willis’ is written on the first one, which happened to be your mother's unmarried name. Should you desire to possess them, they are yours to keep.”
“Oh, thank you—thank you,” Nell cried, clutching the bundle with delight.

“That was everything the house contained,” her hostess stated. “The doctor bills were paid by selling all the furniture, and your ma’s clothes and small possessions were given to Mrs. Thomas. I suppose those things did not last very long with such a crowd of Thomas children. If I remember them correctly, they were destructive young animals.”
“There is not a single item of my mother's in my possession,” Nell said, her voice filled with emotion. “I—I will never be able to offer you sufficient thanks for these letters.”

“I am happy to do it. Goodness, your eyes really resemble your mother's. Hers were capable of practically speaking. Your dad was rather plain-looking, yet extremely pleasant. When their wedding took place, I remember people remarking that a couple had never been so deeply devoted to one another—Poor things, their lives ended not long after; nevertheless, their time together was filled with tremendous happiness, which I reckon is worth a lot.”

Nell yearned to return home so that she might read her cherished correspondence, yet she undertook a brief journey prior to doing so. Solitarily, she visited the verdant section of the “old” Harborough cemetery where her father and mother lay buried, depositing the white blossoms she brought with her upon their grave. Subsequently, she hurried back to Mount Holly, sequestered herself within her chamber, and perused the letters. A portion had been penned by her father, and others by her mother. They were few in quantity—totaling merely twelve—because Edmund and Bertha Harcourt had rarely been apart throughout their courtship. Aged, discolored, and faint, the correspondence was smudged by the passage of time. No deep expressions of intellect were written upon the discolored and creased sheets, which contained solely messages of affection and faith. The charm of bygone moments adhered to them—the distant, affectionate dreams of those lovers who had died long ago. Bertha Harcourt had been endowed with the talent for composing letters that captured the author's delightful character in phrasing and ideas that kept their grace and sweetness across the years. These writings were gentle, private, and hallowed. For Nell, the most delightful among them was the note composed following her arrival into the world and sent to her father during a short trip away. It was packed with a glowing, youthful mother’s descriptions of “baby”—her intelligence, her brilliance, and her innumerable charming traits.

“When she is sleeping, I love her most, and even more when she is awake,” was what Bertha Harcourt had set down in the postscript. It was likely the final line she had ever written. Her end was extremely close.

“This day has been more beautiful to me than any other,” Nell told Cressy later that evening. “My father and mother have been FOUND by me. They have been made REAL to me by those letters. I am no longer an orphan. It feels to me as though I opened a book and discovered sweet, beloved roses of yesterday pressed between its pages.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: Flickering across the kitchen walls of Grey Shutters went the shadows cast by the hearthfire, since coolness marked the spring evening; entering by the unclosed eastern window came the delicate, pleasing sounds of the dark hours. Thirza sat beside the hearth—physically, that is. Mentally, her youthful feet carried her through paths of the past. Recently, Thirza had passed numerous hours in this fashion, despite believing she ought to be crafting knitwear for the twins.

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “I guess I am getting older,” she remarked.

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: Still, Thirza was scarcely altered over those nine years, except for having become somewhat skinnier, and still more sharp-featured; a few additional gray strands showed in her hair, which remained coiled into that very same tight bun, pinned through by two hairpins—could those be the exact same hairpins? Her look, however, had transformed immensely; that quality around her lips that used to suggest a capacity for humor was now remarkably pronounced; the expression in her eyes was softer and kinder, while she smiled with greater frequency and gentleness.

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: Thirza reflected upon the entirety of her past existence, from her restricted yet contented early years, to the secret dreams and crushed aspirations of her youth, and then the enduring, drab, restricted, unvarying period of uninteresting middle age. Afterwards came the arrival of Nell—a bright, creative, passionate youngster possessing a loving heart and a realm of imagination, who brought along hue, heat, and brilliance, transforming the barren expanse of life into something flourishing like a rose. It seemed to Thirza that among her sixty years of life, the only ones she had truly experienced were the nine that came after Nell's appearance. Furthermore, Nell was returning home the next evening.

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: Opening, the kitchen door revealed a figure, and Thirza raised her eyes anticipating Mrs. Sowerby. Instead, Nell was standing in front of her, height impressive and eyes gleaming like stars, while holding an abundance of Mayflowers and violets.

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “Nell Harcourt!” Thirza cried out. Just this once, her customary restraint abandoned her; she embraced her girl, pressing her and her blossoms tightly to her chest, affectionately kissing her radiant hair and lovely face. “I didn’t expect you until tomorrow evening. By what means did you travel from Delford?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “I came on foot, most beloved Thirza. Did I not accomplish this twenty times during the Regent’s era? My luggage will be delivered by the mailman tomorrow; a sudden wave of longing for home simply overtook me, so my arrival was moved up by a day. And ah! That stroll through the May dusk was so wonderful; I paused beside the barrens to gather these Mayflowers; my path led through Violet-Vale, which currently resembles a giant bowl filled with violets—those precious, sky-colored blossoms. Inhale their scent, Thirza—absorb them fully.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: Thirza dutifully took a sniff, yet her curiosity lay far more with Nell than with the aroma of violets.

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “Take a seat, child. You have to be completely exhausted. I’ll go fetch some dinner for you.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “A lovely moon is coming up past the hills this evening, Thirza, and oh, the frogs serenaded me all the way from Delford! The music of the frogs is something I truly love. It appears tied to every one of my fondest memories of past spring nights. And I am always reminded by it of my very first evening here. Is it something you recall, Thirza?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “Indeed, I am,” Thirza replied emphatically, “for it is hardly probable that I will at any point forget it.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “That year, their singing in the brook and the marsh was so wild. From my window during the dusk, I would hear them and ponder how their song could appear simultaneously so joyful and so mournful. Oh, returning home feels truly wonderful! Although Wexcombe was magnificent and Harborough was charming, home is Grey Shutters.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “From what I gather, Hugh won't be returning home this summer,” Thirza remarked.

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “No.” Nell spoke in a voice that caused Thirza to look at her abruptly, yet Nell seemed completely focused on setting her violets inside a bowl. “Look, aren’t they sweet?” she continued with haste. “The year resembles a book, doesn't it, Thirza? Mayflowers and violets write the pages of spring, roses write summer's, red maple leaves write autumn's, and holly and evergreen write winter's.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “Was Hugh successful in his exams?” Thirza continued to ask.

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “Splendidly. He was at the top of his class. But where have the twins and Mrs. Sowerby gone?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “Agatha and Lucy are visiting Mr. Pettifer’s house. Robin has gone down to Boulters’. Right now, I believe I can hear him approaching.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: Robin charged inside, caught sight of Nell, halted, and thereupon threw himself at her with a happy cry.

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “Oh, Nell, seeing you makes me so happy! Listen, Nell, since previous autumn my height has increased by two inches. My measurement was taken by Mrs. Sowerby using her tape today, and listen, Nell, look at my front tooth. I don't have it anymore. After Mrs. Sowerby fastened a piece of string's first end onto it, she attached the opposite end to the door and subsequently closed the door. Two cents were paid to me by Milty when I sold it to him. Teeth are being collected by Milty.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “Why on earth does he need teeth?” Thirza inquired.

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “For a necklace to play Indian Chief,” Robin explained, scrambling onto Nell’s lap. “Fifteen are already in his possession, and all the others have been promised, meaning it is pointless for any of the remaining group to begin gathering them as well. The Boulters are exceptional at business, I am telling you.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “Did you behave well while at Mrs. Gammon’s?” Thirza demanded sternly.

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “Indeed; however listen, Thirza, being good has grown exhausting to me.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “You would grow weary of misbehaving far more quickly, Robin-boy,” Nell remarked.

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “Well, it would be enjoyable for the duration, wouldn't it?” Robin insisted. “Afterward, I could regret it, couldn't I?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “Feeling regret could not eliminate the results of misbehaving, Robin. Have you forgotten that Sunday a year ago in the summer time when you fled from Sunday School? At that time, you mentioned to me that doing wrong was not beneficial. What activity were you and Milty engaged in this afternoon?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “Well, we went fishing and pursued the cat, and searched for eggs, and shouted at the echo. A tremendous echo exists in the bush behind the Gammon barn. Tell me, what is echo, Nell; I wish to know.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “Echo, Robin, is a lovely nymph who resides far off in the forest and chuckles at everyone from amidst the hills.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “How is she described?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “Darkness marks her hair and eyes, yet white as snow describes her neck and arms. The full extent of her beauty remains hidden from every mortal eye. She possesses greater fleetness than a deer, and our knowledge of her is limited solely to that mocking voice of hers. Nighttime brings the sound of her calling; beneath the stars, the sound of her laughter can be heard. Yet she remains forever invisible to you. Should you pursue her, she flies to a distance, continuously laughing at you from just beyond the adjacent hill.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “Is that factual, Nell? Or is it a lie?” inquired Robin, gazing intently.

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “Robin,” Nell asked in desperation, “do you not possess sufficient sense to tell a fairytale apart from a lie?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: “Robin persisted, “I want to know what it is, then, that talks back from the Gammon bush?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
text: Robin’s thoughts were clearly redirected by the reference to age, as following a brief pause for consideration, he uttered in a low, earnest voice:

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters

chapter_title: Chapter XXII Spring and Nell Return to Grey Shutters
