chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People
text: During that summer, living in Brierley proved to be exceedingly delightful, even if Nell felt pursued by a feeling that “something gone which should be there,” right in the middle of all her holiday pleasures. She refused to confess, even within her most private thoughts, that Hugh’s absence brought this about. Nevertheless, whenever she was forced to trek back home by herself following prayer meetings and B.V.I.S. pow-wows, while Isolde together with Gideon, alongside numerous other happy pairs, dawdled down the dark, star-filled rural lanes, her heart suffered a strange, solitary pang that she was unable to clarify. Hugh refrained from even sending her letters, though she had anticipated he perhaps would. She was aware that he sent notes to Isolde now and then, yet she refused to ask regarding him; meanwhile Isolde, assuming that Hugh corresponded with Nell, offered no news. Hugh’s mother—a cheerful, open, buoyant woman who lacked an abundance of tact—possessed a most awkward practice of inquiring of Nell, invariably using a distressingly clear tone and invariably in front of a gathering, whether she had received word from Hugh recently. Unfortunate Nell was left to simply flush terribly and mutter, “not very lately,” a response that everyone, Mrs. Carrow as well, interpreted as nothing more than a modest dodge.

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People
text: Aside from that, Nell was fond of her summer. In June, Honora arrived for a joyful stay; then, after her departure, Mr. and Mrs. Stanhope, Cedric and Belinda the Fourth returned “home” covering July and August.

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People
text: “Miss Rosalind” was unchanged, other than becoming still more charming and lovely. She was worshipped by Cedric, and the bond they shared was a wonderful thing to observe.

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People

Instead, I address her as ‘Mother Rosalind’ and she is second in my affection only to father. In fact—I actually hold her slightly dearer than you, teacher.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People
text: At thirteen years of age, Cedric had grown quite tall for his time of life. His face remained as lovely as before, his eyes were just as handsome, and his imagination continued to act like a prism, turning whatever met it into brilliant rainbows. He enjoyed wonderful strolls with Nell through the woods, fields, and along the coast. No two people were ever more completely “kindred spirits.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People
text: Belinda the Fourth had grown up into a young woman. A massive pompadour was her current hairstyle, and she no longer wore the blue ribbon bows of former times, yet the freckles on her face, the snub on her nose, and the breadth of her mouth and smiles remained completely unchanged.

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People
text: “Miss Harcourt, ma’am, you don’t suppose my speech sounds like a Yankee accent, do you?” she inquired with concern.

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People

I have nothing at all against the Yankees, Miss Harcourt, ma’am. They are genuinely civilized. However, I would choose old St. Brendan’s Island over them any day.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People
text: Cedric passed his initial two weeks at Brierley alongside his grandmother Stanhope. Upon his arrival, Nell was present to greet him, discovering that he was filled with intense excitement to reach the beach—where Nora, the Golden Lady, and the Twin Sailors would be located. Waiting to consume his evening meal was almost impossible for him. Was it not possible for him to glimpse Nora’s fairy-like face looking around the headland, gazing for his arrival with longing? Nevertheless, the Cedric who returned from the beach at dusk was extremely subdued.

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People
text: “Was your search for your Rock People unsuccessful?” Nell inquired.

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People
text: “Oh, Cedric, it is you who are changed,” Nell said. “You have become too old for the Rock People. They only care for children as playfellows. I fear that the Twin Sailors will never come to you again in the pearly, enchanted boat featuring the sail of moonshine; and no longer will the Golden Lady play for you on her golden harp. Even Nora will not meet with you much longer. You have to pay the penalty for growing up, Cedric. You have to leave fairyland behind.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People
text: “The pair of you speak just as much nonsense as you always have,” stated aged Mrs. Stanhope, partly with fondness and partly with admonishment.

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People
text: “Oh, no, we don’t,” Nell said, solemnly shaking her head. “We are becoming extremely, extremely clever, and it is a great shame. We are not nearly as captivating once we discover that speech is provided to allow us to hide what we think.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People
text: “However, it is not—we are granted the ability to share what we think,” Mrs. Stanhope stated in all earnestness. Having no knowledge of Tallyrand, she failed to comprehend epigrams.

During this visit, she managed by chance to quicken Ludovic Speed’s slow courtship of Theodora Dix, an event properly detailed in a different account of her life.(1) Arnold Sherman, an older acquaintance of the Irvings, was staying there during that period as well, contributing significantly to the overall enjoyment of their time.

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People
text: “This has been such a lovely time to play,” Nell remarked. “My strength feels completely renewed. And just two weeks remain before my return to Portmaris, Wexcombe, and Tabby’s Place. Miss Rosalind, Tabby’s Place is the most beloved location. It feels to me as though I possess a pair of homes—a home at Grey Shutters and another at Tabby’s Place. But where did the summer vanish? It feels as though no time at all has passed since my arrival home on that spring night bearing the Mayflowers. During my childhood, I was unable to perceive the far end of summer. The time lay out ahead of me like a period without end. At present, ‘’tis a handbreadth, ’tis a tale.’”

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People
text: “Nell, do you and Hugh Carrow remain as close friends as you once were?” Miss Rosalind inquired softly.

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People
text: “I observe that a problem has arisen, Nell. I will be intrusive and inquire about its nature. Have the two of you had a disagreement?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People
text: “Completely certain.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People
text: “I wonder why everyone appears to believe that I should wed Hugh Carrow,” Nell stated in an irritated manner.

chapter_title: Chapter XXIII Cedric Cannot Find the Rock People
text: “For the simple reason that you were created and destined for one another, Nell—that is the reason. There is no need for you to throw back that youthful head of yours. It is the truth.”
“PROSPECT POINT, “August 20th.

“Dear Nell—spelled—with—an—E,” Cressy penned, “I have to force my eyes to stay open just to send you a note. Honey, I’ve ignored you terribly over the course of this summer, yet I have ignored every one of my other correspondents as well. There is a giant stack of letters awaiting my reply, which means I have to pull myself together mentally and get to work. Please forgive my jumbled metaphors. I am terribly drowsy. Yesterday evening Cousin Emily and I paid a visit to a neighbor. A few other guests were present as well, and the moment those unlucky individuals departed, our hostess alongside her trio of daughters ripped every single one of them to shreds. I was certain they would start picking apart Cousin Emily and me the instant the door was closed after our departure. Upon our return home, Mrs. Lilly let us know that the previously mentioned neighbor’s farmhand was suspected of coming down with scarlet fever. One can consistently rely on Mrs. Lilly for uplifting news of that sort. I am terrified of scarlet fever. Once I got into bed, thoughts of it kept me from falling asleep. I tossed and turned continuously, suffering through terrifying dreams whenever I managed to nod off for a brief moment; then at three o'clock I woke up suffering from a high fever, a raw throat, and a violent headache. I was certain I was sick with scarlet fever; I leaped out of bed in a fright and searched for Cousin Emily’s ‘doctor book’ so I could study the symptoms. Nell, I possessed every single one of them. Therefore I returned to bed, and having learned the worst, slept soundly for the remainder of the night. Even though I have never been able to comprehend why a top would sleep more soundly than any other object. However, when I woke up this morning I felt entirely fine, meaning it could not have been the fever after all. I reckon that even if I contracted it yesterday evening, it would not have manifested that quickly. I am capable of keeping that in mind during the day, but at three in the morning I am simply incapable of reasoning logically.

“I guess you are curious about my presence at Prospect Point. You see, I am fond of spending one summer month by the seaside, and father demands my attendance at the ‘select boardinghouse’ owned by his second-cousin Emily at Prospect Point. Therefore, two weeks back, I arrived as I always do. And in accordance with routine, elderly ‘Uncle Mark Miller’ drove me from the depot using his antique buggy and the creature he describes as his ‘generous purpose’ horse. He is a pleasant aged fellow who presented me with a few pink peppermints. To me, peppermints have a distinctively holy quality—likely because Grandmother Lindsay habitually handed them to me during services when I was small. On one occasion, alluding to the scent of peppermints, I inquired, ‘Is that the odor of sanctity?’ I hesitated to consume Uncle Mark’s peppermints owing to the fact that he merely retrieved them loose from his coat, needing to sort out some corroded nails and additional items from the batch prior to handing them over. However, refusing to wound his precious old emotions under any circumstances, I cautiously scattered them piece by piece along the thoroughfare. After I had discarded the final piece, Uncle Mark remarked, with mild disapproval, ‘Ye shouldn’t a’et all them candies to onct, Miss Cressy. You’ll likely have the stummick-ache.’

“Except for me, Cousin Emily entertains merely five roomers—a single young man alongside four aged women. Mrs. Lilly sits to my right side. She belongs to that class of individuals who appear to derive a morbid delight from describing every single one of their numerous sicknesses, pains, and aches. It is impossible to name a single malady without her uttering, while her head shakes, “Ah, I know too well what that is”—after which every detail is dumped upon you. Ezra asserts that he formerly brought up locomotor ataxia where she could hear, whereupon she claimed she was all too familiar with that condition. It plagued her for a decade before a wandering physician at last healed her.
“Who is Ezra? Just wait, Nell Harcourt. You shall be told everything regarding Ezra when the correct time and place arrive. He must not be confused with respectable old women.

“Mrs. Phinney sits next to me on my left at the table. A lamenting, sorrowful tone marks her speech constantly—you feel a tense anticipation that she will break down weeping at any second. The way she presents herself suggests that existence is truly a valley of grief to her, and that smiling, to say nothing of laughing, constitutes a genuinely blameworthy weakness. Her judgment of me is harsher than Aunt Euphemia's, and she lacks the deep affection to compensate for it that Aunty J. possesses.”

“Directly opposite and to one side of me sits Miss Maria Grimsby. On my very first day here, I mentioned to Miss Maria that rain appeared somewhat likely—and Miss Maria laughed. I observed that the way from the train station was quite lovely—and Miss Maria laughed. I noted that a handful of mosquitoes still seemed to remain—and Miss Maria laughed. I stated that Prospect Point retained all its former beauty—and Miss Maria laughed. Were I to state to Miss Maria, ‘My father has hanged himself, my mother has taken poison, my brother is in the penitentiary, and I am in the last stages of consumption,’ Miss Maria would laugh. It is beyond her control—she came into the world this way; nevertheless, it is deeply gloomy and dreadful.
“Mrs. Hollis is the fifth old lady. She is a sweet old person; however, she is a most uninteresting conversationalist because she speaks only well of everyone.
“And at this moment regarding Ezra, Nell.

“On my very first day there, I observed a youth seated across the table from me, beaming in my direction like someone who had been acquainted with me since my infancy. Because Uncle Mark had informed me, I was aware that Ezra Hale was his name, that he was studying theology at St. Columbia, and that he had assumed responsibility for the Point Prospect Mission Church over the summer.

“He is an extremely unattractive young man—honestly, the most unattractive young man I have ever laid eyes on. He possesses a large, gangly frame featuring ridiculous, elongated legs. His hair is flaxen and limp, his eyes are green, his mouth is large, and his ears—though I refrain from considering his ears whenever possible.
“His voice is delightful—closing your eyes makes him charming—and the beauty of his soul and nature is unquestionable.

“We became close friends immediately. Naturally, he graduated from Wexcombe, which serves as a bond between us. We went fishing and boating with each other; additionally, we strolled along the shore in the moonlight. In the moonlight he appeared less plain, and oh, he was delightful. Delightfulness virtually radiated from him. The elderly women—with the exception of Mrs. Hollis—disapprove of Ezra, since he laughs and jokes—and since he clearly prefers the company of silly me to theirs.

“Somehow, Nell, I do not wish for him to regard me as shallow. This makes no sense. Why ought I to be concerned about the opinion of a flaxen-haired individual named Ezra, whom I had not previously set eyes on?

“On the previous Sunday, Ezra gave the sermon at the church in the village. Naturally, I attended, yet I was unable to grasp that Ezra was about to preach. To me, it continued to feel like an enormous joke that he was a minister—or was preparing to become one.

“Well, Ezra preached. And, once he had been preaching for ten minutes, I felt so tiny and meaningless that I believed I had to be unseen by the unassisted eye. Ezra didn't say a single thing regarding women, and he didn't look my way once. Even so, right then, I understood what an awful, trivial, shallow-spirited little butterfly I was, and the dreadful extent to which I must diverge from the woman of Ezra’ ideals. That woman would be magnificent, powerful, and honorable. He was exceptionally serious, gentle, and faithful. He embodied all that a clergyman should be. I marvelled at how I had ever considered him unattractive—yet he truly is!—what with those impassioned eyes and that scholarly forehead that his unkempt hair concealed on ordinary days.
“The sermon was splendid, allowing me to listen to it for eternity, yet it caused me to feel completely miserable. Oh, how I desire to resemble you, Nell.

“Overtaking me along the path toward home, he smiled with his customary brightness. Yet his expression was no longer able to fool me. The true Ezra had been revealed to me. It made me ponder whether he would ever behold the true Cressy—a person whom no one, not even you, Nell, has yet beheld.

“‘Ezra,’ I uttered—omitting to address him as Mr. Hale. Was it not terrible? Yet during certain moments such details are irrelevant—‘Ezra, being a minister was your destiny from birth. It was impossible for you to be anything different.’

“‘No, I was unable to,’ he stated with gravity. ‘I attempted to be a different person for a extended period—I lacked the desire to be a clergyman. However, I eventually realized that it was the labor assigned to me—and with the assistance of God, I will endeavor to fulfill it.’

“He spoke in a quiet, respectful tone. It occurred to me that he would perform his labor effectively and with noble purpose; a woman possessing the inherent disposition and preparation to assist his efforts would be fortunate indeed. She would not resemble a feather, tossed by each changing breeze of whim. Knowing which hat to wear would never be an issue for her. Likely, a single one would be all she owned. Clergymen are rarely wealthy. Yet, owning merely one hat, or even none, would not bother her, for Ezra would be hers.

“Nell Harcourt, do not dare to utter, suggest, or entertain the thought that Mr. Hale has won my heart. How could I ever harbor feelings for an awkward, impoverished, unattractive theology student—with the name Ezra? In the words of Uncle Mark, ‘It’s impossible, and what’s more it’s improbable.’
“Good night, CRESSY.”

“P.S. Although it cannot be—I am dreadfully fearful that it is real. I feel joyful, miserable, and frightened. It is impossible for him to ever love me, I am certain. Is it possible that I might grow into a decent minister’s wife, Nell? Furthermore, will I be expected to guide the prayers? P G.”
“I’m comparing what’s inside with what’s outside,” Nell said, her gaze shifting from Tabby’s Place’s window toward the park’s far-off pines.

“Aunt Phemie, I have an entire afternoon to devote to pleasant idleness. Is it better to pass it in this spot, featuring a comfortable hearth, a dish piled with tasty russet apples, three purring, contented cats, and a pair of flawless porcelain dogs boasting green noses? Or should I head over to the park, drawn by the attraction of gray forests and gray waves splashing against the rocks of the harbor?”
“I would choose the park if my age matched yours,” Aunt Euphemia remarked, using a knitting needle to tickle the yellow ear of Joseph.
“Aunty, I believed you maintained that you were just as young as the rest of us,” Nell teased.
“Indeed, within my spirit. However, I must concede that my legs lack the youth of your own. Head outside to catch some fresh air, Nell. Your complexion has appeared pale recently.”

“I believe I will head over to the park,” Nell stated impatiently. “Living room quietness does not appeal to me today. My desire is to feel solitary, unrestricted, and untamed. Nobody will be in the park, as all the people are going to attend the football match.”
“For what reason were you absent from it?”

“‘Nobody axed me, sir, she said’—or at least, no one except that dreadful small Dan Ranger. I would not attend anything alongside him; however, instead of injuring his fragile little sensitive emotions, I stated that I was not attending the game whatsoever. It does not bother me. For some reason, I am simply not feeling up for football today.”
“Go out and breathe some fresh air,” Aunt Euphemia reiterated, “yet carry your umbrella with you, because I think rain is coming. My leg has rheumatism.”
“Rheumatism ought to be confined to the elderly, Aunty.”

“A person can easily catch rheumatism in her legs, Nell. However, solely the elderly ought to experience soul rheumatism. Fortunately, I have escaped it entirely. Once your soul is afflicted with rheumatism, you may as well proceed to select your coffin.”

November had arrived—that time of deep, melancholic ocean hymns, crimson sunsets, fierce wind-songs among the pines, and departing birds. Nell wandered along the pineland paths inside the park and, in her own words, allowed that huge, sweeping wind to clear the fogs from her soul. Normally, soul fog did not bother Nell. Yet, for some reason, ever since she had come back to Wexcombe to begin this third year, life no longer reflected her spirit with its former, flawless, brilliant clarity.

On the surface, life at Tabby’s Place continued in its usual enjoyable cycle of labor, learning, and amusement. Every Friday night, many visitors filled the spacious, fire-lit livingroom, which resounded with continuous jokes and merriment, all under the radiant smile of Aunt Euphemia. The person named “Ezra” in Cressy’s letter visited frequently, taking the morning train from St. Columbia and leaving on the night train. Everyone at Tabby’s Place held him in high regard, even if Aunt Euphemia would shake her head and express her opinion that theology students had declined compared to former days.
“My dear, he is extremely pleasant,” she remarked to Cressy, “yet it is necessary for ministers to possess greater gravity and dignity.”
“Is it impossible for someone to be a Christian while also indulging in laughter after laughter?” Cressy asked.

“Oh, men—yes. However, it was of ministers that I was speaking, my dear,” Aunt Euphemia said in a rebuking manner. “Furthermore, you ought not to flirt in that way with Mr. Hale—you truly ought not to.”
“Flirting with him is not what I’m doing,” Cressy argued.
Save for Nell, no one gave her credence. Believing she was merely entertaining herself as she so often did, the rest informed her bluntly that her conduct was extremely poor.
“Cressy, Mr. Hale does not belong to the Hector-and-Orlando category,” Mabel stated sternly. “His approach to life is earnest. It is possible that you will break his heart.”
“Do you truly believe I would be capable of it?” Cressy inquired. “I would delight in believing that.”
“Cressida Lindsay! I never considered you completely heartless. To think you declared that you would delight in breaking a man’s heart!”

“Honey, I never uttered those words. State what I said accurately. My statement was that I would prefer to believe I possessed the ability to shatter it. I wish to be certain that I held the strength required for such an act.”
“Cressy, you make no sense to me. It is obvious you are intentionally encouraging him, yet you are fully aware that your intentions are not serious.”
“If possible, I intend to get him to propose marriage to me,” Cressy stated composedly.
“I surrender to you,” Mabel said with a sense of hopelessness.

Hugh visited from time to time on Friday nights. He appeared to be perpetually cheerful, and he maintained his position during the swift exchange of jokes and witty remarks. He did not chase after Nell, nor did he evade her. Whenever situation placed them together, his conversation with her was agreeable and polite, just as it would be with a fresh acquaintance. Their previous closeness had vanished completely. Nell was deeply hurt by this; nevertheless, she assured herself that she felt immense joy and gratitude regarding how thoroughly Hugh had overcome his letdown concerning her. On that April night among the fruit trees, she had actually feared that she had wounded him severely and that his recovery would take a great deal of time. At present, she perceived that her anxiety had been unnecessary. Men have died and the worms have eaten them but not for love. Clearly, Hugh faced no threat of an early death. He was taking pleasure in living, and he possessed an abundance of drive and enthusiasm. As for him, he would not pine away in misery simply because a lady was beautiful and indifferent. Nell, while hearing the unending teasing that transpired between him and Cressy, questioned whether she had merely pictured that expression in his eyes on the occasion when she informed him that she could not ever love him.

Individuals were not absent who would have willingly taken the empty spot of Hugh. Nell, however, dismissed them devoid of fear and devoid of reproach. Should the genuine Prince Charming fail to ever arrive, she refused to accept any replacement. Thus she rigidly informed herself on that gloomy day within the breezy park.

Aunt Euphemia’s prophesied rain abruptly arrived with a swish and rush. Raising her umbrella, Nell hastened down the slope. A fierce gust of wind swept along the harbor road just as she turned onto it. Her umbrella immediately turned wrong side out. Nell made a desperate grab at it. And then—a voice spoke right beside her.
“Excuse me—could I provide you cover with my umbrella?”

Nell raised her eyes. Standing right in front of her in real life was the exact protagonist of her fantasies—lofty, attractive, and dignified, possessing dark, somber, unfathomable eyes, alongside a tender, melodic, compassionate tone. Had he been created to specification, he could not have matched her perfection more accurately.
“Thank you,” she uttered, feeling bewildered.

“It would be best if we made haste to that small pavilion on the point,” the stranger proposed. “There we can bide our time till this downpour ceases. Such intense rain is improbable to persist for much longer.”
Although the spoken phrasing was extremely ordinary, the voice held such a distinct quality, matched by her expression as she uttered them, that Nell experienced a curious fluttering in her chest.
They hurried as one to the pavilion and settled breathlessly beneath its welcoming shelter. Displaying her imitation umbrella, Nell laughed.
“I become certain that non-living objects are completely evil the moment my umbrella gets blown inside out,” she remarked cheerfully.

Glistening drops of rain gleamed on her glossy hair, whose untethered tresses coiled about her forehead and neck. Glowing cheeks accompanied her wide, luminous eyes. Looking down, her associate regarded her with admiration. His look made her feel her face redden. What was his identity? Look, a fragment of the Wexcombe scarlet and white was attached to his coat lapel. Still, she had believed she was familiar with, at minimum by appearance, every one of the Wexcombe students apart from the Freshmen. And this polite young man certainly was not a Freshman.

“I see that we are schoolmates,” he stated, offering a smile toward Nell’s colors. “That should serve as a sufficient introduction. Royal Lisle is my name. And aren't you the Miss Harcourt who delivered the Tennyson paper at the Philomathic just the other evening?”
“Indeed; however, I am unable to place you whatsoever,” Nell admitted candidly. “Pray, what is your origin?”

“I have the impression that I do not fit in anywhere so far. Two years back, I completed my Freshman and Sophomore years at Wexcombe. I have resided in Europe from that time onward. At present, I have returned so that I can complete my Arts degree.”
“I am also in my Junior year,” Nell said.

“Then we share a class in addition to sharing a college. I am resigned to losing the years destroyed by the locust,” her partner remarked, a universe of significance filling those extraordinary eyes he possessed.

The rain fell without ceasing for almost an hour. Nevertheless, the duration appeared remarkably brief. Nell and her associate journeyed home side by side when the clouds split open and a ray of faint November sunlight swept across the harbor and the pines. Before they arrived at the gate of Tabby’s Place he had requested consent to visit, and it had been granted to him. Nell entered with glowing cheeks, her heart throbbing all the way to her fingertips. Smudge, who scrambled onto her lap attempting to lick her, received a most distracted greeting. Nell, her spirit completely filled with romantic excitement, possessed no focus to bestow upon a crop-eared pussy cat at that moment.

During that same evening, a package was delivered to Tabby’s Place, addressed to Miss Harcourt. Within the box were twelve splendid roses. Cressy boldly seized the card that dropped out, reading both the name and the verse of poetry inscribed upon its reverse side.
“Royal Lisle!” she cried out. “Why, Nell, I wasn’t aware that Cyril Lisle was an acquaintance of yours!”
“I encountered him in the park during the rain this afternoon,” Nell explained hastily. “His umbrella was used to rescue me when mine flipped inside out.”

“Oh!” Cressy took a curious look at Nell. “Does such an exceptionally ordinary event explain his sending us long-stemmed roses by the dozen, accompanied by a highly sentimental poem? Or explain our flushing the most divine rosy-red upon viewing his card? Nell, your face gives you away.”
“Stop speaking absurdities, Cressy. Are you acquainted with Mr. Lisle?”

“I have gotten to know his couple of sisters, and I am aware of him. Everyone of any importance in Portmaris is, too. Among the wealthiest, most elite of Bluenoses are the Gardners. Cyril possesses endearing good looks and intelligence. His mother’s wellness broke down two years back, forcing him to quit university and travel overseas alongside her—his father has passed away. Having to abandon his year must have caused him deep disappointment, yet people claim he acted entirely wonderfully concerning the matter. Fee—fi—fo—fum, Nell. Romance is in the air. I nearly feel jealous of you, though not entirely. When all is said and done, Cyril Lisle cannot compare to Ezra.”

“You goose!” Nell said in a lofty manner. Nevertheless, she remained awake for a considerable time that night, without any desire to sleep. The thoughts of her waking hours held far greater allure than any dreamland vision. Was this, finally, the arrival of the true Prince? As Nell remembered those magnificent dark eyes that had looked so intently into hers, she felt a powerful urge to believe that he had indeed arrived.

The female students at Tabby’s Place were getting outfitted for the party that the Juniors were throwing in honor of the Seniors in February. Nell looked at her reflection in the blue room's glass with feminine pleasure. Her dress was especially lovely. At first, it had been nothing more than an unpretentious small underdress of cream silk beneath a chiffon overdress. However, Cressy had demanded that she carry it to her own house during the Christmas break to stitch minuscule rosebuds across the entire chiffon. Cressy possessed skillful hands, and her work produced a gown that all the other Wexcombe girls coveted. Allie Boone herself, who possessed Parisian frocks, was accustomed to gazing with yearning upon that rosebud creation whenever Nell walked up the principal staircase at Wexcombe wearing it.

Nell was testing how a white orchid looked in her hair. White orchids had been sent to her by Cyril Lisle for the reception, and she was aware that no other Wexcombe girl would wear them that evening—when Cressy entered, looking on with admiration.

“Nell, you are undoubtedly looking handsome tonight. For nine out of ten evenings, I am able to outshine you without difficulty. On that tenth one, you abruptly bloom into a figure that completely overshadows me. By what means do you achieve it?”
“The attire is responsible, my love. Superior plumage.”

“It is not. Your old blue flannel shirtwaist, which Mrs. Sowerby constructed for you, was what you had on the previous time you burst into gorgeousness. Had Cyril not lost his mind and affection for you previously, this evening would surely have accomplished it. However, I am disinclined to see orchids on you, Nell. Nay, jealousy is not the reason. You do not appear to match orchids. Their nature is excessively exotic—far too tropical—overly insolent. At all events, refrain from placing them in your hair.”

“Indeed, I shall not. I must confess to having no personal liking for orchids. It is my belief that they hold no relation to me. Such blooms are rarely dispatched by Cyril—he understands my preference for blossoms suited to daily companionship. One can merely pay a call to orchids.”

“Ezra gave me a few lovely pink rosebuds to wear tonight—however—he will not be attending. He claimed he was required to conduct a slum prayer-meeting! I doubt he desired to attend. Nell, I am terribly concerned that Ezra has no genuine feelings for me. And I am attempting to determine if I should waste away and perish, or proceed to obtain my B.A. and prove sensible and helpful.”
“Cressy, since you are completely incapable of being useful and sensible, it would be better if you just wasted away and died,” Nell remarked with cruelty.
“Heartless Nell!”
“You foolish Cressy! It is perfectly clear to you that Ezra holds affection for you.”

“However—he refuses to say as much to me. And I am unable to force him. He appears to, I must confess. Nevertheless, silent gazes are not a truly trustworthy basis for decorating doilies and stitching borders on tablecloths. I prefer not to start those tasks before I am officially engaged. Doing so would invite bad luck.”

“Cressy, Mr. Hale fears asking for your hand in marriage. Because he lacks wealth, he is unable to provide a dwelling like the one you have always possessed. That single motive has prevented him from speaking up until now, as you well know.”

“I guess that’s true,” Cressy conceded sorrowfully. “Well”—cheering a bit—“should he fail to propose to me, I’ll propose to him, simple as that. Consequently, everything will turn out fine. I refuse to fret. On another note, Hugh Carrow spends all his time with Rowena Calder. Were you aware?”
Nell was attempting to secure a small chain made of gold around her neck. The fastener unexpectedly proved troublesome to handle. Was something wrong with the mechanism—or perhaps with her own hands?
“No,” she casually replied. “Rowena Calder, who is that?”

“She is the sister of Ronald Calder. This winter, she is located in Portmaris to study music. Although I have not set eyes on her, people claim she possesses great beauty and that Hugh is utterly infatuated with her. Nell, I felt so much anger when you turned down Hugh. Yet Cyril Lisle was your destiny. That is clear to me now. Ultimately, you were correct.”

Nell refrained from blushing, contrary to her customary reaction whenever the girls took it for granted that her future wedding with Cyril Lisle was a done deal. Suddenly, she experienced a sense of dullness. The talking of Cressy appeared unimportant, and she found the reception tiresome. She struck poor Smudge’s ears.
“Get off that cushion this second, you cat, you! Why do you not stay down where you are supposed to be?”

Gathering up her orchids, Nell headed to the lower floor, where Aunt Euphemia was overseeing a line of coats suspended in front of the hearth to get warm. Cyril Lisle was standing by for Nell, entertaining himself by bothering the Sarah-cat as he stood there. He was not favored by the Sarah-cat. Her back was invariably turned to him. On the other hand, all the other residents at Tabby’s Place held him in high regard. Aunt Euphemia, completely won over by his constant and respectful manners, along with the appealing cadence of his lovely voice, pronounced that he was the finest young gentleman she had ever met, and that Nell was an exceedingly lucky young woman. Nell felt uneasy when such comments were made. It was true that Cyril’s courtship had possessed all the romance a young woman’s heart could want, but—she preferred that Aunt Euphemia and the girls would refrain from assuming everything was settled. As Cyril whispered a poetic praise while assisting her into her coat, her face did not flush nor did she feel the customary flutter; furthermore, he noticed her reticence throughout their short stroll to Wexcombe. It appeared to him that her complexion was somewhat pale upon leaving the coeds’ dressing room; nevertheless, the moment they stepped into the reception room, her vivacity and vivid hue abruptly reappeared. The look she bestowed on Cyril was her most joyful. He answered her glance with a smile containing what Cressy termed “his deep, black, velvety smile.” Even so, her eyes were not truly fixed on Cyril. She possessed a sharp awareness that Hugh was positioned beneath the palms directly across the hall, engaged in conversation with a young woman who had to be Rowena Calder.

Her beauty was striking, possessing a grand elegance that would eventually turn somewhat heavy in her later years. She was a lofty young woman, featuring expansive navy eyes, pale complexion contours, and a dark sheen upon her sleek tresses.

“She appears exactly how I have forever wished to appear,” Nell reflected in despair. “Complexion of a rose leaf—violet eyes like stars—hair as black as a raven—indeed, every single one is hers. It is surprising that she is not additionally named Lucinda Fitzgerald! However, I doubt that her form equals mine, and without question her nose does not.”
This deduction brought a slight sense of relief to Nell.

That winter, March arrived in the manner of an exceptionally gentle and docile lamb, producing days filled with crisp, golden, and tingling air, with every one giving way to a frosty pink dusk that slowly melted into a magical realm of moonlight.

The loom of April examinations cast a shadow across the young women at Tabby’s Place. Hard study occupied them; even Cressy had devoted herself to notebooks and text with a tenacity that one would not have anticipated from her.

“I’m going to take the Johnson Scholarship in Mathematics,” she declared serenely. “I could win the one in Greek without difficulty, but I prefer to win the mathematical one since I wish to demonstrate to Ezra that I am truly remarkably brilliant.”
“Ezra prefers you for those large brown eyes and that lopsided smile of yours rather than for any of the intelligence held beneath your curls,” Nell remarked.

“During my youth, women were not expected to understand Mathematics,” Aunt Euphemia remarked. “However, the era has shifted. I am unsure if these changes are entirely positive. Do you possess cooking skills, Cressy?”

“No, I have not prepared any food ever in my life, save for a gingerbread that turned out poorly—sunken in the center and raised at the margins. You are familiar with that sort. However, Aunty, once I commence learning to cook in serious truth, do you not suppose that the same intellect allowing me to secure a mathematical scholarship will likewise permit me to master cooking equally well?”

“Perhaps,” Aunt Euphemia remarked with care. “I am not criticizing advanced schooling for women. An M.A. is held by my daughter. Cooking is also within her skill. However, instruction in cooking was given to her by me prior to allowing her to be taught Mathematics by a university professor.”
A letter arrived from Miss Tabby Linden in the middle of March, announcing that she and Miss Maria had chosen to stay overseas for one more year.

“Therefore Tabby’s Place might be yours for the following winter as well,” was her written message. “Maria and my intention is to make a quick trip to Egypt. My wish is to view the Sphinx a single time prior to my death.”
“Imagine those two women ‘travelling around Egypt’! I wonder whether they will gaze up at the Sphinx while knitting,” Honora chuckled.

“I am extremely happy that Tabby’s Place remains ours for one more year,” Mabel remarked. “My fear was that they would return, which would shatter our delightful small haven here, casting us unfortunate, inexperienced young ones back into the harsh realm of boardinghouses.”
“I’m going for a walk in the park,” declared Cressy, throwing her book to one side. “It seems to me that upon reaching eighty, I will be pleased that I took a stroll in the park this evening.”
“In what way?” inquired Nell.
“Accompany me and I will explain, honey.”

In their strolling, they took in every bit of the magic and mystery belonging to a March evening. It possessed a great stillness and mildness, enveloped by a vast, white, contemplative quietude—a quietude that nevertheless had numerous tiny, silvery noises woven through it, which could be detected if one listened using their soul as much as their ears. Down an elongated pine-forested passage, the girls roamed toward what appeared to be the very center of an abundant, deep-red winter sunset.

“If I merely possessed the skill, I’d return home and compose a poem this very instant,” Cressy announced, stopping in a clearing as the green ends of the pine trees were being dyed by a pink glow. “Everything is so marvellous in this place—this vast, pale silence, along with those deep-colored trees that appear to be constantly contemplating.”

“‘The first temples of God were the woods,’” Nell softly quoted. “In a place like this, a person cannot avoid feeling adoring and reverent. Walking among the pines always makes me feel so close to Him.”
“I am the most joyful girl on earth, Nell,” abruptly admitted Cressy.
“So Mr. Hale has finally requested your hand in marriage?” asked Nell composedly.

“Indeed. Furthermore, my sneezing occurred thrice during his proposal. Was that not dreadful? Nevertheless, my answer of ‘yes’ came practically prior to his conclusion—such was my fear that his decision might alter and he would cease. My happiness is absolute infatuation. Previously, it seemed truly unbelievable to me that Ezra could ever harbor affection for someone as lighthearted as myself.”

“Cressy, you’re not really frivolous,” Nell said solemnly. “Deep down below that frivolous surface of yours, you possess a sweet, faithful, womanly little soul. Why do you conceal it to such a degree?”

“Queen Nell, it is impossible for me to act otherwise. Your assessment is correct—my core is not frivolous. Nevertheless, my soul is covered by a kind of frivolous outer layer that I am unable to shed. To quote Mrs. Poyser, changing it would require me to be hatched a second time and hatched in a different way. Ezra, however, understands my true self and affectionally accepts me, including my frivolous nature. My feelings for him are mutual. Discovering my love for him astonished me more than anything else ever has. Loving an unattractive man was something I had previously deemed impossible. Imagine my situation dwindling to a single suitor. Furthermore, a suitor by the name of Ezra! My intention, though, is to address him as Ez. Such a name is delightfully short and sharp. A nickname for Orlando would have been impossible.”
“How do Hector and Orlando figure into this?”

“Oh, at Christmas I informed them that I could not possibly wed either one. Recalling that I once considered it a possibility appears so amusing at present. Because they were so deeply hurt, I wept over the two of them—wailed, in fact. However, I was certain that just a single man existed on earth whom I could ever take as a husband. For a change, I had reached my own decision, and doing so proved quite simple as well. Experiencing such certainty feels wonderful, especially realizing that this conviction belongs to you rather than another person.”
“Are you of the opinion that you can sustain this?”

“Deciding, you are asking? I am uncertain, yet Ez supplied me with a magnificent guideline. He states, whenever I am confused, merely to act in the way I would desire to have acted when I am eighty years old. In any case, Ez is able to decide fast enough, and having an excess of mind within one home would be unpleasant.”
“In what manner will your mother and father respond?”

“Father will not say very much. He believes all my actions are right. Mother, however, will speak. Oh, her tongue is going to be just as Byrney as her nose. Even so, everything will turn out all right in the end.”
“When you wed Mr. Hale, Cressy, there are quite a few things you have always possessed that you will need to surrender.”

“Yet he will be mine. Those other matters won't be missed by me. Our wedding is set for a year from the coming June. You are aware that Ez finishes his studies at St. Columbia this spring. Following that, a small mission church located down on Tanner Street in the slums will be taken over by him. Picture me living in the slums! Nevertheless, I would travel to that place or even to Greenland’s icy mountains alongside him.”
“And here we have the young woman who swore she would only wed a wealthy man,” Nell remarked, addressing a young pine tree.

“Oh, do not bring up the foolish things I did when I was young. The way I have been wealthy is how cheerfully I will be poor. You will witness it. Learning to cook and altering dresses is what I intend to do. Ever since I have resided at Tabby’s Place, I have mastered marketing; and one entire summer, I gave lessons to a Sunday School class. According to Aunt Euphemia, marrying Ez will destroy his career. However, I will not. Although I am aware that I lack substantial sense or seriousness, I possess something far superior—the ability to get people to like me. A man who lisps and regularly gives testimony in prayer-meeting lives in Harborough. His words are, ‘If you can’t thine like an electric thtar thine like a candlethtick.’ Ez will have a small candlestick in me.”
“Cressy, you cannot be reformed. Ah, my affection for you is so deep that delivering pleasant, brief, celebratory remarks is impossible for me. However, your joy brings immense gladness to my heart.”
“I understand. That genuine affection fills your large gray eyes, Nell. Eventually, I will gaze at you with that same expression. Is it true that you will be marrying Cyril, Nell?”

“My beloved Cressida, have you ever known about the renowned Betty Baxter, who ‘refused a man before he’d axed her’? I do not intend to copy that famous woman by either rejecting or taking anyone prior to his ‘axing’ me.”
“Every person in Wexcombe is aware that Cyril is head over heels for you,” Cressy stated openly. “And he has your love, doesn’t he, Nell?”

“I—I suppose so,” Nell admitted unwillingly. It seemed to her that she should have been turning red while admitting this; yet she was not; instead, she invariably flushed deeply whenever anyone mentioned Hugh Carrow or Rowena Calder when she was present. Hugh Carrow and Rowena Calder meant nothing to her—nothing whatsoever. Still, Nell had stopped attempting to examine why she turned red. Regarding Cyril, she was certainly infatuated with him—utterly infatuated. How could she avoid it? Did he not represent her ideal? Who could withstand such magnificent dark eyes, and that beseeching voice? Were not fifty percent of the Wexcombe girls intensely jealous? And what a delightful sonnet he had delivered to her, alongside a box of violets, for her birthday! Nell had committed every single word of it to memory. It was quite fine work for that sort of poetry, as well. Not quite on par with Keats or Shakespeare—even Nell’s infatuation was not so extreme that she believed that. Yet it was quite respectable magazine poetry. Furthermore, it was written for her—not for Laura or Beatrice or the Maid of Athens, but for her, Nell Harcourt. Having someone declare in poetic rhythm that her eyes were morning stars—that her cheek possessed the color taken from the dawn—that her lips were crimson beyond the roses of Paradise, was wonderfully romantic. Hugh would never have considered composing a sonnet to her eyebrows. On the other hand, Hugh possessed an appreciation for humor. She had on one occasion shared a amusing tale with Cyril—and he had failed to get the point. She remembered the friendly laugh she and Hugh had shared over that same story, and questioned with some discomfort whether existing alongside a man lacking humor might turn out to be rather dull eventually. Still, how could anyone anticipate that a somber, mysterious hero would appreciate the funny aspect of life? It would be entirely absurd.

“I wonder what it would be like to live in a world where it was always June,” said Nell, stepping through the dusk-filled orchard's blossoms and fragrance toward the steps of the front door, upon which Thirza and Mrs. Agatha sat discussing the funeral of Mrs. Samson Coates, an event they had gone to earlier that day. Between the two of them sat Lucy, attentively working on her schoolwork; Robin, however, sat cross-legged on the lawn, appearing as somber and downcast as his one dimple permitted.
“It would grow tiresome to you,” Thirza remarked, letting out a sigh.

“I suppose so; however, right at this moment I believe I would need a very long while to grow weary of it, provided it remained entirely as delightful as it is today. June is loved by everything. Robin-boy, what is the reason for this somber November expression during the season of blossoms?”
“I am simply weary and fed up with life,” declared the young cynic.
“By the age of ten? My goodness, that is so tragic!”
“I am not teasing,” declared Robin gravely. “I am dis—dis—disheartened”—producing the lengthy term with a heroic attempt.
“For what reason and to what end?” inquired Nell, taking a seat at his side.

“’sence the substitute instructor who arrived after Mr. Holmes fell ill assigned me ten arithmetic problems to complete by Monday. Working on them will consume my entire day tomorrow. Being forced to labor on Saturdays is unjust. Milty Gammon declared that he would refuse to do them, yet Thirza insists that I must. I really do not care for Miss Carson.”
“Do not speak of your instructor in that manner, Robin Farrow,” Mrs. Agatha remarked sternly. “Miss Carson is an exceptionally good young woman. She has no silliness in her.”

“That sounds far from appealing,” Nell chuckled. “I prefer folks to possess a touch of foolishness. However, I am disposed to think more highly of Miss Carson than you do. My eyes fell on her during last night's prayer-meeting, and her eyes are incapable of looking practical all the time. So, Robin-boy, be of good courage. ‘Tomorrow will bring another day’ and I will assist you with the arithmetic to the best of my ability. Do not squander this beautiful time between dusk and night fretting about sums.”

“Well, I won’t,” said Robin, cheering up. “If you assist me with the sums I’ll get ’em finished soon enough to go fishing with Milty. I wish old Aunt Drusilla’s funeral took place tomorrow rather than today. I wanted to attend it ’cause Milty mentioned his mother said Aunt Drusilla would certainly sit up in her coffin and speak sarcastic things to the people who come to watch her buried. But Thirza claimed she wouldn’t.”

“In her casket, poor Drusilla was lying quite peacefully,” Mrs. Sowerby remarked with gravity. “That is the truth, I had not seen her appear so agreeable previously. Ah, over that poor old woman, not many tears were wept. To be free of her brings gratitude to the Elisha Ducketts, and I am unable to say that I fault them in the least.”
“It appears to me an utterly terrible prospect to depart from this life and leave not a single soul behind who grieves your passing,” Nell stated, trembling.

“No one besides her mother and father ever cared for poor Drusilla, indeed, not even the man she married,” declared Mrs. Sowerby. “She became his fourth spouse. Marrying had turned into a bit of a routine for him. His life ended just a couple of years following their wedding. Indigestion was the cause of death according to the doctor, yet I will constantly insist his passing was brought on by Drusilla’s mouth, precisely that. Poor thing, she was perpetually informed concerning all the details of her neighbors, although she remained quite unfamiliar with her own self. Ah well, she has passed away regardless; and I imagine Isolde’s marriage will be the upcoming commotion.”

“Thinking about Isolde getting married appears strange and dreadful,” Nell murmured, clasping her knees as her gaze went through the opening in the Whispering Wood toward the glow radiating from Isolde’s bedroom.

“She is prospering so much that the situation does not seem terrible to me,” Mrs. Sowerby declared with emphasis. “The farm owned by Gideon Duckett is excellent, and his character as a youth is exemplary.”
“Isolde may have once desired a husband who was wicked, dashing, and wild, but he is surely not that,” Nell said with a smile. “Gideon possesses immense goodness.”
“Precisely what he should be, that is. Is a wicked husband what you would desire for Isolde? Or for your own self?”

“Oh, no. Marrying a person who was evil is not something I would want, yet I believe I would enjoy it if he possessed the ability to be evil but chose not to be. As for Gideon, his goodness is beyond all hope.”
“I hope that one day you will possess greater wisdom,” Thirza expressed.

There was a certain bitterness in Thirza’s tone. Her disappointment was severe. She was aware that Nell had declined Hugh Carrow’s proposal. The rumors in Brierley hummed with this news, which had escaped, though no one could say how. It was possible that Wilfred Mott had surmised the truth and reported his assumptions as facts. Or perhaps Isolde had disclosed the matter to Gideon, who then acted without discretion. Whatever the case, the secret was out; Mrs. Carrow ceased asking Nell, whether in company or in confidence, if she had received recent news from Hugh, choosing instead to ignore her with a cold nod. Nell, who had ever held a fond affection for Hugh’s cheerful, youthful-spirited mother, felt a quiet sorrow because of this demeanor. Thirza kept silent; however, Mrs. Sowerby subjected Nell to numerous sharp, annoyed remarks on the subject, continuing until new rumors arrived to that respectable woman, via the mother of Elias Purdy MacKinnon, claiming that Nell had a different “beau” at university, one who combined wealth, attractive looks, and virtue. Following those reports, Mrs. Agatha kept quiet, even if her deepest desire remained that Nell had agreed to marry Hugh. Wealth was certainly desirable; yet even Mrs. Agatha, despite her pragmatic nature, did not view it as the sole necessity. Should Nell “like” this Handsome Unknown more than she did Hugh, there was no further room for argument; nevertheless, Mrs. Agatha was terribly anxious that Nell might commit the error of taking a husband for financial gain. Thirza understood Nell far too thoroughly to harbor such a worry; yet she suffered a conviction that something within the grand order of the universe had suffered a dismal disruption.

“Whatever is destined to occur will occur,” Mrs. Agatha remarked dejectedly, “and occasionally things that aren't meant to be come to pass anyway. Unless Providence steps in, I cannot refrain from thinking that this will take place regarding Nell, I really do.” Mrs. Agatha uttered a sigh. It was her fear that Providence would fail to step in; and she lacked the courage to do so herself.

Nell had drifted down toward the Nymph’s Well, curling herself up amid the ferns by the base of the large white birch where Hugh and she had spent so many moments together during past summers. Once college ended, he had returned to the newspaper office, making Brierley feel exceedingly dull in his absence. Since he never sent her any mail, Nell pined for those letters that failed to arrive. Naturally, Cyril wrote two times each week; his letters were delicate works of art that would have made wonderful reading inside a memoir or biography. Reading them made Nell feel that she was even more profoundly in love with him than before; nevertheless, her heart did not experience that strange, rapid, aching leap upon seeing his letters that it had felt on the occasion when Mrs. Hiram Mott passed her an envelope bearing Hugh’s dark, vertical penmanship. Nell had rushed back to the east gable and unsealed it with great anticipation—merely to discover a typewritten duplicate of a college society report—“only that and nothing more.” Nell threw the innocent document to the far side of her room and seated herself to compose a particularly sweet message to Cyril.

Five days remained until Isolde’s wedding. The gray dwelling located at Pear Hill was chaotic with baking, brewing, boiling, and stewing, because a grand, old-fashioned wedding was going to take place. Nell, naturally, was going to serve as bridesmaid, fulfilling a pact they had made at twelve years of age, and Hugh was traveling from Portmaris to act as best man. Nell took pleasure in the commotion surrounding the different preparations, yet beneath everything she felt a quiet ache in her heart. In a way, her cherished longtime friend was being lost to her; Isolde’s future dwelling would be located two miles away from Grey Shutters, making their former unceasing closeness impossible to retain. Nell raised her gaze toward Isolde’s light, reflecting on how it had shone like a beacon for her over numerous years; however, it would shortly cease to gleam through the summer twilights. A pair of large, aching tears rose in her gray eyes.
“Oh,” it occurred to her, “how awful it is that individuals must mature—and wed—and transform!”

“When all is said and done, pink ones are the sole genuine roses,” Nell remarked, while binding the bouquet of Isolde with white ribbon inside the gable facing westward at Pear Hill. “Love and faith find their bloom in them.”

In the center of the room, Isolde stood anxiously, dressed in her wedding white, with her dark ringlets dusted by the sheer material of her bridal veil. Nell had placed that veil upon her, honoring the emotional agreement they had made years earlier.

“Things are mostly how I envisioned them a long time back, during the days I cried because of your unavoidable wedding and the separation that would follow for us,” she chuckled. “Isolde, you match the bride in my fantasies, complete with that ‘lovely misty veil’; meanwhile, I am serving as your bridesmaid. However, oh dear! My sleeves aren't puffed—even if the short lace pair I am wearing look better. Furthermore, my heart isn't completely shattered, and I don't precisely despise Gideon.”

“It isn’t truly a separation, Nell,” Isolde objected. “My new home won't be distant. Our affection for one another will remain just as strong. That friendship ‘oath’ we pledged so many years ago has never been broken by us, has it?”

“Yes. We have preserved it loyally. Isolde, our companionship has been lovely. Not a single disagreement, chilliness, or harsh remark has ever ruined it; and my wish is for it to remain that way forever. However, matters are unable to stay entirely unchanged following this. You will possess different pursuits. My place will merely be on the periphery. Still, as Mrs. Agatha remarks, ‘such is life.’ Mrs. Agatha has presented you with a cherished knitted quilt featuring the ‘tobacco stripe’ design, and she states that she will bestow one upon me as well whenever I get married.”
“The unkind aspect of your upcoming wedding is my inability to serve as your bridesmaid,” Isolde mourned.

“Next June, when Cressy weds Mr. Hale, I am scheduled to serve as her bridesmaid, after which I have to cease, because you are aware of the saying ‘three times a bridesmaid, never a bride,’” remarked Nell, looking out the window past the pink and white blooms of the orchard below. “Isolde, the minister is approaching.”

“Oh, Nell,” Isolde puffed out, all at once growing extremely white-faced and starting to shake. “Oh, Nell—I am terribly anxious—I am unable to carry on—Nell, I am certain that I shall lose consciousness.”

“I will haul you over to the rainwater hogshed and plunge you inside if you do,” Nell remarked without sympathy. “Be of good cheer, my sweet. Marrying cannot be exceedingly dreadful if such a great number of individuals live through the service. Observe my calm and collected demeanor, and draw bravery from it.”
“Hold on until it is your turn, Miss Nell. Oh, Nell, my ear catches father walking up the stairs. Hand me my bouquet. Is my veil positioned correctly? Do I look extremely pale?”
“You look truly beautiful. Izzy, my dear, give me a final farewell kiss. Never again will Isolde Pembroke kiss me.”
“However, Isolde Duckett is going to. Look, mother is shouting for us. Let's go.”

Adhering to the straightforward, traditional custom common at the time, Nell descended to the drawing room leaning on Hugh’s arm. Having arrived just that day, Hugh had not seen her since their departure from Portmaris until they encountered each other at the stairhead. Hugh extended a polite handshake. He appeared to be in good health, even if, as Nell observed right away, he seemed somewhat lean. Far from being pale, a color had flared upon his cheek when Nell had approached him in the corridor, dressed in her gentle white gown with lilies-of-the-valley tucked into the glowing piles of her hair. When the pair stepped into the filled parlor, a faint hum of approval swept through the gathered guests. “What a fine-looking pair they are,” murmured the easily touched Mrs. Agatha to Thirza.

Gideon strolled inside by himself, his countenance extremely flushed, after which Isolde entered grandly attached to the arm of her father. She avoided passing out, and no improper incident happened to disrupt the service. A period of eating, drinking, and celebrating came next; afterwards, when night was drawing to a close, Gideon and Isolde traveled by carriage under the moonlight toward their place of residence, while Hugh accompanied Nell on a walk to Grey Shutters.
A bit of their former fellowship had come back amid the relaxed gaiety of the night. Ah, walking along that familiar path alongside Hugh once more felt wonderful!

Because the night was exceptionally quiet, a person ought to have caught the rustle of blooming roses, the giggling of daisies, the chirping of grass—numerous lovely noises, entirely blended with one another. The splendor of the moonlit sky over well-known fields illuminated the earth.

“Could we not go for a walk along Lovers’ Lane before you head inside?” Hugh inquired while the pair traversed the bridge spanning the Lake of Glassy Waters, wherein the moon rested like a huge, sunken flower of gold.

Nell gave her prompt agreement. Lovers’ Lane existed as a genuine trail in a realm of magic that evening—a glistening, secretive area, brimming with sorcery within the pale-spun spell of moonbeams. There was an earlier period during which taking a stroll like that alongside Hugh along Lovers’ Lane would have proved much too perilous. However, Cyril and Rowena had rendered it exceedingly secure at present. Nell caught herself giving a great deal of thought to Rowena while she conversed pleasantly with Hugh. She had encountered her on a few occasions prior to departing Portmaris, and she had acted delightfully amiable toward her. Rowena had likewise acted delightfully amiable. In truth, they formed an exceptionally warm couple of individuals. Yet despite this, their familiarity had failed to develop into a close bond. Clearly, Rowena did not qualify as a soulmate.
“Will Brierley be your location for the whole summer?” Hugh inquired.

“No. I’m heading down east to Coombe Road next week. Esther Haythorne wants me to cover her teaching throughout July and August. They run a summer term at that school, and Esther is unwell. Therefore, I will be substituting for her. In a way, I don't mind. Do you realize that I am starting to feel somewhat like an outsider in Brierley these days? It saddens me—yet it is real. It is truly dreadful how many children have grown into big boys and girls—actual young men and women—over the last two years. Half of the students I taught are now adults. Seeing them occupying the spots that you and I and our friends once held makes me feel terribly ancient.”

Nell chuckled and breathed a sigh. She considered herself to be extremely aged, adult, and sagacious—a feeling that merely demonstrated her youthfulness. She asserted to herself that she yearned immensely to return to those cherished joyful times when existence was viewed via a pink haze of expectation and fantasy, and held an elusive quality that had vanished eternally. Where had it gone now—the splendor and the vision?

“‘Thus the world wags on,’” Hugh cited with a practical and somewhat distracted air. Nell questioned whether Rowena occupied his thoughts. Ah, Brierley would become extremely desolate from this point forward—now that Isolde had departed!

Nell disembarked from the train at Coombe Road station and searched the surroundings to check whether somebody had arrived to greet her. She was supposed to lodge with a particular Miss Thora Sweet, yet no individual present matched even slightly the mental image she had built of that woman based on the letter from Esther. The sole human visible was an aged female, seated within a wagon that had mail bags stacked all around her. Estimating her weight at two hundred pounds would have been generous; her countenance was as circular and crimson as a harvest-moon, possessing nearly as few distinct features. She was dressed in a snug, black, cashmere gown, crafted according to the style from a decade prior, a slightly dusty black straw hat ornamented with yellow ribbon bows, and bleached black lace mits.
“Over here, you,” she shouted, gesturing toward Nell with her whip. “Is the new Coombe Road schoolma’am you?”
“Yes.”

“Indeed, that was my belief. Attractive schoolma’ams are famous on Coombe Road, in the same way that Millersville is famous for ugly ones. Thora Sweet inquired of me earlier today whether I was able to drive you out here. I replied, ‘Sartin I kin, if she don’t mind being scrunched up some. This rig of mine’s kinder small for the mail bags and I’m some heftier than Thomas!’ Allow me a moment, miss, to move these bags around slightly, and I will fit you in one way or another. Thora’s place is merely two miles away. The hired boy belonging to her next-door neighbor will retrieve your trunk this evening. I am called Skinner—Amelia Skinner.”
Nell was finally nestled into bed, swapping entertained grins with her own reflection as it happened.

“Move faster, black mare,” ordered Mrs. Skinner, as her plump hands took hold of the reins. “I have never driven the mail rowte before. Today, Thomas wished to hoe his turnips, which led him to ask that I take his place. Consequently, I simply sat down, grabbed a quick bite while standing, and set off. It pleases me somewhat. Naturally, it proves somewhat tedious. During certain moments I sit and ponder, whereas during others I simply sit. Move faster, black mare. Getting home early is my goal. Being without me makes Thomas extremely lonely. After all, our marriage took place quite recently.”
“Oh!” Nell uttered in a polite tone.
“Only one month. Yet Thomas pursued me for a rather long period. The whole thing was truly romantic.” Nell attempted to imagine Mrs. Skinner engaged with romance, but she could not.
“Oh?” she uttered once more.

“Indeed. You see, a second gentleman pursued me afterwards. Keep moving, dark horse. Having been a widow for such an extended period, people no longer anticipated my remarriage. However, upon the departure of my daughter—a schoolteacher like yourself—to the West for a teaching job, I experienced true loneliness and was not at all opposed to the prospect. In due course, Thomas started calling on me, as did that other man—William Obadiah Seaman was what he was called. A lengthy duration passed during which I was unable to decide which one to choose, while they continued to visit repeatedly, and my anxiety persisted. You see, W.O. possessed wealth—his property was splendid, and he maintained quite a grand manner. He was easily the superior prospect. Keep moving, dark horse.”
“What stopped you from marrying him?” inquired Nell.
“Indeed, you see, I wasn't loved by him,” Mrs. Skinner gravely replied.
Nell’s eyes widened as she gazed toward Mrs. Skinner. Yet no trace of amusement could be seen upon that woman's features. Clearly, Mrs. Skinner found no humor in her personal situation.

“For three years he had been a widower, with his sister running his household. After she wed, he simply desired a person to manage his residence. You ought to keep in mind that it was a place truly worth caring for. The dwelling is quite splendid. Move along, black mare. On the other hand, Thomas lacked money, and if his dwelling failed to leak during dry spells that was nearly the only good thing to mention, even if it appears somewhat picturesque. You see, however, my love belonged to Thomas, while I had no regard whatsoever for W.O. Consequently, I debated the matter internally. ‘Sarah Crowe,’ say I—Crowe was my maiden name—‘you are able to wed your wealthy suitor if you wish, yet happiness will elude you. People are unable to endure life together in this world lacking a small amount of affection. Your best course is simply to unite with Thomas, because his love is yours, your love is his, and no other outcome will suffice.’ Move along, black mare. Therefore, I informed Thomas that I would accept his proposal. Throughout my period of preparation, I refrained from ever driving by W.O.’s home because I was afraid that seeing his grand residence would plunge me into hesitation once more. At present, though, it never crosses my mind, and my existence with Thomas is completely comfortable and joyous. Move along, black mare.”
“What was William Obadiah’s reaction?” Nell asked.

“Well, he made a little fuss. However, he is on his way to visit a lean old spinster in Millersville at present, and my belief is she will snap him up quickly. That woman will prove a superior spouse compared to his former one. W.O. had no desire to wed her originally. He merely requested her hand because his dad desired it, fully expecting her to refuse him. Yet listen here, she accepted. You can imagine what a fix that was. Keep moving, black mare. Excellent at managing a home though she was, she proved dreadfully stingy. Eighteen years passed with her wearing a single bonnet. Following that, she acquired a replacement, and upon encountering her along the way, W.O. failed to recognize her. Keep moving, black mare. It seems to me my own dodge was a close one. Had I wedded him, my wretchedness might have been as terrible as my unfortunate cousin’s, Odette Ann. Having taken a wealthy husband for whom she felt nothing, Odette Ann leads a dog's life. Upon visiting me this past week, she remarks, remarks she, “Sarah Skinner, I envy you. I’d rather live in a little hut on the side of the road with a man I was fond of than in my big house with the one I’ve got.” The spouse of Odette Ann isn't entirely terrible either, despite possessing such a stubborn streak that his fur coat stays on when ninety degrees is marked on the thermometer. Persuading him to act requires coaxing him toward the reverse behavior. Still, affection is lacking to ease the friction, making for a miserable existence. Keep moving, black mare. Down in the dip stands the residence of Thora—“Wayside,” according to her name for it. Pretty as a picture, wouldn't you say? My guess is you'll rejoice to depart from this spot, given the way those mail bags keep crowding you.”
“Indeed, but driving alongside you was something I truly enjoyed,” Nell remarked with sincerity.

“Get along now!” Mrs. Skinner uttered, feeling immensely pleased. “Just wait until Thomas hears about that. Receiving a praise always delights him tremendously. Trot along, black mare. Well, this is our stop. It is my hope that you do well at the school, miss. Behind Thora’s house, a shortcut runs through the marsh. Should you go by that path, exercise extreme caution. Getting trapped in that dark mire just once would draw you straight under, leaving no trace or word of you until judgment day, just like what happened to Adam Palmer’s cow. Trot along, black mare.”
“Nell Harcourt sends greetings to Cressida Lindsay.

“Dearest, I really ought to have written to you before now. In this place, I have settled in again to the life of a rural ‘schoolma’am’ located at Coombe Road, taking up lodging at ‘Wayside,’ which belongs to Miss Thora Sweet. Thora is an affectionate person who possesses very attractive looks; her height is tall, though not excessively so; she is somewhat plump, but retains a particular control of silhouette that implies a frugal spirit who will not be overly generous even regarding body weight. A bun of soft, wavy, brown hair containing a strand of grey adorns her head, above a cheerful face boasting pink cheeks, along with large, gentle eyes that match the blueness of forget-me-nots. Furthermore, she belongs to that charming, traditional class of cooks who are completely unconcerned about ruining your stomach provided that they can supply you with luxurious banquets.
“She is to my liking; and I am to hers—mainly, it appears, for the reason that a sister of hers called Nell passed away at an early age.

“‘It makes me truly happy to meet you,’ she remarked with energy upon my arrival in her yard. ‘Goodness, my expectations of your appearance were completely off. I felt certain your hair would be dark—darkness was a trait of my sister Nell. Yet red is the color of yours!’

“At first, I believed my initial expectation of Thora might not hold, and that I would dislike her for a brief time. Shortly after, I told myself I ought to act more reasonably instead of holding a grudge against a person merely for labeling my hair red. It was likely that Thora did not even have the word ‘auburn’ in her vocabulary.

“‘Wayside’ is a charming kind of small place. Set down in a lovely little depression that slopes down from the road, the home is white and small. An orchard and flower-garden, completely blended together, lie between the house and the road. Quahog clam-shells—which Thora refers to as ‘cow-hawks’—border the walk to the front door; Virginia Creeper grows over the porch, and moss covers the roof. Located ‘off the parlor,’ my room is a tidy little space—containing just enough room for me and the bed. A picture hangs over the head of my bed showing Robby Burns as he stands at Highland Mary’s grave, shaded by a huge weeping willow tree. Because Robby’s face looks so mournful, it is not surprising that I experience nightmares. Indeed, during my initial night in this place, I had a dream where laughing was impossible for me.

“The parlor is small and tidy. A massive willow heavily shades its single window, giving the room a cave-like appearance of green darkness. Fantastic tidies rest on the chairs, colorful mats lie on the floor, books and cards are neatly set out on a circular table, and containers of dried grass sit on the mantel-piece. Positioned between the containers is a bright ornament made of saved coffin plates—a total of five, belonging individually to the father of Thora, her mother, a brother, her sister Nell, and a farmhand who once passed away in this place! Should I unexpectedly lose my mind one of these days ‘know all men by these presents’ that my madness was brought on by those coffin-plates.

“However, every bit of it is wonderful, and I expressed that very thought. Thora adored me on account of it, in the exact manner that she loathed unfortunate Esther for having remarked that an excessive amount of shade was unsanitary and for refusing to rest upon a feather bed. As for me, I delight in feather-beds, and my delight increases the more unsanitary and filled with feathers they become. Thora mentions that observing me dine brings her great solace; she was terribly worried that I might resemble Miss Haythorne, who refused every food except fruit and warm water when eating breakfast and attempted to persuade Thora to abandon frying food. In truth, Esther is a sweet young woman, yet she possesses a habit of following whims. Her difficulty stems from a lack of creativity combined with an inclination toward indigestion.

“I was informed by Thora that the parlor was available to me whenever any young men visited! However, I doubt there are numerous ones to visit. No young man has been seen by me in Coombe Road so far, with the exception of the hired boy next door—Sam Toliver, a youth who is very tall, lank, and tow-haired. A short time ago, he came over one evening to sit for an hour on the garden fence, close to the front porch where fancy-work was being done by Thora and me. During that entire duration, the sole comments offered by him were, ‘Hev a peppermint, miss! Dew now-fine thing for cararrh, peppermints,’ and, ‘Powerful lot o’ jump-grasses round here ternight. Yep.’

“Yet a romantic involvement is taking place right here. Appearing to be involved, to a greater or lesser degree, in late-life romances seems to be my destiny. That their wedding was caused by me is something Mr. and Mrs. Stanhope constantly claim. Continuing to be exceedingly thankful to me for an idea that another person would likely have offered had I not done so is Mrs. Stephen Clark of Delford. Nevertheless, it is my genuine belief that, had I not assisted him and Theodora Dix, Ludovic Speed would have made no additional progress beyond serene courting.

“Regarding the current matter, my role is merely that of a passive observer. Having attempted to assist once before, I caused a dreadful disaster. Consequently, I will refrain from further interference. When we see each other, I will share the entire story with you.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: During the initial Thursday evening that Nell spent at Coombe Road, Thora requested her company at a prayer-meeting. Thora opened up like a flower to go to that gathering. Her attire consisted of a light-blue muslin gown adorned with pansies, featuring a quantity of frills that exceeded anything one would expect from thrifty Thora, alongside a white leghorn hat decorated with three ostrich plumes and pink roses. Nell was thoroughly astonished. At a subsequent time, she discovered the reason behind Thora dressing up in such a fashion—a reason that dates back to Eden.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: The prayer-meetings at Coombe Road appeared to be largely made up of women. In addition to the minister, thirty-two women, two boys who were half-grown, and a single man attended. Nell caught herself observing this man. Neither handsome, young, nor graceful, he possessed extraordinarily long legs—legs so lengthy that hiding them required keeping them wound around the base of his chair—and he stooped at the shoulders. He had large hands, hair that needed a haircut, and a messy moustache. Even so, Nell believed his face appealed to her; its quality was kind, honest, and tender, containing an additional element that Nell struggled to pinpoint. Ultimately, she decided that he had endured suffering with strength, an experience that had left its mark upon his features. A kind of patient, witty fortitude showed in his look, suggesting he would endure being burned at the stake if required, yet maintain an agreeable demeanor until the moment he actually had to start writhing.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: As soon as the prayer-meeting concluded, the man approached Thora and remarked,

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
