chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: Thora grabbed his arm, with Nell subsequently mentioning to the young women at Tabby’s Place that it was “with the exact reserved modesty of a sixteen-year-old being walked home by a boy for the very first time.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: “Miss Harcourt, allow me to present Mr. Fairlie,” she stated rigidly.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: A nod came from Mr. Fairlie, who remarked, “Miss, while observing you during the prayer-meeting, I thought about how lovely a young girl you were.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: Hearing this kind of statement from almost anyone else would have deeply irritated Nell; nevertheless, Mr. Fairlie’s manner of delivering it gave her the impression of having been given a truly genuine and delightful tribute. She offered him a grateful smile and accommodated him by stepping back on the moon-drenched thoroughfare.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: It turned out that Thora possessed a suitor! Nell felt thrilled. Thora was bound to become the ideal spouse—joyful, frugal, patient, and an absolute master in the kitchen. For Nature to allow her to remain a perpetual spinster would constitute a glaring misuse.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: “It was requested of me by John Fairlie that I bring you to visit his mother,” Thora mentioned on the following day. “For much of the time she is confined to bed, and she does not ever leave her home. However, she possesses a great fondness for visitors and constantly desires to meet the people staying with me. Are you able to make the trip up tonight?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: Nell agreed; however, Mr. Fairlie arrived later that day representing his mother to extend an invitation for them to come for tea on Saturday evening.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: “Oh, why didn’t you put on your pretty pansy dress?” inquired Nell, as they departed from home. The day was sweltering, and poor Thora, amidst her state of excitement and her thick black cashmere dress, appeared to be roasting alive.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: “Old Mrs. Fairlie would regard it as dreadfully frivolous and inappropriate, I fear. Nevertheless, John is fond of that dress,” she appended with a wistful air.

text: A half-mile distance separated "Wayside" from the old Fairlie homestead, which sat atop a windswept hill. Large, comfortable, and sufficiently aged to possess dignity, the dwelling was surrounded by orchards and groves of maple. Neat, spacious barns stood to its rear, and evidence of wealth was everywhere. Whatever the meaning behind the patient endurance visible on Mr. Fairlie’s face, Nell mused that it had not signified duns or debts.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: John Fairlie greeted them at the entrance and escorted them to the sitting-room, in which his mother sat as if on a throne in an armchair.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: Because Mr. Fairlie was tall and slender, Nell had anticipated that aged Mrs. Fairlie would also be. On the contrary, she proved to be a minuscule bit of a female, featuring gentle rosy cheeks, gentle blue eyes, and an infant-like mouth. Attired in a lovely black silk gown of modern cut, a light white shawl draped across her shoulders, and a delicate lace cap atop her snow-white hair, she could have served as a model for a grandmother doll.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: “Thora, my darling, how are you?” she inquired affectionately. “Seeing you once more brings me such joy, sweetheart.” She offered her lovely, aging face for a kiss. “And here is the new teacher. Meeting you gives me great pleasure. So constantly has my son extolled your virtues that I am almost envious, while Thora, I am certain, should be completely envious.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: Unfortunate Thora turned red, Nell uttered some civil and standard remarks, and after that all of us took seats and engaged in conversation. Laborious effort was required, even from Nell, because no one appeared comfortable save elderly Mrs. Fairlie, who assuredly experienced no trouble in speaking. She required Thora to take a seat beside her and touched her hand now and then. Thora remained seated and wore a smile, appearing terribly ill at ease in her awful garment, while John Fairlie remained seated without any smile.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: By the tea table, Mrs. Fairlie elegantly requested that Thora serve the tea. Thora flushed even more deeply than before, yet she complied. Nell penned an account of that dinner to Mabel.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: “There was cold tongue, chicken, strawberry preserves, lemon pie, tarts, chocolate cake, raisin cookies, pound cake, and fruit cake—along with several other items, which included extra pie—I believe it was caramel pie. Once I had consumed double the amount that I should have, Mrs. Fairlie let out a sigh and remarked that she was worried she possessed nothing to entice my appetite.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: “‘I fear dear Thora’s culinary skills have ruined you for anyone else’s,’ she offered charmingly. ‘Naturally no one on Coombe Road aims to compete with her. Will you not take an additional slice of pie, Miss Harcourt? You have consumed nothing.’

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: “Mabel, my meal consisted of a serving of tongue along with one of chicken, three biscuits, a liberal portion of preserves, a slice of pie, a tart, plus a square of chocolate cake!”

With a sigh, she made herself comfortable in her armchair.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: “Miss Harcourt, I am a exceptionally infirm old woman. I have endured immense suffering for more than twenty years. I have been perishing bit by bit for twenty long, exhausting years.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: “What a shame!” Nell remarked, endeavoring to show empathy yet merely managing to feel foolish.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: “There have been many nights where they believed I would not survive until the morning,” Mrs. Fairlie continued gravely. “No one understands what I have endured—no one is able to know except me. Ah well, it is unable to continue much longer at this point. My exhausting journey will come to an end shortly, Miss Harcourt. It brings me immense solace that John will be provided with such an excellent wife to take care of him once his mother has passed away—an immense solace, Miss Harcourt.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: “Thora is a lovely woman,” Nell said with warmth.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: “Delightful! An exquisite personality,” agreed Mrs. Fairlie. “And an ideal housekeeper—a role I failed to achieve. My physical condition prevented it, Miss Harcourt. I am truly grateful for the sensible selection John has executed. It is my expectation and trust that joy will be his. Being my sole male offspring, Miss Harcourt, his welfare resides extremely close to my soul.”

text: “Naturally,” Nell uttered foolishly. She was being foolish for the very first time in her existence. Still, she was unable to conceive the reason. It appeared she had completely no words for this gentle, beaming, heavenly elderly woman who was caressing her hand with such kindness.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXII Tea with Mrs. Fairlie
text: “Pay me another visit before long, dear Thora,” Mrs. Fairlie remarked affectionately, as they departed. “Your visits are far too infrequent. However, I imagine John will bring you to reside here permanently before long.” Catching sight of John Fairlie while his mother was speaking, Nell jerked in sheer horror. His expression resembled that of a suffering individual whose torturers turned the rack to its utmost limit of human tolerance. Certain that he was sick, she quickly led poor, red-faced Thora off.

text: “Does old Mrs. Fairlie not seem like a sweet woman?” inquired Thora, while they walked along the road.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIII “He Just Kept Coming and Coming”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIII “He Just Kept Coming and Coming”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIII “He Just Kept Coming and Coming”
text: “He has done so. And he has not once brought up the topic of marriage to me. Furthermore, I doubt he will at this point. I have never uttered a single word regarding this to any living soul, yet it feels as though I must finally discuss it with somebody or lose my mind. John Fairlie started courting me two decades ago, prior to mother's death. Well, his visits continued repeatedly, and following a period of time, I started sewing quilts and other items; however, he failed to ever mention marriage, merely continuing to visit over and over. I was completely helpless. Mother passed away after we had been courting for eight years. I anticipated that he might express his intentions at that time, considering I was left by myself in the world. He proved to be truly compassionate and empathetic, doing all he possibly could on my behalf, yet he never uttered the word marry. And that is precisely how things have proceeded up to the present. I am blamed for this by people. They claim that I refuse to marry him owing to his mother being so frail and my desire to avoid the trouble of caring for her. Why, taking care of John's mother would bring me joy! Nevertheless, I permit them to hold that belief. Having them blame me is preferable to having them pity me! The fact that John refuses to propose to me is so terribly embarrassing. And what is his motive for not doing so? It feels to me that if I simply understood his rationale, it would not bother me nearly as much.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIII “He Just Kept Coming and Coming”
text: “It could be that his mother prefers he remains unmarried,” Nell offered.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIII “He Just Kept Coming and Coming”

text: “It’s beyond me,” Nell admitted helplessly. Her thoughts turned to Ludovic Speed. The two situations, however, were not alike. John Fairlie differed greatly in character from Ludovic.

text: Nell’s eyes were fixed on John Fairlie; and, beneath that vivid moon, the final turn of the rack was visible to her once more. Silently, he swung around and marched away along the path.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIII “He Just Kept Coming and Coming”
text: “Stop! Stop!” Nell shouted frantically behind him, paying no attention whatsoever to the rest of the stunned spectators. “Mr. Fairlie, stop! Return.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIII “He Just Kept Coming and Coming”
text: John Fairlie came to a halt, yet he refrained from returning. Nell rushed along the road, grabbed his arm, and practically pulled him back toward Thora.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIII “He Just Kept Coming and Coming”
text: “You have to return,” she begged. “This is entirely a error, Mr. Fairlie—the fault is all mine. I forced Thora to do it. She was unwilling—however everything is fine now, isn’t it, Thora?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIII “He Just Kept Coming and Coming”
text: Thora grabbed his arm and departed silently. Submissively following them back to the house, Nell crept inside through the rear entrance.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIII “He Just Kept Coming and Coming”
text: “Indeed, you support me so wonderfully,” Thora uttered with sarcasm.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIII “He Just Kept Coming and Coming”
text: “Thora, I was helpless to prevent it,” Nell stated with remorse. “It simply seemed to me that I had passively witnessed a murder taking place. Running after him became my only choice.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIII “He Just Kept Coming and Coming”
text: “Oh, I am equally pleased that you did so. As I watched John Fairlie departing along that road, it seemed to me that all the remaining joy and happiness in my life were departing alongside him. That feeling was terrible.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIII “He Just Kept Coming and Coming”
text: “Was there any question from him about your reasons?” Nell inquired.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIII “He Just Kept Coming and Coming”
text: “No, he didn’t ever mention it,” Thora answered listlessly.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: Nell possessed a faint expectation that some result might yet emerge. However, none occurred. John Fairlie arrived to take Thora out in his carriage, and he accompanied her on foot from the prayer-meeting, continuing the routine he had pursued for twenty years, and one he appeared destined to maintain for another twenty. Summer drew to a close. Nell conducted her school, composed letters, and engaged in some study. Her journeys to and from the schoolhouse were enjoyable. She invariably traveled through the swamp; it formed a delightful spot—a marshy ground, verdant with the most vivid mossy mounds; a shimmering stream turned and twisted across it, and spruce trees grew straight, their branches draped with grayish-green moss, their roots covered with every variety of forest beauty.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: Even so, Nell considered her existence on Coombe Road to be somewhat dull. Of course, a single amusing event did occur.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: She had not laid eyes on the gangly, flaxen-haired Samuel who had brought the peppermints since the night he visited, except for occasional encounters along the path. However, on a humid night in August he showed up, quietly sitting down upon the wooden bench near the porch. He was dressed in his customary work clothes, which were made up of mended pants, a blue denim shirt that was frayed at the elbows, and a tattered hat made of straw. A straw was tucked in his mouth, which he continued to chew as he gazed seriously at Nell. Nell put down her book with a sigh and picked up her doily. Having a dialogue with Sam was truly impossible.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: Following an extended period of quiet, Sam abruptly broke the silence.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “I am moving away from that place,” he stated suddenly, gesturing with his straw toward the adjacent home.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “Oh, do you happen to be?” Nell asked in a polite manner.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “Yep.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “And to what place are you heading at present?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “Well, I’ve given some thought to acquiring a spot for myself. A location that would fit my needs exists in Millersville. However, should I take the lease, having a wife will be necessary.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “I guess that’s true,” Nell remarked absently.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “Yep.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: A further extended period of silence ensued. At last, Sam took his straw out once more and remarked,

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “Will yeh hev me?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “Wh—a—t!” Nell gasped.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “Will yeh hev me?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “Are you suggesting—that I MARRY you?” asked miserable Nell weakly.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “Yep.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “Why, I’m barely acquainted with you,” cried Nell indignantly.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “However, ye would become familiar with me once our wedding was over,” Sam said.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: Nell summoned what remained of her modest pride.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “I will most definitely not marry you,” she stated with a haughty air.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “Well, you could certainly do worse,” protested Sam. “I work hard, plus I have saved some money in the bank.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “Never bring this up to me another time. What could have possibly planted that notion in your mind?” inquired Nell, as her anger was overcome by her amusement. The circumstance was utterly preposterous.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “You seem like a promising girl, and you move along at a good pace,” Sam stated. “A lazy woman isn't what I'm looking for. Give it some thought. My opinion won't be changing anytime soon. Anyway, I need to head off. The cows need milking.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: Recent years had chipped away at Nell’s notions about marriage offers, leaving her with hardly any remaining. Consequently, this particular proposal amused her entirely, without causing her any underlying pain. Later that evening, she performed an imitation of unfortunate Sam for Thora, causing the two of them to indulge in uncontrolled laughter at his sudden burst of emotion.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: It was one afternoon, as Nell’s stay at Coombe Road was coming to an end, that Hector Ward drove in great hurry down to “Wayside” to fetch Thora.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “They need you over at the Fairlie place right away,” he stated. “It’s my genuine belief that old Mrs. Fairlie is finally going to pass away, having feigned it for two decades.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: Thora darted off to retrieve her hat. Nell inquired whether Mrs. Fairlie was feeling worse than her normal state.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “Her condition is far worse,” Hector declared gravely, “which leads me to believe it is grave. On previous occasions, she would scream and thrash about frantically. Right now, she just lies there without making a sound. You can be certain that whenever Mrs. Fairlie falls quiet, she is extremely ill.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “Is old Mrs. Fairlie someone you dislike?” Nell inquired with curiosity.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “I enjoy cats when they are cats. I do not enjoy cats when they are women,” Hector answered mysteriously.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: In the dusk, Thora returned to the house.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “Mrs. Fairlie has passed away,” she stated with fatigue. “Her death occurred shortly following my arrival. Only a single time did she address me—‘I suppose you’ll marry John now?’ was what she remarked. Nell, that pierced me deeply. Imagine that his very own mother believed I refrained from marrying John on account of her! Nor was I able to utter anything in response—additional women were present. It was a relief to me that John had left.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: Thora started weeping dismally. However, Nell made her a warm beverage of ginger tea to console her. Indeed, Nell realized afterward that white pepper had been used by her rather than ginger; nevertheless, the distinction was never known by Thora.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: When the sun was setting on the evening following the funeral, Thora and Nell sat together upon the steps of the front porch. Within the pinelands, the wind had grown still, while vivid flashes of heat-lightning pulsed over the skies to the north. Wearing her unattractive black dress, Thora appeared at her absolute worst, her eyes and nose showing red from her tears. Few words passed between them, as Thora appeared slightly to begrudge the attempts Nell made to comfort her. It was clear she favored remaining unhappy.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: Without warning, the latch on the gate clicked, and John Fairlie marched into the garden. Crossing directly over the bed of geraniums, he moved in their direction. Thora rose to her feet. Nell did as well. A tall girl, Nell was dressed in white; yet John Fairlie took no notice of her.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “Thora,” he asked, “would you become my wife?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: Those statements erupted as though twenty years of eager suppression forced them to be voiced instantly, prior to all else.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: Because Thora’s face was already as red as it could possibly get from weeping, it became an exceedingly unattractive shade of purple instead.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “How come you failed to inquire earlier?” she asked deliberately.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “I was unable to. She extracted a vow from me against it—mother extracted a vow from me against it. Nineteen years back, a dreadful illness seized her. We believed she would not survive it. She begged me for a vow that I would not request your hand in marriage during her lifetime. I was unwilling to make such a vow, even with our shared belief that her remaining time was brief—the doctor assigned her a mere six months. Yet she pleaded for it upon her knees, ill and in pain. I was forced to give my word.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “What reason did your mother have to dislike me?” Thora exclaimed.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “It is nothing—absolutely nothing. She simply refused to have a different woman—whichever woman it might be—present during her lifetime. She claimed that without my vow, her death would occur instantly, making me her murderer. Consequently, I gave my word. Ever since, she has bound me to that pledge, despite my own moments of falling to my knees to plead for my release.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “Why was I not told about this?” Thora inquired with a choke. “If I had merely been aware! Why did you not simply let me know?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “I gave her my word that I would keep it completely secret,” John uttered in a raspy voice. “She had me swear upon the Holy Book; Thora, had I imagined it would last for such a lengthy time, I would have refused. You cannot comprehend the agony I have endured throughout these nineteen years, Thora. It is clear to me that I caused you pain as well, yet you will still become my wife, won't you, Thora? Please, Thora, will you not? As quickly as possible, I arrived to seek your hand.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: In that instance, the dazed Nell regained her composure, recognizing that her presence there was inappropriate. Sneaking off, she avoided seeing Thora until the following morning, at which time Thora recounted the remainder of the tale to her.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “That old woman is deceitful, relentless, and cruel!” Nell cried.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “Be quiet—she has passed away,” Thora stated gravely. “If that weren't the case—however it is. Therefore we are forbidden to talk ill of her. All the same, I have finally found joy, Nell. And I would not have cared about enduring such a lengthy wait in the least had I merely understood the reason.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “When is your wedding to take place?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “In the coming month. Naturally, it is going to be extremely muted. I imagine folk are going to gossip dreadful. It will be said by them that I rushed to grab John the moment his unfortunate mother was no longer around. John wished to inform them of what actually happened, however I uttered, ‘No, John; after all she was your mother, and we’ll keep the secret between us, and not cast any shadow on her memory. I don’t mind what people say, now that I know the truth myself. It don’t matter a mite. Let it all be buried with the dead’ says I to him. Therefore I persuaded him to concur with my view.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “I could never be nearly as forgiving as you are,” Nell remarked, in a somewhat irritated manner.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXIV John Fairlie Speaks at Last
text: “Your perspective on numerous matters will change once you reach my age,” Thora remarked with tolerance. “Learning how to forgive is among the lessons age brings us. Doing so is simpler at forty than it was at twenty.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: Taking a seat upon a travel bag while exhaling with delight, Cressy remarked, “We have all returned to this spot, pleasantly tanned and delighting like a powerful athlete entering a contest.” She continued, “Is it not wonderful to behold this beloved former Tabby’s Place once more—along with Aunty—and the felines? Has Smudge not suffered the loss of yet one more portion of his ear?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “If he were completely without ears, Smudge would be the sweetest cat anywhere,” stated Nell faithfully from her trunk, as Smudge twisted around her lap in a wild burst of greeting.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Aren’t you happy to see that we have returned, Aunty?” asked Cressy.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Yes. However, I want you to put things in order,” Aunt Euphemia said mournfully, regarding the dense tangle of trunks and suitcases that enveloped the four laughing, babbling girls. “You are able to speak equally well at a later time. My rule when I was a girl was work before play.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Oh, we’ve only inverted that in our generation, Aunty. Our principle is to enjoy your fun before applying yourself. Your tasks can be done far more effectively once you’ve enjoyed a proper stretch of recreation.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “If a minister is to be your husband,” Aunt Euphemia remarked, gathering Joseph alongside her knitting work and surrendering to what was bound to happen with the captivating elegance that rendered her the finest of housemothers, “words like ‘dig in’ must be abandoned by you.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Why?” Cressy groaned. “Oh, why is a minister’s wife expected to speak nothing but prunes and prisms? I will not. Everyone on Tanner Street uses slang—which means, metaphorical language—and if I failed to do so, they would consider me unbearably arrogant and stuck up.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Have you broken the news to your family?” Honora asked, offering pieces from her lunchbasket to the Sarah-cat.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: Cressy gave a nod.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “In what manner did they react to it?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Oh, mother flew into a rage. However, I remained steadfast—even I, Cressida Lindsay, who had never previously been able to stand firm on anything. Father proved more composed. Father’s very own father served as a minister, which explains why he possesses a warm feeling toward the clergy. Following mother’s cooling down, I brought Ez to Mount Holly, and both of them adored him. Nevertheless, mother dropped several terrifying insinuations during each chat about the expectations she had held for me. Oh, my holiday trail has not precisely been sprinkled with roses, dear girls. Still—I have triumphed and I possess Ez. No other thing counts.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “For your part,” Aunt Euphemia uttered grimly.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “And not to Ez, either,” Cressy fired back. “You continue to feel sorry for him. For what reason, if I may ask? I believe he is worthy of envy. In me, he is gaining intellect, loveliness, and a heart made of gold.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “We are fortunate to understand how your remarks should be received,” Aunt Euphemia remarked with patience. “I trust that you refrain from speaking in such a manner in the presence of strangers. What impression would be made upon them?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Oh, discovering their thoughts is not something I desire. Seeing my own reflection through the eyes of other people holds no appeal for me. It would, I am certain, prove terribly unpleasant on most occasions. Furthermore, Burns’s sincerity regarding that plea seems doubtful to me.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Ah, it seems to me that everyone asks in prayer for certain outcomes that are actually undesired, provided we possess sufficient honesty to examine our inner selves,” Aunt Euphemia admitted frankly. “My belief is that those kinds of petitions fail to ascend very high. In times past, I offered prayers for the ability to pardon a particular individual, yet I am currently aware that pardoning her was not my genuine wish. Once I at last reached the point of truly desiring to do so, my forgiveness was granted to her devoid of any need for prayer.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “It is hard for me to imagine you holding a grudge for very long,” Mabel remarked.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Oh, I was in the past. However, bearing a grudge appears to be a waste of time as one grows older.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “That brings it to mind,” remarked Nell, and related the story of John and Thora.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “And now give us the details of that romantic encounter you alluded to so mysteriously in a letter of yours,” Cressy requested.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: With vivid energy, Nell performed Samuel’s marriage offer. The girls uttered shrill cries of mirth, and Aunt Euphemia let out a smile.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Deriding your suitors lacks propriety,” she declared sternly; “however,” she continued composedly, “it was my own constant habit.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Aunty, do tell us about your beaux,” Cressy begged, adding, “There must have been so many of them.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “They aren’t in the past tense,” Aunt Euphemia countered. “I still have them. Back home, three elderly widowers have been eyeing me affectionately for a while now. You young people shouldn’t assume that all the world's romance belongs to you.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “ Aunty, widowerhood and making eyes at someone hardly seem romantic.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Well, no; yet young people are not always full of romance either. A few of my suitors definitely were not. I would laugh at them outrageously, poor young men. Saul Elwood was one—he existed in a kind of waking trance constantly—never appeared to grasp what was happening around him. He failed to realize that I had answered ‘no’ until a year had passed after I said it. Once he actually got married, his spouse tumbled out of the sleigh a certain night while they were traveling back from church, and he failed to notice she was gone. Next came Dan Winston. He possessed too much knowledge. He was aware of everything in this world along with the majority of what exists in the hereafter. He had the ability to provide an answer to any query, even had you inquired of him the date of the Judgment Day. Milton Edwards was truly pleasant and I was fond of him, yet I did not become his wife. On the one hand, he required a week to comprehend a joke, and on the other hand he failed to ever propose to me. Horatio Reeve proved to be the most captivating suitor I ever possessed. However, whenever he related a tale he embellished it so thoroughly that you were unable to discern it beneath the adornments. I was never capable of determining if he was fabricating or merely allowing his fantasy to wander free.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “And as for the rest of them, Aunty?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Depart and open your bags,” Aunt Euphemia uttered, accidentally brandishing Joseph in their direction instead of a needle. “The rest possessed too much kindness to mock. I will hold their memory in honor. A box containing blossoms is located in your room, Nell. Their arrival occurred approximately sixty minutes back.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: Once the initial week had passed, the students residing at Tabby’s Place established a routine of rigorous academic work; indeed, this marked their final year at Wexcombe, requiring continuous effort to secure commencement accolades. Nell applied herself to English studies, Honora immersed herself in the classics, and Cressida labored intensively at Mathematics. At times weariness overtook them, at times despair set in, and at times no goal appeared deserving of their exertions. It was during a period of such despondency that Mabel made her way up to the blue room on a wet night in November. Nell was seated on the floor within a small ring of illumination produced by the lamp situated next to her, encircled by a multitude of discarded, balled-up papers.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Whatever are you up to?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “I was merely examining a few old Story Club tales. My goal was to find a bit of cheer and inebriation. Having studied to the point where everything appeared azure, I headed up here to retrieve these from my trunk. Because they are so thoroughly soaked in tragedy and tears, they prove to be excruciatingly funny.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “I’m feeling down and disheartened too,” Mabel stated, flinging herself onto the sofa. “Nothing appears to have any value. Even my thoughts are ancient. I’ve already pondered every single one. What purpose does life serve anyway, Nell?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Darling, our feeling like this is simply caused by brain fatigue, as well as the weather. Following a tough day of work, a night with heavy rain such as this one would crush the spirits of anybody except a Mark Tapley. You are aware that life is worth living.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Ah, I guess that is the case. Still, I am unable to demonstrate it to my own satisfaction at this moment.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Only consider every one of the grand and virtuous spirits that have existed and labored throughout the earth,” Nell remarked in a dreamy manner. “Is it not valuable to follow in their footsteps and receive the legacy of their achievements and lessons? Is it not valuable to believe that we are able to partake in their encouragement? Furthermore, what about every grand spirit destined to arrive in times to come? Is it not valuable to labor a bit and pave the road for those individuals—rendering merely a single stride along their course simpler?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Oh, Nell, my intellect concurs with what you say. Nevertheless, my spirit continues to be gloomy and lacking in creative spark. Rainy evenings perpetually leave me feeling filthy and unkempt.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “On certain nights the rain appeals to me—lying in bed, I enjoy listening to it tap against the roof and sweep among the pine trees.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “I am fond of it when it remains upon the roof,” Mabel stated. “That is not invariably the case. During the previous summer, I passed a dreadful night inside an ancient country farmhouse. Rain trickled through the leaking roof and tapped against my bed. That held no romance at all. In the ‘mirk midnight’ I was forced to rise and bustle about to drag the bedstead away from the leak—and it happened to be a heavy, old-fashioned bed that weighed roughly a ton. Following that, the continuous drip-drop, drip-drop persisted through the whole night until my nerves were completely shattered. You cannot imagine how spine-chilling a sound a large raindrop produces when it hits an uncovered floor with a mushy thud during the night. It resembles spectral footsteps and similar horrors. Why are you laughing, Nell?”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Such tales. As Cressy might remark, they are dyingly funny—in multiple ways, because every character perished within them. What exceptionally beautiful heroines were ours—and in what fashion we attired them!

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Silks, satins, velvets, jewels, and laces were the only things they ever put on. In one of Odette Pullen’s tales, a narrative portrays the protagonist as slumbering in a gorgeous nightshirt made of white satin and adorned with seed pearls.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Continue,” Mabel urged. “It seems to me that existence remains valuable so long as it contains something to laugh at.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “I wrote this particular one. My female protagonist is enjoying herself at a dance, ‘glittering from head to foot with large diamonds of the first water.’ Yet of what use were beauty or expensive clothing? ‘The paths of glory lead but to the grave.’ It was unavoidable that they be killed or perish from a broken heart. For them, no way out existed.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Allow me to look through a few of your tales.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “Well, here is my masterpiece. Take note of its happy title—‘My Graves.’ Quarts of tears were shed by me when I wrote it, and gallons were shed by the other girls when it was read by me. Odette Pullen’ mother gave her a frightful scolding due to the fact that she possessed so many handkerchiefs in the wash during that week. A harrowing tale, it concerns the wanderings of the wife of a Methodist minister. The reason I made her a Methodist was that it was required for her to wander. In every place she resided, she buried a child. Nine of them existed, and their graves, severed far apart, ranged from Newfoundland to Vancouver. The children were described by me, their several death beds were pictured, and their tombstones and epitaphs were detailed. The burial of the entire nine had been intended by me, but after eight had been disposed of by me, my invention of horrors ran out, and the ninth was permitted by me to live as a hopeless cripple.”

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: As Mabel perused My Graves, breaking up its mournful passages with quiet laughs, and Smudge enjoyed the righteous slumber of a feline that had spent the whole night curled atop an Odette Pullen story about a lovely fifteen-year-old girl who left to care for lepers—naturally succumbing to the terrible illness in the end—Nell skimmed the remaining manuscripts and remembered the past at Brierley school, where the members of the Story Club used to compose them while seated beneath the spruce trees or nestled amid the brookside ferns. What an enjoyable time they had shared! The warmth and joy of those former summer days flooded back to her as she read. Neither all the splendour of Greece nor all the majesty of Rome possessed the power to cast a spell like those amusing, sorrowful stories from the Story Club. Within the collection of manuscripts, Nell discovered one recorded on pieces of packing paper. Amused laughter flooded her gray eyes when she remembered when and where it was created. It was the piece she had composed on the day she dropped through the roof of the Cobb duckhouse along the Tory Road.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: Nell cast a quick look at it, and then she began reading it with deep concentration. The piece was a short conversation among asters, sweet-peas, wild canaries occupying the lilac bush, and the protective spirit of the garden. Having finished reading it, she remained seated, gazing blankly ahead; then, once Mabel had departed, she pressed flat the wrinkled manuscript.

chapter_title: Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens
text: “I think I shall,” she stated with determination.

“Aunt Phemie, a letter bearing an Indian stamp has arrived for you,” Cressy said. “Mabel has three, Nonie has two, and I have a wonderful thick one sent by Ez. Nell, you have received only a circular.”

No one observed the color rising in Nell's cheeks when she caught the slim envelope that Cressy casually threw to her. Shortly afterwards, however, Cressy raised her eyes and saw that Nell was completely transformed.
“Sweetheart, what nice event took place?”

“A short piece I transmitted to The Youth’s Friend two weeks back has been taken by them,” stated Nell, attempting with great effort to sound as though she had pieces taken with every post, though failing to fully pull it off.
“Nell Harcourt! How wonderful! What was the piece? When will it be printed? Were you paid for it by them?”

“Indeed; a check amounting to ten dollars has been dispatched by them, and the editor states in his letter a desire to examine additional pieces of my writing. Kind gentleman, he certainly will. The piece was a former sketch that I discovered inside my trunk. After re-writing it, I submitted it—though I actually held no expectation that it might be taken owing to its lack of plot,” stated Nell, remembering the painful ordeal regarding Evadne’s Atonement.
“What will you do with those ten dollars, Nell? How about we all head up town and get drunk,” Cressy proposed.

“I intend to waste it on a soulless, wild party of some kind,” Nell cheerfully announced. “Whatever happens, it is not corrupt cash—unlike the payment I received for that awful Reliable Baking Powder tale. I bought needed garments with that money and despised them whenever I wore them.”
“Imagine hosting an actual living writer at Tabby’s Place,” Honora remarked.
“Taking this on involves a significant duty,” Aunt Euphemia remarked with gravity.

“Truly, that’s so,” concurred Nonie, matching my gravity. “Writers are tricky creatures. Predicting the time or manner of their outbursts is impossible. It could be that Nell will use us as material.”

“The capacity to compose material for the Press represented a heavy charge,” Aunt Euphemia stated sternly, “and I trust Nell comprehends this. Prior to departing for the foreign field, my daughter was accustomed to composing tales, yet currently she has directed her mind toward loftier matters. She was wont to remark that her guiding principle was ‘Never write a line you would be ashamed to read at your own funeral.’ It would be wise for you to adopt that as your own, Nell, provided you intend to launch yourself into literature. Although, to be certain,” Aunt Euphemia appended in a puzzled manner, “Elizabeth was in the habit of laughing whenever she uttered those words. She was perpetually laughing to such an extent that I cannot comprehend how she ever arrived at the choice to become a missionary. I am grateful for her decision—I offered prayers that she would—yet—I would prefer that she had not.”
Aunt Euphemia then inquired about the reason for the laughter of those silly young women.

Nell’s eyes gleamed throughout that entire day; literary aspirations began to grow and flourish within her mind; the excitement of them went along with her to Jennie Cooper’s walking party, and even seeing Hugh and Rowena, who were strolling right in front of her and Cyril, was unable to completely dampen the shimmer of her bright hopes. All the same, she was not so detached from earthly matters that she failed to observe how Rowena’s manner of walking was unequivocally clumsy.
“However, I imagine her face is all that Hugh sees. That is so typical of a man,” Nell mused with contempt.
“Will you be at home on Saturday afternoon?” Cyril inquired.
“Yes.”
“Your presence will soon be sought by my mother and sisters,” Cyril remarked softly.

A sensation went through Nell that could perhaps be called a thrill, though it was scarcely an agreeable one. None of Cyril’s family had ever been met by her; the importance of what he said was realized by her; and it possessed, in some way, an unalterable quality that gave her a chill.

“I shall be glad to see them,” she stated without emotion; and then she questioned whether she actually would be glad. Naturally, she should be. Yet would it not prove to be a bit of a trial? Rumors had reached Nell concerning how the Gardners regarded the “infatuation” of their son and brother. Cyril had surely exercised some influence to arrange this visit. Nell was aware she would be scrutinized. From their agreement to visit, she gathered that, whether voluntarily or involuntarily, they considered her a potential addition to their family.

“I will simply be who I am. I will not attempt to leave a favorable impression,” Nell reflected with superiority. However, she was pondering which dress it would be wiser to put on Saturday afternoon, as well as whether the recent fashion of piling her hair up would be more becoming to her than the previous manner; and the excursion on foot was somewhat ruined as far as she was concerned. When evening arrived, she had come to the conclusion that she would put on her brown chiffon come Saturday, yet she would arrange her hair in a low style.

On Friday afternoon, none of the girls at Wexcombe had classes. Taking advantage of the occasion, Mabel was composing an essay intended for the Philomathic Society; she occupied a seat at the corner table in the living room, surrounded by a messy scatter of manuscript pages and notes upon the floor. Mabel consistently maintained that she was incapable of writing anything without tossing every page to the ground upon finishing it. Positioned directly in the center of the floor, Nell—attired in a serge skirt and flannel blouse, her hair somewhat ruffled by the breezy stroll back—was playing with the Sarah-cat using a wishbone. Snuggled together in her lap were both Smudge and Joseph. Because Honora was preparing food in the kitchen, a cozy scent of plums pervaded the entire home. Shortly afterward, draped in a massive work apron and bearing a mark of flour on her nose, she entered to display to Aunt Euphemia the chocolate cake that she had recently iced.

At this favorable juncture there came a knock at the door. No person gave it a thought except Cressy, who jumped to her feet and answered it, anticipating a messenger delivering the headwear she had purchased earlier that day. Positioned on the doorstep were Mrs. Lisle and her daughters.

Somehow managing to scramble to her feet, Nell dumped a pair of outraged cats from her lap while automatically moving her wishbone into her left hand from her right. Having to traverse the room to get to the kitchen door, Honora panicked, frantically shoved the chocolate cake beneath a cushion on the inglenook sofa, and bolted up the stairs. Mabel started frantically collecting her manuscript. Solely Aunt Euphemia and Cressy stayed composed. Owing to their efforts, all were shortly seated comfortably, Nell included. Honora descended, stripped of her apron and free of smudges, Mabel restored her corner to order, and Cressy rescued the moment with a torrent of prompt small talk.

An elegant, slender, and attractive woman, Mrs. Lisle was impeccably dressed, displaying a friendliness that appeared slightly strained. A youthful version of her mother, Aline Lisle possessed none of that friendliness. Her efforts to be pleasant resulted merely in an arrogant and condescending demeanor. Dorothy Lisle was slender, cheerful, and somewhat boyish. Recognizing that she was the sister Cyril preferred, Nell felt drawn to her. Had her lively hazel eyes been dreamy dark ones, she would have closely resembled Cyril. Owing to her and Cressy, the visit actually proceeded quite smoothly, apart from a minor feeling of tension in the room and a pair of somewhat unfortunate events. Allowed to run free, Smudge and Joseph initiated a game of tag, leaping wildly onto Mrs. Lisle’s silk-clad lap and off again during their frantic dash. Mrs. Lisle raised her lorgnette and watched their retreating shapes as though felines were entirely foreign to her, while Nell, stifling somewhat anxious laughter, offered the best apology she could manage.
“Are you keen on cats?” inquired Mrs. Lisle, her tone carrying a subtle hint of indulgent surprise.

Even though she cared for Smudge, Nell did not particularly care for cats, yet the manner of Mrs. Lisle’s speaking irked her. Irrationally, it came to her mind that Mrs. John Carrow held such a fondness for cats that her home contained every one her spouse permitted.
“Aren’t they adorable animals?” she asked mischievously.
“Cats have never been to my liking,” Mrs. Lisle said distantly.
“I love them,” Dorothy said. “They possess such a wonderful selfishness. Dogs show too much goodness and selflessness. They cause me to feel uneasy. Cats, however, are magnificently human.”

“You have two delightful old china dogs there. May I look at them closely?” said Aline, moving across the room to the fireplace and thus unwittingly causing the next mishap. Taking up Magog, she took a seat on the cushion that hid Honora’s chocolate cake beneath it. Agonized glances were shared between Honora and Nell, yet they were helpless. Sitting on the cushion, the majestic Aline kept talking about china dogs right up to the moment she left.
Dorothy stayed behind for a second so she could press the hand of Nell and utter a sudden whisper.

“I am certain you and I will become good friends. Ah, Cyril has filled me in on everything concerning you. Poor lad, I am the sole family member he opens up to—after all, no one is able to entrust secrets to mamma and Aline. What marvelous experiences you girls are sure to enjoy in this place! Will you allow me to visit frequently and participate in them?”

“Visit as frequently as you wish,” Nell answered warmly, grateful that a single sister of Cyril’s proved agreeable. She could never feel affection for Aline, of that she was sure; nor would Aline ever care for her, even if Mrs. Lisle could perhaps be gained over. On the whole, Nell let out a sigh of release once the trial had ended.
“‘Out of every melancholy phrase expressed by voice or quill, none carry more sorrow than it might have been,’”

lamented Honora in a tragic tone, raising the pillow. “What we have here in this cake is what one could term an utter collapse. Furthermore, the pillow has also been destroyed. Don't ever try to convince me that Friday isn't an unpropitious day.”
“Those who announce their arrival for Saturday ought not to show up on Friday,” Aunt Euphemia remarked.
“I believe Cyril made a blunder,” Cressy remarked. “The lad truly cannot be held accountable for his words while speaking with Nell. What has become of Nell?”

Nell had walked up to the higher floor. A strange sensation made her want to weep. However, she forced a laugh from herself rather than shedding tears. Smudge and Joseph had behaved so terribly! Furthermore, Dorothy was truly a sweetheart.
“May I pass away, or let the following evening arrive,” Cressy moaned.
“Provided that your life is sufficiently long, both desires shall be fulfilled,” Nell remarked serenely.
“You can easily remain calm, being comfortable with Philosophy. I am not, and contemplating that dreadful exam tomorrow makes me shudder. What will Ez say if I do not pass?”
“You will not be unsuccessful. In what manner did you fare in Greek today?”

“I am unsure. It might have been a fine composition, or it might have been poor enough that Homer turned in his resting place. My studying and pondering of notebooks have reached a point where I cannot judge anything at all. Little Cressy will feel so grateful once this entire process of examining comes to an end.”
“Examinating? Such a word has never come to my ears.”
“Well, am I not just as entitled to invent a word as anyone else is?” asked Cressy.
“Words are grown rather than made,” remarked Nell.
“Forget about it—I am starting to dimly perceive open sea up ahead where no test waves threaten. Girls, do you—are you able to grasp that our existence at Wexcombe has nearly come to an end?”

“I am unable to,” Nell stated, filled with sorrow. “It feels like only yesterday when Nonie and I found ourselves isolated among all those Freshmen at Wexcombe. And presently we have become Seniors taking our last tests.”
“‘Wise, potent, and reverend Seniors,’” Cressy recited. “Is it your belief that we are truly even a bit wiser than on our arrival at Wexcombe?”
“By times you don’t act like it,” Aunt Euphemia said severely.
“Oh, Aunt Phemie, taking us all in all, haven’t we been fairly good girls during the three winters you’ve acted as a mother to us?” Cressy pleaded.
“The four of you have been the sweetest, dearest, best girls who ever attended college as a group,” declared Aunt Euphemia, who never ruined a flattering remark with uncalled-for thriftiness.

“However, I suspect you still lack a good deal of judgment. Naturally, that is only to be anticipated. Judgment comes from experience. A college education cannot impart it. You have attended college for four years while I never did, yet I possess far greater knowledge than you do, young ladies.”

“‘There is a great deal that fails to adhere to standard rules, A immense amount of wisdom exists That is completely unattainable at university, A vast quantity of information remains untaught in the classroom,’”
cited Mabel.
“Was there anything you acquired at Wexcombe besides geometry, dead languages, and similar rubbish?” asked Aunt Euphemia.
“Oh, indeed. My belief is that we have done so, Aunty,” Nell objected.

“What Professor Woodleigh shared with us this past Philomathic has now been proven true to us,” Cressy remarked. “The statement he made was, ‘In the banquet of life, humor serves as the most zesty seasoning. Let your errors amuse you while teaching you, find amusement in your hardships while drawing power from them, and turn your obstacles into a laughing matter while mastering them.’ Is that not a lesson of value, Aunt Phemie?”
“Indeed, it is, my dear. If you have acquired the ability to smile at matters deserving of laughter, while refraining from laughing at those that do not, you possess both wisdom and comprehension.”
“Nell, what did you gain from the course you took at Wexcombe?” Honora softly asked off to the side.

“It is my belief,” Nell uttered deliberately, “that I have truly come to regard every minor obstacle as a joke and every major one as a sign of impending triumph. Taking everything into account, I believe that is the gift Wexcombe has bestowed upon me.”

“Expressing what it has accomplished for me requires me to rely once more on a quote from Professor Woodleigh,” Honora stated. “Do you recall him saying during his speech, ‘If we but possess the vision to perceive it, the soul to cherish it, and the reach to claim it for our own, the world offers us so very much—an abundance within mankind, an abundance within creative works and writings, an abundance in every place to bring joy and inspire gratitude.’ Nell, I believe that Wexcombe has imparted that lesson to me to a certain degree.”

“Based on what everyone is saying,” Aunt Euphemia observed, “it boils down to the fact that four years of college can impart to you—provided you possess sufficient innate common sense—the same knowledge that roughly twenty years of life experience would take to instill. Well, as far as I am concerned, that validates higher education. Prior to this, I had always held doubts regarding the issue.”
“Aunt Phemie, what about the folks who lack natural gumption, though?”

“Individuals devoid of innate common sense never acquire it,” Aunt Euphemia shot back, “whether in university or throughout existence. Should they survive until a century old, their actual knowledge remains no greater than it was at birth. It is a calamity for them, not a failing, wretched creatures. Nevertheless, those among us blessed with a degree of common sense ought to properly express gratitude to the Almighty for it.”
“Aunt Phemie, would you mind explaining the meaning of gumption?” Cressy inquired.
“No, I will not, young woman. Whoever possesses gumption understands its meaning, while whoever lacks it will remain perpetually ignorant of its meaning. Consequently, defining it serves no purpose.”

The packed days passed quickly, and tests reached their conclusion. Nell earned High Honors in English. Honora earned Honors in Classics, whereas Cressy did so in Mathematics. Mabel achieved a respectable overall performance. Subsequently, Convocation took place.

“This is what I would once have called an epoch in my life,” Nell remarked while removing Cyril’s violets from their box and contemplating them deeply. Intending to wear them, naturally, she nevertheless let her gaze drift toward a second box sitting on her table. Filled to the brim with lilies-of-the-valley, they were just as fresh and sweetly scented as the ones that blossomed in the yard at Grey Shutters whenever June arrived in Brierley. Adjacent to the box rested Hugh Carrow’s card.

Nell pondered the reason Hugh had gifted her flowers for Convocation. Throughout the previous winter, she had encountered him on very few occasions. Since the Christmas holidays, his visits to Tabby’s Place amounted to just a single Friday evening, and their encounters in other locations were infrequent. It was clear to her that his intense focus on his studies was aimed at achieving High Honors and the Cooper Prize, leaving him minimal involvement in Wexcombe's social activities. In contrast, Nell’s own winter had contained a great deal of social entertainment. Her interactions with the Gardners had been frequent; her bond with Dorothy was extremely close; and within college circles, the news of her engagement to Cyril was anticipated at any moment. Nell was anticipating it as well. Nevertheless, right before departing Tabby’s Place to attend Convocation, she discarded Cyril’s violets and substituted Hugh’s lilies-of-the-valley. The motive behind her action was something she was unable to explain. For some reason, as her long-held ambitions were being realized, past Brierley times, aspirations, and companionships felt remarkably near. In former times, she and Hugh had playfully imagined the occasion when they would both be graduates in Arts, wearing caps and gowns. That extraordinary day had finally arrived, and Cyril’s violets did not fit into it. Only the blossoms from her long-standing friend appeared to suit this realization of early-blooming dreams that he had formerly shared.

This date had enticed and charmed her for years; yet when it arrived, the sole, sharp, lasting recollection it imparted to her was not the gasp-inducing instant in which the dignified president of Wexcombe presented her diploma and cap while greeting her as a B.A.; nor was it the sparkle in Hugh’s eyes upon noticing her lilies, or the bewildered, hurt look Cyril cast toward her while passing her on the platform. It was not Aline Lisle’s patronizing felicitations, nor Dorothy’s passionate, spontaneous expressions of goodwill. It was a single peculiar, inexplicable ache that ruined this long-anticipated date for her, leaving within it a specific subtle yet lasting trace of resentment.

The graduates in Arts hosted a dance for their graduation that evening. As Nell got ready for the event, she set aside the pearl beads that she normally put on and removed from her trunk the little box delivered to Grey Shutters on Christmas day. A gold chain as thin as a thread, featuring a tiny pink heart in enamel for a pendant, was inside it. The card included with it bore the inscription, “With all good wishes from your old chum, Hugh.” Nell—who had laughed at the recollection the enamel heart brought to mind of that disastrous day when Hugh dubbed her “Carrots” and unsuccessfully attempted to reconcile using a pink sugar heart—had sent him a pleasant, brief message of gratitude. However, she had yet to wear the piece of jewelry. On this night, displaying a dreamy smile, she secured it around her fair neck.
Together, she and Cressy made their way on foot to Wexcombe. While Nell proceeded without speaking, Cressy prattled about various topics. Unexpectedly, she remarked,
“I was told today that the news of Hugh Carrow’s betrothal to Rowena Calder would be made public right after Convocation ended. Have you heard anything about that?”
“No,” Nell said.
“I believe that is accurate,” Cressy remarked in a light tone.

Nell kept silent. She could feel her face glowing hot within the dark. Sliding her hand beneath her collar, she grasped the chain made of gold. It snapped after a single forceful twist. Nell jammed the fractured piece of jewelry into her pocket. Her eyes stung while her hands shook.

Yet among the joyous partygoers that evening, her mirth surpassed everyone else's, and she expressed no regret when informing Hugh that no dances remained on her card when he approached to request one. Later on, while joining the girls by the fading fire at Tabby’s Place to warm their satin skins against the chill of spring, her talk about the day's happenings was as cheerful as anyone's.

“Elias Purdy MacKinnon came by this evening following your departure,” remarked Aunt Euphemia, having remained awake to maintain the fire. “The commencement dance was news to him. That young man should wear an elastic strip around his skull at night so his ears learn to lie flat. A former suitor of mine used one, which benefited his appearance tremendously. Because I was the person who recommended the idea to him, he followed my counsel, yet he held it against me for the rest of his days.”
“Elias Purdy is an exceptionally solemn young man,” Honora remarked with a yawn. “He occupies himself with more weighty issues than his ears. You are aware he intends to become a minister.”

“Well, I suppose the Lord doesn’t regard the ears of a man,” Aunt Euphemia remarked solemnly, ceasing any additional disapproval of Elias Purdy. Aunt Euphemia maintained a suitable deference toward the clergy, even when it concerned an unseasoned preacher.

“Only think—seven days from tonight I will find myself in Brierley—what a charming prospect!” exclaimed Nell, leaning above the crate where she was storing away the quilts belonging to Mrs. Agatha Sowerby. “On the other hand, only think—seven days from tonight I will have departed eternally from Tabby’s Place—what a dreadful prospect!”
“I ponder whether the spirit of every laugh we shared will resonate in the youthful reveries of Miss Tabby and Miss Maria,” Cressy conjectured.
Miss Tabby and Miss Maria were returning to their residence, following their journey across nearly the entirety of the inhabited world.

“We will return during May’s second week,” Miss Tabby had written. “Though Tabby’s Place might feel somewhat tiny following Karnak's Hall of the Kings, I have always disliked large dwellings. Besides, returning home will be a great relief. Beginning your travels at an advanced age often leads to overdoing it, given the awareness that little time remains, and the habit easily takes hold. Maria, I fear, will never find contentment again.”

“I shall leave here my fancies and dreams to bless the next comer,” Nell remarked, casting a longing glance across the blue room—that lovely blue room in which she had passed three years of such joy. Upon her knees by its window she had offered her prayers, and leaning out from it she had observed the sun setting beyond the pine trees. She had listened as fall rain dashed against the glass, and she had greeted the robins of springtime on its ledge. She pondered whether previous dreams might linger in rooms—whether, upon departing eternally from the place where a person had experienced happiness, pain, laughter, and tears, a part of her, unseen and ungraspable, but fully actual all the same, might linger like an echoing recollection.

“I believe,” Cressy remarked, “that any space in which a person experiences dreams, grief, joy, and life grows bound up with those occurrences and gains a distinct character. Were I to step into this room half a century in the future, I know it would whisper ‘Nell, Nell’ in my direction. We’ve shared such wonderful moments in this spot, sweetie! All the conversations, laughs, and warm, friendly gatherings! Oh, goodness! My wedding to Ez takes place in June, and I am certain my joy will be absolute. Yet at this very moment, my wish is for this delightful Wexcombe existence to continue without end.”

“I am sufficiently illogical at this moment to desire that as well,” Nell conceded. “Regardless of whatever more profound happiness might await us in the future, we will never experience this precise charming, carefree life we have shared here again. Cressy, it has ended permanently.”
“What will be done with Smudge?” Cressy inquired, just as that favored feline stepped into the space.

“I shall bring him to my house to be with Joseph and the Sarah-cat,” stated Aunt Euphemia, pursuing Smudge. “Separating those cats after they have mastered coexisting would be a pity. Cats and people find that a difficult lesson to master.”

“I regret having to give up Smudge,” Nell stated sorrowfully, “however, bringing him to Grey Shutters would serve no purpose. Cats are loathed by Thirza, and Robin would torment him incessantly. Furthermore, my time at home will likely be short. The position of principal at the Eastmere High School has been extended to me.”
“Will you be accepting it?” Cressy asked.
“I—I have not made up my mind yet,” Nell replied, flushing with confusion.

Cressy gave an understanding nod. Of course, it was impossible to finalize Nell’s future until Cyril had expressed himself. He would do so shortly—there was certainly no uncertainty about it. Nor was there any uncertainty that Nell’s response would be “yes” once he asked “Will you please?” Nell viewed the situation herself with a composure that was rarely disturbed. She possessed a deep love for Cyril. To be sure, it differed from her initial expectations of love. Yet Nell questioned herself tiredly, did anything in existence resemble a person's mental picture of it? It mirrored the previous diamond disenchantment of her youth—matching the exact letdown she experienced upon first beholding the cold gleam rather than the violet magnificence she had expected. “That’s not my idea of a diamond,” she had declared. Nevertheless, Cyril was a wonderful man and their life together would be filled with great happiness, despite the absence of a certain nameless excitement from her existence. When Cyril arrived that night and requested that Nell join him for a stroll through the park, all the residents at Tabby’s Place understood his intentions; and all of them understood, or believed they understood, how Nell would reply.
“Nell is an extremely lucky girl,” Aunt Euphemia remarked.
“I guess that’s right,” Mabel remarked with a shrug of her shoulders. “Cyril is a good guy and everything like that. However, he actually lacks any real substance.”
“Mabel Colby, that sounds remarkably like a jealous comment,” Aunt Euphemia said in a tone of rebuke.

“It does—yet I entertain no jealousy,” Mabel stated placidly. “I hold affection for Nell, and Cyril pleases me. Everyone asserts that her marriage will be a splendid one, and at present even Mrs. Lisle finds her delightful. Everything appears as though it were fashioned in paradise, though I harbor my reservations. Take whatever you can from that, Aunt Euphemia.”

Cyril requested that Nell become his wife inside the small pavilion located by the harbor shore, the very place of their conversation during the rainy day when they first met. Nell considered his choice of that location to be extremely romantic. Furthermore, the phrasing of his proposal was so exquisite that it seemed as though it might have been transcribed from a Deportment of Courtship and Marriage, just as a lover of Opal Pettigrew had once done. Its total impression was entirely perfect. It possessed sincerity as well. That Cyril truly intended his words was beyond question. No discordant tone existed that might disrupt the symphony. Nell believed that a head-to-toe shudder of excitement should be coming over her. Yet it was not; an awful composure possessed her. As Cyril waited for her response, her lips parted so she could utter her momentous yes. At that instant—a shaking came over her as though she were recoiling from the edge of a cliff. A moment arrived for her in which a person understands, as if struck by a dazzling burst of insight, far more than all earlier years combined have revealed. She yanked her hand away from Cyril’s.
“Oh, I am unable to marry you—I am unable—I am unable,” she exclaimed, hysterically.
Cyril grew pale, looking quite silly as well. He had been exceedingly confident, though he could hardly be faulted for it.
“In what way do you intend that?” he gasped out.
“I am saying that marrying you is impossible for me,” Nell reiterated frantically. “I believed it was possible—yet it isn’t.”
“What is the reason you are unable to?” inquired Cyril, with greater composure.
“Because—you do not matter enough to me.”
A red flush appeared on Cyril’s face.
“Then you have merely been entertaining yourself throughout these past two years?” he uttered unhurriedly.

“No, no, I haven’t,” poor Nell panted. Oh, what way was there for her to clarify? Clarification was impossible for her. Certain matters simply defy all explanation. “I believed I was fond of you—I really did—yet now I am certain I am not.”
“My life has been destroyed by you,” Cyril said with bitterness.
“Pardon me,” begged Nell in misery, her cheeks burning and her eyes smarting.
Cyril turned around and spent a few minutes gazing toward the sea. By the time he returned to Nell, his face had grown extremely pale once more.
“Is there no hope you can offer me?” he asked.
In silence, Nell gave a shake of her head.

“Well then—farewell,” Cyril uttered. “It is beyond my comprehension—it is impossible for me to accept that you aren't the lady I thought you were. However, upbraiding one another is useless now. No other female will ever have my affection. I am grateful to you for your companionship, if nothing else. Farewell, Nell.”

“Good-bye,” Nell stammered. After Cyril departed, she remained seated in the pavilion for many minutes, observing a pale fog stealthily and unyieldingly drifting toward the shore up the harbor. She was experiencing her moment of degradation, self-disdain, and embarrassment. Their surges swept across her. Nevertheless, beneath every bit of it, lay a strange feeling of regained liberty.
She stole inside Tabby’s Place during the twilight and retreated to her chamber. Nevertheless, Cressy was present upon the window seat.
“Hold on,” uttered Nell, her cheeks reddening as she foresaw the moment. “Hold on until I tell you my news. Cressy, Cyril wanted me to be his wife-and I said no.”
“You—you turned him down?” Cressy asked with a blank expression.
“Yes.”
“Nell Harcourt, have you lost your mind?”
“I believe I do,” Nell uttered tiredly. “Oh, Cressy, please do not lecture me. You fail to comprehend.”

“I truly am baffled. For a pair of years, you have given Cyril Lisle every form of encouragement—only to inform me now that you turned him down. It means you were simply engaging in a disgraceful flirtation with him. Nell, I would never have expected such behavior from you.”
“It wasn’t flirtation on my part—until the very final moment, I truly believed my feelings were genuine—and after that—well, it simply became clear that becoming his wife was impossible for me.”
“It is my guess,” Cressy stated maliciously, “that his wealth was the reason you planned to wed him, but your higher nature intervened to stop you.”
“I didn’t. His money never crossed my mind. Oh, I cannot make you understand it, just as I was unable to make him understand.”
“Indeed, it seems to me that your treatment of Cyril has been disgraceful,” Cressy declared, annoyed. “He possesses good looks, intelligence, wealth, and virtue. What else could you desire?”

“I desire a person who fits into my existence. He does not. Initially, his attractive appearance and skill at offering romantic praise swept me off my feet; and subsequently, I assumed I was required to be enamored since he represented my dark-eyed perfection.”
“Not knowing what I want makes me bad, yet your behavior is even worse,” Cressy stated.
“My own mind is well known to me,” Nell objected. “My mind alters, which is the problem, forcing me to become familiar with it once more.”
“Well, I guess talking to you is completely pointless.”

“Cressy, there’s no necessity for that. My spirit is broken. Everything in the past has been ruined by this. It will be impossible for me to ponder the time at Wexcombe without remembering how I was humiliated tonight. I am despised by Cyril—as well as by you—and I hold myself in contempt.”

“You poor darling,” said Cressy, softening. “Just come over here and allow me to comfort you. I have no right to reprimand you. I would have wed Hector or Orlando had I not encountered Ez. Oh, Nell, matters are so tangled in actual life. They are not neatly defined and trimmed away, like they are in books.”
“I hope that no person will ever ask for my hand in marriage again for the rest of my life,” cried unfortunate Nell, deeply convinced that her words were true.

To Nell, existence seemed to resemble an anticlimax throughout the initial weeks following her journey back to Grey Shutters. The cheerful fellowship of Tabby’s Place was something she longed for. Over the course of the previous winter, she had harbored several splendid dreams, which now rested in the dust surrounding her. Given her current state of self-loathing, she was unable to start dreaming anew right away. Furthermore, she found out that, although solitude accompanied by dreams is magnificent, solitude lacking them possesses little appeal.
Following their distressing farewell at the park pavilion, Cyril had not been seen by her again; nevertheless, prior to departing Portmaris, Dorothy visited her.

“I’m terribly sorry that Cyril won't be your husband,” she said. “Having you as a sister was something I truly wanted. However, your decision is entirely correct. You would be bored to death by him. Although I love him and find him to be a dear sweet boy, he actually lacks any interest whatsoever. It seems as though he should be interesting, yet he is not.”
“Our friendship won't be ruined by this, will it, Dorothy?” had been Nell’s wistful question.

“No, truly. You are far too wonderful to forfeit. Should I be unable to possess you as a sister, my intention is to retain you as a pal regardless. Furthermore, do not worry about Cyril. He is suffering dreadfully at present—I am forced to hear his ventings daily—yet he will recover from it. He constantly does.”
“Oh—always?” Nell asked, her tone shifting just a bit. “So before this, he has ‘got over it’?”

“Dear me, yes,” Dorothy stated candidly. “On two prior occasions. And he babbled to me in the exact same manner on each occasion. It was not that the other women truly turned him down—they merely made public their engagements to different men. Naturally, upon meeting you, he swore to me that he had never truly experienced love until then—that those earlier relationships were nothing more than youthful infatuations. Even so, I do not believe there is any reason for you to be anxious.”

Nell chose to cast her worries aside, experiencing a blend of resentment and relief. It was true that Cyril had assured her she was his sole love, and he unquestionably thought so himself. Still, knowing it was probable she had not destroyed his existence brought her solace. Alternative goddesses existed, and Dorothy claimed that Cyril was bound to be adoring at a different altar. All the same, a few additional illusions were stripped from life, which Nell gloomily started to view as quite empty.
On the night she got back, she stepped down from the porch gable wearing a sad expression.
“Thirza, what occurred to the former Frost Maiden?”

“Oh, I was aware that would make you feel terrible,” Thirza remarked. “It made me feel terrible too. Ever since I was a little girl, that tree had stood there. The severe gale we experienced in March knocked it down. At its center, it was decayed.”

“I am going to miss it so much,” Nell mourned. “Without it, the room in the porch gable feels different. Whenever I look out of its window from now on, I will always feel that something is missing. And oh, this is the first time I have ever returned to Grey Shutters without Isolde being here to greet me.”
“Isolde’s mind is occupied with other matters at the moment,” Mrs. Sowerby remarked meaningfully.
“Well, tell me all the Brierley news,” said Nell, taking a seat on the porch steps, as the evening sunshine poured down upon her hair like a delicate golden shower.

“Aside from what we wrote to you, news is scarce,” Mrs. Sowerby remarked. “I imagine it hasn't reached you that Simon Fletcher had his leg broken last week. His family benefits immensely from this. A hundred tasks, which they had constantly longed to accomplish but were unable to while he was around, are now being completed, the old crank.”
“His family was a frustrating one,” Thirza observed.

“Annoying? Yes, quite! His mother was accustomed to standing in prayer-meeting, revealing every one of her kids’ flaws and requesting prayers on their behalf. Naturally, this infuriated them, making their behavior even worse.”
“Nell hasn’t heard the news regarding Odette from you yet,” Thirza pointed out.

“Oh, Odette,” Mrs. Sowerby sniffled. “Well,” she reluctantly admitted, “Odette Pullen returned from the West—she arrived last week—and her wedding will be to a millionaire from Winnipeg. Be certain that Mrs. Gorham spread the news everywhere immediately.”
“My dear, faithful Odette—it brings me such joy,” Nell stated with warmth. “Every blessing in life ought to be hers.”

“Oh, I am not speaking ill of Odette. She is a pleasant girl. However, she does not belong to the millionaire category, and you will discover that except for his wealth, that man has little to offer, that is the truth.
